How the body’s own immune system can attack the brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Peter Jones once treated a patient with strikingly vivid hallucinations of animals. During ward visits, the patient would stroke and interact with the critters “in as real a way as he was with me,” says Jones, an academic psychiatrist at the University of Cambridge in England.
Antipsychotic drugs did nothing to dissolve these Snow White-esque visions. But when the patient receivedplasma exchange –– a treatment normally reserved for a misbehaving immune system –– his hallucinations dissipated.
Clearly, this was not a textbook case of schizophrenia. Rather, the patient’s symptoms stemmed from autoimmune encephalitis, a rare form of brain inflammation that can, in some cases, cause hallucinations and other symptoms of psychosis. When these patients are treated with drugs that tamp down the immune system, the psychotic symptoms often disappear.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Autoimmune encephalitis is usually first identified through testing blood or spinal fluid for certain types of antibodies. If patients test positive for these antibodies, it’s a sign that their immune system may be attacking the brain. Other signs can help to solidify diagnosis: bright patches of inflammation on MRI scans, quickly worsening psychotic symptoms and — importantly — clear neurological symptoms such as seizures.
But Jones’ patient didn’t have those obvious neurological symptoms. If Jones hadn’t suspected an autoimmune cause, the case likely would have been missed.
Some experts suspect that the field of psychiatry is overlooking a small number of patients like this, and they are working to find more of them. They’re considering screening a broader array of psychiatric patients and seeking out new antibodies that may be involved in autoimmune encephalitis.
At the same time, many worry that there’s a risk of planting false hopes and diverting patients from the psychiatric treatments the vast majority will actually need, should autoimmune encephalitis become overdiagnosed.
Landmark research paper
The “artificial divide” between the body and the mind that separates the fields of psychiatry and neurology is starting to break down, says Michael Zandi, a neurologist at University College London. Psychosis, for example, can be caused by a mix of mental and biological factors, from psychological trauma to drug abuse to physical diseases or infections (such as syphilis) that alter brain activity. Around 3 percent of people will experience a psychotic episode in their lifetime.
Brain inflammation caused by the body assaulting itself, as in autoimmune encephalitis, has been recognized for the past couple of decades. In the early stages of this condition, many patients develop the core features of psychosis –– hallucinations, delusions and agitation –– and so are initially sent to psychiatric services.
A landmark paper about this condition came in 2007, when researchers described the cases of 12 women with autoimmune encephalitis. Nine of the patients initially presented with a number of psychosis-like symptoms, while the others mainly had memory loss. All but one devolved into seizures. The researchers found that the women’s conditions were caused by antibodies that bind to the brain’s NMDA receptors, proteins that are involved in many processes in the brain, such as learning and the formation of memories.
The trigger for autoimmune encephalitis, in this case, seemed to be tumors in these patients, 90 percent of which were ovarian. All five tumors the researchers examined contained nerve tissue complete with NMDA receptors. This confused the immune system, which came to recognize the NMDA receptor as foreign and ramped up the manufacture of antibodies that bind to it.
But those antibodies also bound to NMDA receptors in healthy brain tissue, interfering with brain function. Other cells of the immune system gathered to the area, sparking inflammation that, in many of these cases, caused psychosis.
In autoimmune encephalitis, an immune chain reaction may be triggered by tumors, previous infections or unclear causes. Most cases of the condition are linked to a brain-targeting autoantibody, which leads to inflammation that may result in neurological or psychiatric symptoms.
Beyond tumors, experts also think that classic autoimmune encephalitis may be triggered by previous infections such as herpes simplex virus in the brain. But root causes are often mysterious. Only a tiny sliver of psychosis cases are due to autoimmune causes — most experts cap it at 1 to 2 percent of patients. If untreated, these patients may decline into a coma and even die, so to avoid missing them, savvy psychiatrists look for other neurological symptoms, most notably seizures, but also features like catatonia or mouth-twitching.
If these telltale signs of brain inflammation emerge, blood or spinal fluid may be tested for autoantibodies (antibodies that attack the patient’s own tissues). If these tests, often coupled with signs on MRI or EEG brain scans, point to autoimmune encephalitis, patients are rushed into immunotherapy: treatments with drugs to tamp down the overreactive immune system. Many fully recover: “We can get them completely better,” says Zandi.
Autoimmune encephalitis is commonly caused by antibodies that bind to the NMDA receptor, known as NMDAR antibodies. But researchers have uncovered dozens more antibody types that are associated with encephalitis, some of which also appear to produce psychiatric symptoms.
One leading example is LGI1 antibodies, which were discovered in 2010. These antibodies latch onto LGI1 proteins in the brain, preventing them from passing signals between nerve cells. This form of autoimmune encephalitis often causes dementia-like symptoms, leading to initial misdiagnosis. Zandi says he’s had patients whose apparent dementia has disappeared after immunotherapy, leaving them “fully independent, back to driving, normal.”
University of Oxford psychiatrist Belinda Lennox has observed similarly striking transformations. Around the time of the 2007 paper, she began conducting antibody tests on psychiatric patients whose symptoms seemed to overlap with signs of autoimmune encephalitis,such as quickly shifting psychotic symptoms or neurological features like seizures.
One of Lennox’s first patients to test positive for NMDAR antibodies was a young female librarian who had rapidly descended into paranoia, stopped sleeping and then went mute. Antipsychotic drugs made her condition worse. After the antibodies were detected, the patient was given treatment to remove them from her blood. Within about a week, she was completely better. “That was the sort of mind-blowing moment,” Lennox says.
Today, Lennox is fascinated by the possibility of a larger population of psychosis patients whose illness is owed to autoimmune issues that are missed. This might explain why some patients don’t respond well to psychiatric treatments. “It’s an unexplored tip of the iceberg,” she says.
In search of missed patients, for the last decade Lennox has been running a clinical trial called SINAPPS2 to probe whether antibodies can be causing psychosis even in patients who don’t have other obvious neurological symptoms such as seizures and comas. Jones of the University of Cambridge is another investigator on the trial.
The researchers have been screening patients who have been experiencing psychotic episodes for less than two years, for four types of antibodies, including NMDAR and LGI1. At testing, none of the participants had severe neurological issues. Lennox says the team has detected the antibodies in the blood or spinal fluid of around 5 percent of around 5,000 psychiatric patients who have been screened.
Blood tests aren’t always reliable, however. Some of these detections may be false positives — meaning that despite the positive score, the body doesn’t truly have those autoantibodies in it. Others may have some antibodies floating around but they’re harmless and not driving their illness. A third population, though, may be in the same camp as Jones’ memorable patient.
One outstanding — and contested — question is whether a wider swath of early psychosis patients should be tested for these antibodies.
So far, 70 participants have been recruited to receive either immunotherapy or a placebo treatment. After treatment, researchers track their progress for up to 1½ years. (Jones stresses that if any patients start having seizures or other clear neurological symptoms, they will be treated with immunotherapy even if they were in the placebo group.)
The results, which are expected in 2027, will hopefully help map out the risks and benefits of immunotherapy treatment for psychosis patients with detected autoantibodies, guiding future care, says Jones. One outstanding –– and contested –– question is whether a wider swath of early psychosis patients should be tested for these antibodies, already a norm in Germany and Australia.
New antibody clues
Researchers are also continuing to search for new brain-targeting antibodies. Their hope is to understand patients who don’t have known antibodies but do have symptoms that look like autoimmune encephalitis. Detecting such new antibodies doesn’t prove they are driving the symptoms — cause and effect takes time to disentangle. But it gives researchers clues.
“Every year, there are a handful of new antibodies that are discovered, and some are more relevant to psychosis than others,” says Jonathan Rogers, a neuropsychiatry researcher at University College London. For example, in 2024, researchersdiscovered an antibody that binds to a protein in the brain called CAMKV. They detected this rare antibody in five patients with cancer, three of whom had psychosis or other psychiatric changes.
A variety of scientists also are turning to methods used in basic research to test patients who they suspect may have an autoimmune condition. The method involves sweeping a patient’s blood across a slice of rodent brain, incubating it for an hour and then washing off the blood. Then researchers check if any antibodies in the patient’s blood have stuck to the rodent brain tissue.
If they have, that implies there’s something in the blood that reacts against something in the brain. And even if the antibody type isn’t identifiable, it suggests potential immune activity in the patient’s brain.
Given the differences between rat and human brains, this detection technique isn’t perfect. But these rat brain tests can help build evidence for encephalitis in unclear clinical cases, says Eoin Flanagan, a neurologist at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota. When his clinic uses this method, around 5 to 10 percent of antibody activity detected is “unclassified,” meaning it’s not certain what the antibodies bind to. That suggests there may be more autoantibodies still to be found that are involved with autoimmune encephalitis.
To determine whether antibodies are present in a patient’s blood or spinal fluid, the fluid may be washed over a slice of rodent or primate brain. Different antibodies will stain this tissue in distinct patterns, making this a useful method for antibody discovery. In this image, staining patterns in rat brains are shown for three of the most common antibodies in autoimmune encephalitis: NMDAR, LGI1 and Caspr2.
As antibody discovery work continues, others in the field are pushing for improved treatments for autoimmune encephalitis. “If we’re going to do the work to discover the antibodies, we have to use that data to actually improve patients’ lives,” says Tammy Smith, a neurologist at the University of Utah. She argues for more targeted therapies, rather than a “kitchen sink approach, where everyone gets everything thrown at them.”
Smith is working on an ongoing clinical trial called ExTINGUISH that is testing a treatment for encephalitis caused by NMDAR antibodies. Even this, the poster child of autoimmune encephalitis, still isn’t fully understood, she says.
An important early step in treatment is to find and treat any tumors triggering the brain inflammation, if necessary. There’s generally a round of anti-inflammatory steroids, combined with a treatment such as plasma exchange, which flushes out antibodies, or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, which neutralizes them.
Next, patients often receive treatment with groups of identical antibodies — called monoclonal antibodies — that target and eradicate the immune cells that birth antibodies.
But Smith says there isn’t strong evidence that the monoclonal antibody treatment step improves all patient outcomes, even though it’s common to give the treatment right away, without waiting to see if the previous steps were enough. ExTINGUISH aims to rigorously test this: All of the trial’s 116 participants diagnosed with autoimmune encephalitis receive the earlier treatment rounds, but only half receive monoclonal antibody treatment. The other half get a placebo. The researchers won’t know who’s in each group, but if patients don’t notably improve, they’ll receive a different kind of intense immune-suppressing therapy.
Comparing all of these outcomes will help to clarify whether early monoclonal antibody treatment is necessary. This will ensure that patients aren’t burdened with unnecessary side effects, Smith says.
Smith has another concern. She is worried that, rather than missing patients, the field is tilting toward overdiagnosis — “treating something that’s not clearly autoimmune as autoimmune,” she says. If so, patients who actually need standard psychiatric care or other kinds of treatment won’t receive the help they require.
Patients are also getting tested in labs that may not be reputable. One patient came to Smith with test results indicating she had tested positive for 12 different autoantibody types –– a result Smith says is impossible. When the patient was tested at a lab Smith trusts, only one kind of antibody was detected.
Other experts are similarly concerned about potential overdiagnosis. Some cite high-profile cases of autoimmune encephalitis, such as that of former New York Post journalist Susannah Cahalan, as the cause, as well as continued stigma around mental illness. “If people think it might be an autoimmune cause, that’s more of a biological explanation,” says the Mayo Clinic’s Flanagan.
“If people think it might be an autoimmune cause, that’s more of a biological explanation.” — EOIN FLANAGAN
And then there are physicians themselves, Flanagan says: Initially, patients were missed, but now that practitioners are aware of the disease, they are more likely to overdiagnose.
Noticing more patients with incorrect autoimmune encephalitis diagnoses showing up in his clinic, Flanagan, with his colleagues, examined misdiagnosis across six specialty clinics. Reporting in 2022, the team found that just over a quarter of patients diagnosed with autoimmune encephalitis didn’t have it, and most of that one-quarter didn’t meet established criteria for the disease.
Immunotherapy isn’t risk-free, says Flanagan. The treatments lower the immune system’s defenses, increasing the possibility of infection, and steroids in particular can worsen psychosis. (This is one reason Jones and Lennox’s trial isn’t giving patients steroids.) In his study, 20 percent of the 84 patients who had received immunotherapy had some kind of negative reaction.
In addition to burdening patients with unnecessary risks, treatment for their “real disease” was also skipped over or delayed, Flanagan adds.
Refining levels of diagnosis
Tom Pollak, a psychiatrist at King’s College London, has led the charge to establish criteria for diagnosing less clear-cut cases of autoimmune encephalitis –– a wider category some researchers have dubbed “autoimmune psychosis.” But beyond identifying missed patients, he says, these criteria are also meant to clarify who shouldn’t be diagnosed.
When the autoimmune antibodies were first being discovered, he recalls, many in the scientific community believed the antibody blood test would revolutionize treatment for schizophrenic patients.
“It turned out to be not at all as simple as that,” he says. “I still see patients from that era who I think have been misdiagnosed and who have been given a diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis that they’ve lived with for 10 years, even though it’s inaccurate.”
But though the significance of these rare cases shouldn’t be overinflated, it also shouldn’t be reduced to a “nothingburger,” Pollak says. “There doesn’t seem to be one easy kind of story.”
Today, Pollak is skeptical that another antibody as prevalent as NMDAR will be discovered and illuminate an enormous hidden community of patients. But he has grown increasingly interested in something different but related: a broader link between immune system function and mental illness.
“I still see patients from that era who I think have been misdiagnosed and who have been given a diagnosis of autoimmune encephalitis that they’ve lived with for 10 years, even though it’s inaccurate.” — TOM POLLAK
He recently published a study that found an association between poor mental health and more static immune responses. When faced with stressful situations (such as a car accident or a more chronic psychosocial stressor), patients whose white blood cell counts jumped in response to the stressor, then leveled out afterwards, were less likely to develop depression and anxiety than those whose immune responses were more stagnant. Pollak is hoping to investigate the phenomenon in people at high risk for psychotic disorders.
As the research on autoimmune encephalitis inches along, a group of psychiatrists in New York is searching for, then trying to treat, an even less-studied population: patients diagnosed with long-term, severe schizophrenia that may have a hidden autoimmune cause.
Steven Kushner, a psychiatrist and codirector of Columbia University’s Stavros Niarchos Foundation Center for Precision Psychiatry and Mental Health, believes that such people exist in small numbers and is determined to find and help them. Since last fall, he has been leading an initiative to screen severe psychiatric patients across 15 New York state-run hospitals for signs of autoimmune-related illness, including lupus and autoimmune encephalitis, as well as a handful of other disorders.
The initiative, Kushner says, is starting to identify a few cases and to treat them with immune-suppressing drugs, after multiple rounds of testing. He says that so far, they’ve screened a few hundred people.
At some point in the future, Kushner says his team will share how many patients they’re finding with autoimmune conditions, and how those patients are faring after treatment. But he says that the primary goal of the project isn’t science; it’s patient care. “We’re trying to help people,” he says.
Jones, for one, doesn’t believe this work should be done outside of a research setting. But he’s sympathetic to the idea of helping the most severely affected patients, for whom no other treatment has worked.
“Trying some heroic treatments may well be worthwhile in that group, but I’d still say you should do it within the context of a trial, so that you can learn from it,” he says.
After all, despite the dramatic recovery of his patient with animal hallucinations, Jones also remembers similar cases that didn’t end up being autoimmune encephalitis.
While he believes in this wider unrecognized population, anecdotes can only go so far in science, he adds. “We don’t have that gold standard evidence from a trial. So the whole thing remains an unanswered question at the moment.”

All operational British Rivet Joint spy planes near Russia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
13:50:59 BST
21:50:59 KST

Britain deployed its entire operational RC-135W Rivet Joint intelligence fleet on missions around Russia on 25 September, with both aircraft currently available to the RAF flying separate sorties over the Baltic and Black Sea while the third British Rivet Joint remains in the United States for refit and maintenance work.
Open-source flight tracking identified the aircraft as ZZ664 and ZZ666, both operating from RAF Waddington. ZZ664 flew around the Baltic region and close to the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, while ZZ666 operated over the Black Sea before both aircraft began their return towards the UK. Neither aircraft was shown entering Russian airspace.
The UK operates three RC-135W Rivet Joint aircraft, meaning the two sorties represented the RAF committing its entire immediately available Rivet Joint force to intelligence-gathering activity around Russia on the same day. The third aircraft is currently in the United States undergoing refit and maintenance work, leaving the two aircraft seen over eastern Europe as the complete operational British fleet at that point.
The visibility of the sorties is also part of the point before someone asks if this should be secret, civilian services such as Flightradar24 build their tracking picture from sources including ADS-B, where an aircraft broadcasts information such as identity, altitude and position, and multilateration, or MLAT, where a position is calculated from the timing of transponder signals received by several ground stations. Both British aircraft were readily visible on civilian tracking networks for substantial parts of their missions, meaning these were not flights whose broad presence was being concealed from public view. Military aircraft can reduce the information available to civilian trackers, although MLAT can still plot an aircraft transmitting suitable transponder signals, so public visibility does not necessarily reveal every element of the mission. Had there been a requirement to minimise that visibility, however, the tracking picture could have been considerably less complete.
The Baltic aircraft followed a route around eastern NATO territory and Kaliningrad, an area containing a concentration of Russian military facilities, while the second aircraft operated over international waters in the Black Sea.
The RC-135W Rivet Joint is the RAF’s principal signals intelligence aircraft and is designed to intercept, locate and analyse electromagnetic emissions generated by military activity. Rather than relying primarily on cameras, the aircraft carries an extensive suite of receivers and processing equipment used to collect communications and electronic signals, including radar emissions, allowing crews to build a picture of activity at considerable distance.
Mission specialists aboard the aircraft can detect and classify signals while the sortie is under way, helping identify radar systems, communications networks and other emitters. This allows Rivet Joint to collect intelligence while remaining in international or allied airspace rather than entering the territory being monitored.
The three British aircraft are operated by No. 51 Squadron from RAF Waddington and are closely related to the RC-135 fleet operated by the US Air Force. British Rivet Joints are regularly used for intelligence missions around NATO’s eastern flank, but the simultaneous appearance of both operationally available aircraft around Russia placed the whole immediately usable UK fleet on missions covering Russia’s western and southern approaches.

Built by Ukrainian officers from real combat, DWAC course is now “NATO Selected”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

21:50:19 KST

A drone-warfare course written by Ukrainian officers from real combat has earned NATO status. The English-language Drone Warfare Awareness Course, built on Ukraine's war experience, is now "NATO Selected" and has been taught to officers from more than 10 countries, the General Staff said.
Ukraine's combat experience is flowing into NATO's classrooms, and the alliance is starting to treat Kyiv as a teacher rather than only a recipient. It follows a broader shift of Ukrainian lessons into allied curricula.
Combat lessons become a course
The course came out of Ukraine's International Peacekeeping and Security Center, whose instructors at its "Partnership for Peace" training center wrote the syllabus, formally titled "Fundamentals of the Combat Use of Unmanned Systems", based on the Armed Forces' own experience.
In November 2025, the Ukrainian team presented it at a seminar in Sweden attended by NATO commanders and analysts.
The next year, it passed international trials with officers from more than a dozen countries and earned its NATO Selected mark, a recognition that it meets Alliance standards and can be offered to member-state officers, short of the full accreditation the center is still pursuing.
Sweden and Finland lend a hand
Two Nordic partners helped get it there. Sweden's SWEDINT began working with the center in 2024, teaching international methods for course development and preparing courses for accreditation.
Finland's FINCENT joined in 2025, sharing insights on building a military education system and assessing training needs. In the fall of 2026, delegations from both countries visited the center and signed plans for further joint work.
Ukraine teaches the Alliance
The course is one piece of a wider reversal. Ukrainian officers have trained Polish and German counterparts in drone and electronic warfare, and at the joint NATO-Ukraine center in Poland, they have set their battlefield practice against NATO doctrine, exposing where the Alliance's assumptions no longer fit in a modern war.

Category 5 Hurricane Polo threatens Mexico’s coast, landfall expected Monday
BUENOS AIRES, Sept 26 - Hurricane Polo moved away from Mexico's Pacific coast on Saturday after it regained the highest Category 5 strength, before an expected return to make landfall in Baja California Sur on Monday, forecasters said.
On Saturday morning, Polo was about 425 miles south west of the Mexican resort town of Cabo Corrientes, with maximum sustained winds of 160 mph, according to the US National Hurricane Center. The storm was moving north west at 10 mph.
AccuWeather, a private forecaster, reported that 24 hours after hitting Baja California, the hurricane was expected to make a second landfall along the coast of mainland northwestern Mexico, bringing potential life-threatening flash flooding to parts of Baja California Sur, Sinaloa, Sonora and Chihuahua.
The hurricane’s heavy rain and strong winds along Mexico’s Pacific coast forced evacuations, port closures and school cancellations this week. In the resort city of San Jose del Cabo, police officers restricted access to a beach on Friday as the hurricane generated high waves and dangerous surf conditions.
Hurricane conditions are possible on Monday afternoon from Punta Eugenia to Santa Fe in Baja California, the NHC said.
Polo is expected to dump 4 to 8 inches of rain across parts of Baja California Sur, with maximum amounts of 10 inches, which could produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, the NHC said. It could also cause life-threatening surf, rip currents and coastal flooding. REUTERS

German Olympic Committee names Munich as bid city choice
September 26, 2026
The German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) on Saturday announced it chose Munich as Germany's entry to bid for at least the next three Olympic Summer Games.
Ahead of the vote, former Olympic champion and new Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said: "We have an international task to fulfill and must enter the race with the city or region that gives Germany the greatest chances internationally. The decision on that is made by sport, and I assume that it will make it with a great deal of responsibility."
Germany's president Frank-Walter Steinmeier said the olympic bid represented a huge opportunity for all of Germany to "show that we are a land of opportunity."
According to the Munich bid, all competitions would take place in Bavaria, except for the football matches which would be played in Stuttgart and the sailing competitions in the nothern city of Kiel.
Berlin bowing out created two-horse race
Munich and a Cologne-led bid by the Rhine-Ruhr region were the only two in contention.
As many as 17.6 million tickets could be sold for the Games in Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr, more than ever before at a Games, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia said recently.
Munich was campaigning after two failed bids for the 2018 and 2022 Winter Games and having previously hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.
Up until Thursday, Berlin had been among the cities in contention, but the city's mayor announced that the city would withdraw from the race.
The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in the German capital's elections last weekend. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.
Sports minister has sights set on 2040
On Friday, Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said he would welcome a German Olympic bid for the 2040 Games, with it coinciding with an important historical milestone.
"2040 will mark the 50th anniversary of reunification. Here we could send a great signal that also aligns with the values of the Olympic Games," Rauhe told German news agency dpa ahead of the deciding vote on Saturday.
"Based on my personal history, 2040 would be my favorite date. That has to do with the fact that I'm a Berlin child. As a schoolchild, I experienced what happens to people when a wall falls, when people grow together again, when two population groups that had been separated become a community again,” Rauhe said.
"Ultimately, though, one thing matters above all: bringing the Olympic and Paralympic Games back to our country. No matter when," Rauhe said.

Why has the Yemen government called for a general mobilisation?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:46:18 UTC
21:46:18 KST

Why has the Yemen government called for a general mobilisation?
Yemeni government offers amnesty to Houthi defectors, aiming to weaken rebel ranks and rebuild national unity.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has called for a general mobilisation of the population as part of its long-anticipated pushback against the Houthis.
In his first speech since government forces were routed from the Red Sea coast, Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council, made a national call to arms and asked citizens to “contribute in every way possible” in the fight against the Houthis.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
- list 2 of 4Families fleeing Yemen’s war face displacement, hunger and water shortages
- list 3 of 4Yemeni leader urges public to enlist, offers amnesty to Houthi defectors
- list 4 of 4Yemen’s government offers amnesty to Houthi defectors
Al-Alimi also offered an amnesty to defecting Houthi fighters, effective immediately.
It comes as the Houthis made dramatic advances in western Yemen in September, including capturing the city of Mocha and Mayyun Island. The assault follows the recent collapse of a 2022 government and Houthi truce, which had paused 12 years of fighting between the two sides.
The Houthis’ Red Sea offensive has given them control over Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the busiest shipping routes in the world, a narrow waterway linking the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
The strait is also of crucial economic and strategic importance to Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government.
Through the mobilisation of the general population, al-Alimi pledged to recapture Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, which it lost to the Houthis in 2014, and restore government sovereignty over the whole of Yemen.
“Our objective is clear to everyone both at home and abroad: to restore state institutions and exercise their sovereignty over the entire country, including Sanaa,” al-Alimi said.
So, why has the government decided to call for a general mobilisation now and why has the government offered Houthi fighters an amnesty? Here’s what we know.
Why has al-Alimi ordered a general mobilisation?
In the eyes of most analysts, the government’s position has rarely been weaker. Pushed out of Mocha, Mayyun Island and the wider Bab al-Mandeb coastline, the Houthi advance jeopardises the authority of the internationally recognised government and brings its Saudi ally deeper into the conflict. Riyadh and other Saudi cities have now become regular targets of Houthi rockets and drones.
Even the government’s rare victories have proven short-lived. Hays district in al-Hodeidah was briefly taken by government forces in early September before falling again to the Houthis just days later.
Ahmed al-Shalafi, Al Jazeera Arabic’s Yemen affairs editor, described al-Alimi’s comments as a “war speech”, calling for Yemenis to join the military’s ranks and take part in the liberation of Houthi-held Sanaa.
Government forces currently remain bogged down in fighting in Taiz and Marib, far from the capital.
How significant is the offer of amnesty?
In 2024, before the current lightning advance, a United Nations panel of experts estimated that Houthi fighters numbered somewhere around 350,000, bolstered by the recruitment of fighters sometimes aged under 18.
It is unlikely that these fighters will defect to the government side any time soon, analysts have said, but the offer of amnesty might grow more attractive if the Houthis begin to lose ground.
“You need to remember that, despite everything, Yemen remains a tribal society,” Baraa Shiban, a researcher and political analyst on Yemen and the Gulf at the Royal United Service Institute (RUSI), said. “The offer of amnesty is the government signalling that it won’t be seeking revenge upon fighters in a way that could risk the conflict descending into tribal warfare.”
How will Saudi Arabia respond?
Saudi Arabia has a lot to lose. In the last 24 hours, Riyadh claimed to have intercepted six Houthi ballistic missiles targeting the Yanbu area on the Red Sea and Taif, to the country’s West.
The potential for further strikes upon Saudi Arabia threatens Riyadh’s ability to export oil through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia’s west coast has gained greater significance since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran on February 28, with Tehran responding by closing the Strait of Hormuz, blocking access by sea to the kingdom’s oil-rich Eastern Province.
The brief closure of Saudi Arabia’s East-West Crude Oil Pipeline following an attack on three pumping stations earlier this month has also exposed vulnerabilities for Riyadh.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan – who signed their Mecca Joint Defence Agreement in August – announced that an emergency meeting of military chiefs would be held to address the threat.
However, what level of intervention the three countries might take in Yemen, if any, remained far from certain.
“Even at the peak of the fighting [before the 2022 ceasefire], Saudi only deployed very limited ground forces in support of the government, preferring to rely on air strikes instead,” Shiban said.
“I really can’t imagine Yemeni citizens reacting all that well to the sight of armed Turkish, Pakistani and Saudi forces on their soil, which could even risk taking the conflict in a very different direction.
“I would be surprised if their [Turkiye and Pakistan] involvement did extend beyond technical support and intelligence sharing.”
Are other countries affected?
The Houthis have said they would keep Bab al-Mandeb open and indicated that any attacks would be limited to Saudi vessels. However, addressing the United Nations General Assembly last week, the vice-president of Yemen’s internationally recognised government council, Abdullah Abdulkader Al Alimi-Bawzer, said the rebels were not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” he told world leaders in New York on Thursday.
Protecting the strait “is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation,” Alimi-Bawzer said.
Saudi Arabia has announced a naval coalition for the Red Sea, but details of the scale and scope of the armada remain largely unknown.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have reportedly sent a letter to the European Union promising that ships linked to the bloc would not be targeted, in an apparent attempt to isolate Saudi Arabia from its allies.

The president made the remarks in an exclusive interview with CBS News’ “Face the Nation,” broadcast late on Friday. On Iran’s nuclear program and inspection of its sites in return for sanctions relief, Pezeshkian said that Iran has never sought nuclear weapons. He said that the US and Israel assassinated the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei, whose religious decree bans the development of nuclear weapons.

Israel says in their own speech, what they’re doing is neutralizing the government, not negotiating,” he said, according to a transcript shared on the CBS News website.
“We are doing everything humanly possible, but not through bullying and coercion intended to force us into submission. We’re already negotiating. Why are they concurrently attacking us?” Pezeshkian said, according to the same transcript.
On Iran’s seven-day plan to re-open the Strait of Hormuz – a proposal conveyed to the US by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi through mediator Qatar on the sidelines of the UNGA – President Pezeshkian said that the implementation of the plan will begin as soon as the US accepts the plan.

He said that the US tore apart the 2015 nuclear deal and twice attacked Iran, in 2025 and 2026, when the two sides were in the midst of negotiations, and then breached the memorandum.

Asked whether Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Khamenei had advised Pezeshkian to pursue diplomacy, the president said all discussions and decisions had been coordinated.
Pezeshkian said a six-member team had been formed in Iran, comprising representatives from the military, parliament, administration and other institutions. The team has the authority to make decisions and implement them in coordination, he added.
Asked why he came to New York despite the risks, Pezeshkian rejected claims that Iranian officials had been hiding in shelters during the war. He said he remained active, visiting several ministries each day and holding meetings with ministers.

Cyberattack gains access to University of Tartu library's online store customer data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Cyberattack gains access to University of Tartu library's online store customer data
The University of Tartu Library informed users of its e‑bookstore that an external attacker gained access to their online store and most likely downloaded the store's customer data.
The Director of the University of Tartu Library, Jaanika Anderson, told online store users that on 11 September they detected a data security incident: an attacker had illegally accessed the store.
The university immediately notified the Information System Authority (RIA) of the incident and suspended access to the online store. The Data Protection Inspectorate was also informed.
"In additional analysis of the incident, the university determined that the attacker very likely also illegally downloaded the online store's customer data, which includes your first and last name, email, phone number, online store username and the encrypted version of the password associated with it, as well as data related to the use of the online store, such as purchase history, IP addresses, etc.," Anderson wrote to online store users.
The attacker likely also accessed customers' usernames and passwords, and although passwords were stored in encrypted form, the library recommends changing them as soon as possible if the same username‑password combination has been used for other accounts, and monitoring for any suspicious activity.
Anderson added that the attacker did not gain access to payment instrument data related to purchases.
The university has suspended access to the online store and will restore it only after a full security analysis has been carried out and security vulnerabilities have been eliminated.

Cheaper Patriot partners: U.S. Army names 30 finalists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:41:55 UTC
21:41:55 KST

- The U.S. Army named 30 finalists in xTech|Apex Intercept, a competition for low-cost interceptors to work alongside the Patriot air defense system.
- Finalists get $25,000 each and will demonstrate their technology in October and November, with up to 18 winners due by Dec. 31.
The U.S. Army has picked 30 finalists, from defense giants such as RTX and Northrop Grumman to startups in Australia and the United Kingdom, in a prize competition to find cheaper interceptors that could fly alongside the Patriot air defense system.
The Army’s xTech program announced the finalists for xTech|Apex Intercept this week. Each receives $25,000 and a chance to demonstrate its technology to Army and Department of War experts and end users between Oct. 1 and Nov. 30. The Army plans to name up to 18 winners by Dec. 31.
The competition is run by the Army’s FUZE xTech program with the Capability Program Executive for Defensive Fires. The Army says it wants low-cost interceptors to add to Patriot’s work against aircraft and drones, cruise missiles, and close-range and short-range ballistic missiles. It has not published a target price per interceptor.
The Army split the contest into four topics. The largest, with 10 finalists, covers complete low-cost interceptors, called all-up rounds, together with their fire control. Those finalists include RTX, which builds Patriot, as well as Anduril, AeroVironment, QinetiQ, UDD Tech, Wardstone, Greenjets, Furientis, AEON Industries and AirX Robotics, which entered its Katana interceptor.
Seven companies are competing on low-cost solid rocket motors: Northrop Grumman, L3Harris, General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems, Ursa Major, X-Bow Systems, Australia’s DefendTex and Britain’s Cambridge Aerospace. Six are working on low-cost seekers, the sensors that guide an interceptor onto its target, including Leonardo DRS, Toyon and Technology Service Corporation. One seeker entry, a radio-frequency design, is listed under Cherrill Consulting Group with the logo of Israel Aerospace Industries.
The final seven are working on fire control and flight guidance, the software and hardware that aim and steer an interceptor. They include Australia’s Advanced Navigation, which proposed guidance that works without GPS, radio maker Persistent Systems and Australian firm Rocket Fast Drones.
Winners of the complete-interceptor topic can receive up to $1 million each, and winners in the other three topics up to $750,000 each, with $7.25 million set aside for the final round. The total prize pool is up to $8 million. The Army says winners may be considered for follow-on prototype agreements or contracts, and finalists may be invited to submit separate proposals for further development.
The competition was open to small, medium and large businesses in the United States and allied countries. Companies submitted white papers of up to five pages between July 7 and July 24, along with an optional five-minute video.

Swiss finance minister downplays talk of UBS relocation

Swiss finance minister downplays talk of UBS relocation
A move abroad by UBS due to stricter capital requirements is unlikely, according to Karin Keller-Sutter.
“We have granted UBS significant concessions under the Capital Adequacy Ordinance,” the Swiss finance minister said in an interview in the Aargauer Zeitung newspaper on Saturday.
“The Federal Council has also opted against any further general tightening of capital ratios, as recommended by experts following the Credit Suisse crisis,” Keller-Sutter continued. “Despite this, UBS described all our proposals as ‘extreme’. It staked everything on an aggressive strategy, presumably assuming it would in any case win out in parliament: after all, that’s always been the case in the past.”
More
What the too-big-to-fail Swiss parliament vote means for UBS
This time, however, parliamentarians – at least in the Senate – took a different stance. “UBS certainly doesn’t have to leave Switzerland for this reason,” Keller-Sutter told the newspaper. “Many analysts and experts agree the requirements are reasonable and easily manageable for the bank. Leaving Switzerland would be far more costly and legally much more complex. Furthermore, UBS would no longer be a Swiss bank: yet its model is based on Switzerland, on ‘Swissness’, on our rule of law and political stability. When we hear about private banks and the capital inflows registered during the Middle East conflict, this clearly demonstrates the confidence placed in Switzerland as a place of business.”
Keller-Sutter said she has not called or been in contact with UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti since the recent Senate decision. “This isn’t necessary,” she explained. In November, she will meet with the chairman of UBS’s board of directors, Colm Kelleher, as part of a regular exchange with financial centre representatives. “But now is not the time for negotiations: the matter is in parliament,” she said.
More
A brief history of Swiss banking oversight and its scandals
Speculation about a possible relocation of UBS from Switzerland – potentially involving a merger, for instance with US giant Morgan Stanley – caused the share price to rise by 3.5% on the Swiss stock exchange on Friday. There had already been recurring rumours of a possible move of UBS headquarters to the US, and UBS itself has never completely ruled out this possibility.
In September, at the Swiss Bankers Association’s annual meeting in St Gallen, Kelleher said the objective was to remain in Switzerland. “However, if we were to find ourselves in a situation where we are no longer competitive, we would naturally have to give the matter thought,” said Kelleher, himself a former Morgen Stanley CEO.

Michigan firm to build 4,000 attack drones for U.S. troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:34:34 UTC
21:34:34 KST

- Swarm Defense Technologies received an order for 4,000 Kiwi one-way attack drones worth at least $25 million under the Drone Dominance Program.
- The Michigan company placed fifth in the deep strike category at Gauntlet II testing at Fort Carson, Colorado, in August.
Michigan drone maker Swarm Defense Technologies has received an order for 4,000 Kiwi one-way attack drones under the U.S. Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, the company announced Sept. 22. The prototype delivery order has a minimum value of $25 million, including munitions, which works out to about $6,250 per drone at that minimum.
The Kiwi is a small quadcopter built to fly to a target and explode on impact. The company will build the order at its 3,700-square-meter (40,000-square-foot) plant in Auburn Hills, Michigan. It did not give a delivery schedule or say which units will receive the drones.
The award follows Gauntlet II, the program’s second competitive round, held at Fort Carson, Colorado, in August. Military operators flew 1,858 sorties across 23 drone designs from 19 companies in unscripted missions, including strikes from 15 km (9.3 miles) away, attacks in confined spaces, night flights and runs against jamming and counter-drone systems. Swarm Defense placed fifth on the deep strike leaderboard with 66.0 points. The program’s order schedule set 4,000 drones for fifth place in each mission area.
“Receiving an order for 4,000 Kiwi aircraft is a major milestone for Swarm Defense,” said Kyle Dorosz, CEO of Swarm Defense Technologies. “The Drone Dominance Program has placed its confidence in both our aircraft and our ability to deliver them at scale.”
The company’s main pitch is volume per operator. Its Strike Deck ground control software lets one person manage dozens of drones at once, automating navigation and the flying of relay drones that extend radio range while keeping the aircraft from colliding. The drones can guide themselves on the final approach to a target, but operators choose the targets and authorize each strike, the company said.
“Combat units need to bring volume to the fight. Swarming allows a single pilot to accomplish what it normally takes several pilots to do,” said Adam Wright, president of Swarm Defense Technologies and a former U.S. Navy SEAL.
Swarm Defense grew out of Firefly Drone Shows, which the company describes as the largest U.S. maker of light-show drones. Firefly has built more than 20,000 swarming drones since 2017, and the two companies share engineering and manufacturing in Auburn Hills. Swarm Defense designs its own flight controllers, motor controllers, battery electronics, firmware and control software in-house.
The order covers only the strike version of the Kiwi. The company says the drone can also be fitted for reconnaissance, as an airborne radio relay or as a reusable drone that drops munitions and returns. Separately, it holds a Phase I prototype agreement with the Defense Innovation Unit to develop containers of drones that could sit dormant at forward positions until a remote operator launches them.
The Drone Dominance Program is a $1.1 billion, two-year effort to buy large numbers of cheap, U.S.-made attack drones for combat units. The first round, Gauntlet I at Fort Benning, Georgia, in February and March, produced about $150 million in orders for roughly 30,000 drones from 11 companies. For Gauntlet II, the department plans to buy about 60,000 drones from 10 companies, worth roughly $300 million. To reach Fort Carson, each of the 19 finalists had to deliver 120 drones fitted with explosive payloads within about five weeks.
Two more rounds, Gauntlet 3 and Gauntlet 4, are planned at roughly six-month intervals, along with a separate competition for bomber drones scheduled to start in October.

Is Ukraine Really Running Out of Money?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:34:00 UTC
21:34:00 KST

Journalists often make mistakes. As someone who dropped a bit of a clanger this week (I said there was a deal on the EU’s sanctions on Russian oligarchs 24 hours before there actually was one), I’m especially eager to avoid repeating one I made just a few months ago.
Early this year I repeatedly wrote that Ukraine was set to run out of money in April, or – when I felt like being more specific – in “early” April. Nor was I alone: European Commission officials, Ukrainian officials, and many of my fellow journalists said the same thing.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In retrospect, however, the claim never really made much sense.
For one thing, it was never clear what it actually meant. (That Kyiv would default on its debt? If so, why not just say that? And if not, what?) For another, Ukraine’s behavior didn’t really fit that of a country that was on the brink of fiscal armageddon.
On Feb. 20, Hungary shocked Ukraine and its European allies when it announced that it would veto a €90 billion loan to Kyiv, citing the latter’s failure to restart oil flows through a damaged pipeline that transits Ukraine on its way from Russia to Hungary.
Rather than dropping to its knees and begging Budapest to back down – or asking Brussels to break the impasse or (the most obvious solution) repairing the pipeline – Kyiv simply shrugged.
“What’s the point of rebuilding [it]?” Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, said five days later.
Why the Baltics Are Right to Worry About Putin’s Latest Reassurances
For a country on the brink of bankruptcy, this was (to put it mildly) a very weird thing to say. But for a country that wasn’t, it wasn’t.
As it later transpired, Ukraine wasn’t close to “running out of money,” at least in any meaningful sense. (Moreover, even if some kind of a fiscal crunch were imminent, Kyiv could have issued bonds to state banks or forced its central bank to print money to remain temporarily afloat.)
Ultimately, Kyiv’s actions were not driven by economics, but by politics.
First, Ukraine was understandably reluctant to facilitate oil deliveries to a country (Hungary) whose pro-Moscow government had regularly sabotaged the EU’s Ukraine policy, and whose oil purchases would further enrich the country (Russia) that was attempting to destroy it.
Second, and as Zelensky effectively admitted, blocking the crude transit was deemed an effective way of tilting Hungary’s parliamentary elections in mid-April in favor of Péter Magyar, the nemesis of then-premier Viktor Orbán. Magyar’s subsequent landslide victory suggests Zelensky was right.
Not coincidentally, ten days after the elections, Kyiv finally allowed the oil to flow, causing Budapest to immediately lift its veto. Ukraine then spent the better part of two months haggling over the loan’s technical details with EU officials.
Finally, on June 25, the first loan payout – €3.2 billion in budget support – was made. No other budget support from the loan has been disbursed since then (although €11.7 billion has been paid out for defense procurement).
And, last time I checked, Ukraine still hasn’t run out of money. At least not yet.
Kyiv, give me a break!
Why do I tell this story?
In part, because I have a penchant for public self-flagellation. More importantly, though, I think recalling this history is crucial to understanding what’s happening today.
Last month, Zelensky stunned his European allies when he announced that Ukraine faced a “budget shortfall” this year of $27 billion (€24 billion) – a sum equivalent to more than 10% of the country’s GDP.
Once again, however, the claims don’t add up. Literally.
According to Zelenskyy, “$8-10 billion” is required to buy “weapons and everything necessary” to ensure a “normal start” to next year, while “nearly $20 billion” is needed to pay soldiers’ salaries, the families of fallen soldiers, and “other areas of funding.”
Zelensky has never defined what he means by “necessary”, “normal”, or “other areas of funding”. Nor has he explained how “$8-10 billion” + “nearly $20 billion” = $27 billion. (Why not, say, $28 billion? Or $29 billion? Or “nearly” $30 billion?)
Tellingly, neither the European Commission nor the International Monetary Fund has been able to confirm Zelensky’s figures, despite weeks of intensive discussions. Even more tellingly, Brussels has resisted calls from some EU countries to plug the gap by accelerating payouts this year from the €90 billion loan – a clear sign that it doesn’t think any “shortfall” is imminent.
In an interview with me this week, Valdis Dombrovskis, the EU’s economy commissioner, strongly implied that Ukraine’s financing needs are less dire than Kyiv is suggesting.
“By and large, [the] budgetary needs for Ukraine for this year seem to be broadly covered,” Dombrovskis said, adding that the country nevertheless requires additional military support.
Kyiv’s demand for extra cash is especially puzzling when one recalls that so much funding for this year is still available.
Maksym Samoiliuk, a senior economist at the Center for Economic Strategy, a Kyiv-based think tank, points out that around $29.5 billion in external financing (much of it from the EU) is currently being held up by the Ukrainian parliament’s failure to pass reforms. Why, then, demand more when you’re not taking what you can already get?
Much like earlier this year, the key to this puzzle is to realize that politics, rather than economics, is driving Zelensky’s behavior.
First, his demand plays well domestically. Calling for higher salaries for soldiers and bereaved families is always a sure-fire political winner. Asking foreigners to pay for this also exempts Zelenskyy from the awkward task of having to ask Ukrainians to pay for it themselves.
Second, it is aimed at Ukraine’s allies – in particular, it is intended to make Western governments, media, and citizens recognize (and ideally address) Ukraine’s increasingly dire economic situation.
Mind the gap
Viewed in this light, Zelensky’s actions are also perfectly reasonable.
After all, Russia’s naval blockade of the Black Sea has starved Kyiv’s economy of export revenue from wheat and other goods in recent months. Moscow’s drone and missile strikes have also devastated Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and destroyed numerous tax revenue-generating businesses. Financial support from Europe’s allies, particularly the US, has also dried up.
In other words, Ukraine does need help.
But it can also help itself.
As Dmytro Andriienko and Viktoriia Klimchuk of the Kyiv School of Economics have noted, Ukraine could seek to harness domestic sources of revenue, namely by cutting or postponing non-critical government expenditure and broadening its own tax base. By a happy coincidence, these latter measures are precisely among those demanded by the EU and the IMF.
Boosting domestic revenue, then, will help unlock foreign funding – a financial double blessing.
Or as Dombrovskis put it: “When we are discussing additional funding gaps and possible additional funding sources, it [is] important that Ukraine actually uses the funding or receives the funding which is already available.”
Ukraine’s failure to pass reforms, then, might prove to be the biggest mistake of all. It also risks being significantly more costly than mine – unless, of course, I’m very much mistaken.

War’s next tech leap: Person who built Ukraine’s “Army of Drones” is now building “Army of Robots”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:33:05 UTC
21:33:05 KST

The person who built Ukraine's "Army of Drones" is now building an "Army of Robots". Myhailo Fedorov, the former defense minister, has launched a private-sector push to robotize the war, wanting machines to take the deadliest jobs, evacuating the wounded, laying and clearing mines, and fighting, so soldiers come home, he wrote, announcing the effort at the IT Arena conference in Lviv.
The pitch rests on a track record. Fedorov's Army of Drones, launched in 2022, helped make drones the weapon behind more than 95 percent of Ukraine's battlefield hits. Over 700 makers now building them, and he is betting robotization is the next such leap.
Army of Robots is meant to be an ecosystem, not a company: investing in defense-tech firms, standing up R&D, testing with troops, and scaling fast, whatever works. Fedorov is running it from outside government, having left the defense ministry in July and started building a defense-tech company backed by Palantir chief Alex Karp.
Robots take the deadliest jobs
Fedorov's vision is a battlefield where machines go first. A sensor spots a threat, then a robot enters the danger zone, he says. Humanoid robots would carry ammunition and pull out the wounded, lay and clear minefields, scout, hold positions, and strike, taking the roles that today cost soldiers their lives. For now, it is a vision more than a fielded capability: Fedorov is describing where he wants the battlefield to go, not a robot force already in the fight.
The Army of Drones sets the model
The aim, Fedorov says, is to gather the best engineers, combat experience, and capital and point them at one goal: making robots fight instead of people. The obstacle is Russia, which he said has learned to quickly copy and scale military technology, so Ukraine must keep inventing the next cycle before the enemy does.
"Russia will stop only when we can break its backbone," he says, arguing that it will take Western capital, world-class engineers, and private initiative.

SBU’s Alpha Special Forces Claim Hit on Rostov’s Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant
Unknown

2026-09-26
12:31:00 UTC
21:31:00 KST

Ukrainian forces said they
struck the Azov Optical-Mechanical Plant in southern Russia’s Rostov region overnight into Saturday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said its Alpha Special Operations Center hit the plant in a joint operation with the Ukrainian Navy.
The SBU called the facility a key supplier of components used in precision weapons.
“This enterprise is one of the key optoelectronic sites of the Russian Tactical Missile Weapons Corporation. The plant produces radar and infrared homing heads for guided missiles, thermal imaging devices, and electronic systems for high-precision artillery,” the agency wrote in its press release.
The attack reportedly damaged the plant’s “optical and foundry production facilities, the assembly area, the galvanic shop and the printed circuit board manufacturing shop,” it added.
The plant was also reportedly struck in a Ukrainian attack on July 10.
The SBU also claimed it hit a Pantsir-S2 air defense system in the same region, likely as part of an operation to suppress local air defenses.
The agency also claimed involvement in hitting the Ilsky Oil Refinery in Russia’s Krasnodar Krai overnight.
Domestic missiles used
The operation used an array of domestically built weapons, including the Ruta, Palanytsia and Bars drone missiles, as well as Neptune anti-ship missiles, according to the SBU.
The Neptune missile was used to sink the flagship of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, the Moskva, in April 2022. Ukraine unveiled an updated version in August 2025, with reports suggesting it has a range of up to 1,000 km (621 miles) – a jump from the 300 km (186 miles) range listed in a 2020 brochure for the original model.
Russia’s 7th-Largest Refinery in Perm Reportedly Offline After Friday Attack
The Palanytsia, which Kyiv described as a drone-missile hybrid, was first unveiled in 2024 and later upgraded in 2025, bringing the reported range to 650 km (400 miles).
The Ruta and Bars are classified similarly, with President Volodymyr Zelensky announcing successful tests of the former in late 2024.
Confirmed combat use of the Ruta was reported in 2025, followed by upgrades in 2026 that included a heavier warhead, a reported range of over 450 kilometers (280 miles), and a guidance system said to be immune to electronic warfare (EW) jamming.
The Bars, with a 700-800 kilometers (435-500 miles) range and a 50-100-kilogram (110-220-pound) warhead, was unveiled in April 2025.

Russian strikes on Kyiv data centers disrupt operations at several Ukrainian media outlets

Unknown Publisher

Russian strikes on Kyiv data centers disrupt operations at several Ukrainian media outlets
Several Ukrainian media outlets reported disruptions to their operations on Sept. 26 following Russian strikes on data centers in Kyiv.
Russian forces intensified attacks on data centers in Kyiv in September, causing internet outages across the capital and disrupting access to some online services.
TV channel Novyny.Live said it had temporarily suspended broadcasting due to disruptions affecting some of its services following a Russian attack on infrastructure in Kyiv.
Military media outlet Armiia TV also suspended operations on Sept. 26 following Russian strikes.
Public broadcaster Suspilne said its website's video players were not working because they were operated by Cosmonova, whose data center was damaged on Sept. 25. On the following day, Cosmonova said its data center had been damaged by a Russian attack for the second time and was knocked out of operation.
A Russian attack on Sept. 23 damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions. The attack also affected cloud service Fex.net and disrupted internet access for around 100,000 households in Kyiv and the surrounding region, the Digital Transformation Ministry said.
After another Russian attack on Kyiv on Sept. 24, providers Domonet, Kievnet, and Faust reported infrastructure damage and internet outages. Russia also destroyed a data center hosting MiroHost's infrastructure, with the company saying it could not yet estimate when services would be restored.
Another Russian attack damaged a Datagroup data center on Sept. 25.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said following a meeting with senior military officials on Sept. 25 that the Ukrainian government had decided to strengthen the protection of data centers and other critical communications infrastructure.
"This is the beginning of a phase where, since September, they have started taking it out systematically," Anatolii Frolenkov, a representative of the 1-IX internet exchange point, told the Kyiv Independent.
Despite the recent damage, Frolenkov said knocking out internet access across Ukraine would be extremely difficult.
Providers can limit the impact of individual strikes by duplicating network equipment, maintaining backup communications routes, and distributing infrastructure across different locations, including outside Ukraine, he said.
But that strategy is expensive, leaving many providers without sufficient backup infrastructure, more vulnerable when equipment is destroyed.
"The internet will not disappear completely," Frolenkov said. "There will be outages, there will be problems. It won't work as smoothly or as quickly, things may glitch, and operators may go down for a couple of hours because the infrastructure is being physically destroyed."

Parental leave idea makes signature threshold, backers say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:27:14 UTC
21:27:14 KST

Parental leave idea makes signature threshold, backers say
A people’s initiative for parental leave has reached the required number of signatures, according to one of its backers, the Liberal Green Party.
A total of 136,000 signatures have been collected for handing in to the Federal Chancellery next week, the Liberal Greens said in a press release on Saturday.
The text of the initiative was published in the Federal Gazette in April 2025, meaning a deadline of October 1, 2026 for collecting 100,000 signatures required for a public vote. The proposal has been put forward not just by the Liberal Greens, but also by the Greens, Alliance F, Travail Suisse and Women of the Centre.
It is also supported by the Social Democrats and the Evangelical Party, among other organisations.
More
Having children is a luxury in Switzerland. Is the US next?
The initiative calls for adequate, paid parental leave for mothers and fathers following the birth of a child. Funding is to be provided through income replacement insurance. Should their constitutional proposal be approved, implementing legislation must be in place within five years. For the first ten years, the text calls for 18 weeks’ leave for both fathers and mothers, to be take in principle one after the other. A maximum of one quarter of this period may be taken together, and the leave will not be transferable between them.
The amount of the allowance would be based essentially on the rates provided for military and civilian service; but for those on lower wages, the text provides for an allowance equal to a full month’s salary. In autumn 2024, when presenting the proposal, Liberal Green politician Kathrin Bertschy, who is also the co-head of the women’s organisation Alliance F, calculated that payroll contributions would need to rise by 0.25 percentage points to 0.75%. A study by the Ecoplan research group has estimated the annual costs at around CHF1 billion ($1.2 billion).
Calls for paid parental leave has been on the table for years. Today, working mothers are entitled to 14 weeks’ maternity allowance. In 2020, Swiss voters also approved two weeks’ paternity leave, which came into force at the start of 2021. The initiative which sparked that vote initially called for four weeks’ paid paternity leave.

Ukraine's former defence minister Fedorov unveils new Army of Robots project: what is known
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
15:26:00 EEST
21:26:00 KST

Ukraine's former defence minister Fedorov unveils new Army of Robots project: what is known
Former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has announced a new defence project called Army of Robots. The concept involves developing humanoid robots capable of carrying out simple frontline tasks instead of soldiers. Fedorov presented the project on 26 September at the IT Arena 2026 conference in Lviv.
Source: Oboronka, a defence industry project created within Ukrainska Pravda's holding company
Details: The new project is a continuation of the Air. Land. Economy concept that Fedorov's team has been working on since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Quote: "There will be humanoid robots that will perform simple tasks: reloading a machine gun, replacing a battery or installing a sensor. These are things a robot can be taught quickly and carry out after a rapid deployment to the battlefield."
More details: Fedorov said the first goal of the Army of Robots project was for a humanoid robot to kill a Russian soldier within six months of the programme's launch. The project also aims to conduct its first operation involving robots and drones within the first 12 months, with the systems "communicating" through algorithms. Fedorov's team believes the project could change perceptions of what warfare will look like.
The project envisages creating a technological ecosystem to be developed by a "large private technology company", whose name will be announced later. The idea is for humanoid robots to operate autonomously alongside UAVs, unmanned ground vehicles and other classes of unmanned weapons.
Fedorov said the Army of Robots project is currently seeking engineers, teams and specialists in Ukraine and the West, as well as investment to develop robots capable of replacing Ukrainian infantry soldiers on the battlefield.
Project announcement. Video: Fedorov
In addition to this line of work, the Army of Robots project also envisages developing low-cost interceptor missiles and AI-based strike systems. Ukrainian and foreign defence companies specialising in software, weapons manufacturing and other technologies are being invited to take part in the project.
Background:
- In early September 2026, Fedorov announced plans to establish his own defence-tech company, with Alex Karp, CEO of US technology company Palantir, set to become its key investor.
- A venture fund is also being established in Kyiv to invest in defence companies and finance both startups and established manufacturers.

Ukraine’s rescue UGV gets better from soldiers, not AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:21:37 UTC
21:21:37 KST

- AIDronesUA's CEO said soldier feedback, not AI, has driven most improvements to the MAUL casualty evacuation UGV.
- The company plans to build 400 to 500 MAUL vehicles a year in Sweden with local partner NJORD Technology.
The biggest improvements to MAUL, a Ukrainian unmanned ground vehicle built to carry wounded soldiers off the front line, have come from the troops using it rather than from artificial intelligence, the head of the company behind it said.
An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a remotely controlled or partly autonomous vehicle that moves on land without a crew aboard. Ukrainian forces use UGVs to deliver ammunition and supplies, lay mines and evacuate casualties through areas where Russian drones make it too dangerous to send medics or crewed vehicles.
Kostyantyn Hushcha, chief executive of AIDronesUA, wrote that feedback from soldiers on real missions can move quickly from a conversation with engineers to a new fix, a prototype and another round of testing. Much of that work, he said, is far more basic than AI and deals with how the vehicle moves, how the casualty is secured and protected, how the onboard systems fit together, and how fast the vehicle can be repaired and sent back out.
“These details may look less impressive than a new AI feature, but they are what determine whether an evacuation can actually be completed,” said Kostyantyn Hushcha, CEO of AIDronesUA.
Hushcha said the company is still looking at where autonomy and AI could improve MAUL, adding that any new technology has to make the platform more reliable, safer for the wounded soldier and better at completing the evacuation.
MAUL is a four-wheel-drive UGV with a combustion engine, designed from the start for casualty evacuation. The wounded soldier lies inside an armored capsule, held in place by three straps, while an interior camera lets operators watch the patient during the trip. The vehicle is 2.3 m (7.5 feet) long, carries up to 200 kg (440 pounds) and runs on airless metal wheels meant to survive mines and rough ground, and Ukraine’s 1st Medical Battalion says it can reach 70 km/h (43 mph).
The 1st Medical Battalion developed the original design, and Ukrainian manufacturer DevDroid later bought a license to build it, selling each unit for about $19,000.
MAUL drew wide attention in November 2025, when the battalion used it to rescue a soldier who had spent 33 days wounded behind Russian lines with a tourniquet on his injured leg. During the six-hour mission, the vehicle drove over an anti-personnel mine that blew off a wheel and then took direct hits from a Russian drone on the way back, but its armor held and the soldier reached Ukrainian medics, who stabilized him before his limb was later amputated.
AIDronesUA is expanding production outside Ukraine. At the Eurosatory defense show in June, the company signed a memorandum with Sweden’s NJORD Technology to build MAUL in Sweden, targeting 400 to 500 vehicles a year for Ukraine’s armed forces. Earlier this month, Ukrainian combat medics took MAUL to Sweden for the first time to show the Swedish Life Guards how UGVs are used to recover casualties.

Eleven charged with murder aggravated by speech against ‘white race’ in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:16:48 UTC
21:16:48 KST

Eleven defendants will face trial in France after being accused of killing a 16-year-old in 2023 while engaging in speech “against the white race and the French nation,” according to a judicial order seen by POLITICO.
The death of Thomas Perotto in the village of Cr´epol quickly became a political flashpoint, with far-right figures like Eric Zemmour framing the incident as an example of the threat posed by immigrants.
President Emmanuel Macron called it a “terrible assassination,” while far-right leader Marine Le Pen described the attack as the work of an “armed militia.”
Advertisement
The killing later fueled far-right mobilization, including an attempted “punitive expedition” by identitarian militants in nearby Romans-sur-Isère.
French judges have sent 11 defendants to the juvenile assize court over the 2023 stabbing to death of 16-year-old Thomas Perotto, with the case involving a racial aggravating factor in the reference to “the white race and the French nation,” French media reported Friday.
The order sending them to trial, seen by POLITICO, accuses the defendants of murdering Perotto at a village fête in Crépol, attempting to kill three other people and violently attacking others. Judges seek to trial them as a group because the investigation hasn’t determined who is alleged to have delivered the fatal blow, AFP reported.
The judges’ order states the alleged killing was “preceded, accompanied or followed by words, writings, images, objects or acts of any kind” harming the honor of victims or a group because of their supposed race, ethnicity, nation or religion — “in this case, the white race and the French nation.”
Some defendants were minors when the attack took place. All are presumed innocent. The Valence prosecutor’s office had initially sought trial on murder and attempted murder charges without the aggravating factor, saying witness statements supporting it were “in the minority” and “imprecise.”
Denis Dreyfus, a lawyer representing a group of attendees claiming damages, told POLITICO that the charges matched arguments his side had made. “We welcome the considerable work carried out by the investigating judges,” he said, adding that the case should now proceed with “the dignity due to Thomas and the victims.”
The defense pushed back on the charges. “How can our client be sent to trial for murder aggravated by a racial circumstance when neither the fatal blow nor any racist remarks are personally attributed to him?” lawyers Seydi Ba and Diala Al-Shaman, who represent one of the defendants, said, according to AFP.
A trial date has not been set. Elise Rey-Jacquot, a lawyer representing another defendent, told RTL on Saturday she would appeal the charges, potentially delaying proceedings.

Russia’s air defenses can’t protect all its strategic sites once Ukraine’s ballistic missiles are ready, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
12:16:31 UTC
21:16:31 KST

Russia's best defenses against ballistic missiles ring Moscow, leaving much of the rest of the country exposed to Ukraine's growing missile arsenal. That concentration is why Ukraine's homegrown ballistic missiles could cause Russia real trouble beyond the capital, even as Russia's air defenses show gaps elsewhere, expert Vadym Kushnikov says, Ukrainian Radio reports.
Russia has the systems to stop ballistic missiles, Kushnikov continues, but it has massed the best of them around Moscow: the S-500 "Prometey", with interceptors adapted from the A-135, the Soviet-era shield built to defend the capital from missiles.
Other regions, by his assessment, are left more open to Ukraine's massed and combined strikes. That matters now that Ukraine's own ballistic missile, such as the Sapsan, is entering combat.
The best defenses ring Moscow
"If you analyze the characteristics, Russia today has concentrated its most modern S-500 complexes, with 77N6-N and 77N6-N1 interceptors, in Moscow Oblast," Kushnikov says.
Elsewhere, he said, Russia is short of air-defense complexes, the S-400 among them, a shortfall he said is visible in satellite imagery.
Ukraine's ballistic program grows
Ukraine's deep-strike arsenal has been shifting from foreign-supplied systems to homegrown ones. Alongside its Neptune and Flamingo cruise missiles, it now fields the Sapsan, an Iskander-class ballistic missile with a range of about 500 kilometers, which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed was in combat late last year.
A domestic ballistic missile will let Ukraine strike deep inside Russia without waiting for a Western green light.
Production faces hard hurdles
Building them is the hard part. Ukraine's rocket-engineering tradition runs deep, Kushnikov suggests, but its production sites, mostly in the east, are direct targets of Russian strikes.
The missiles also depend on components that are difficult to make, chiefly solid-fuel rocket engines and the guidance that steers a warhead flying at five times the speed of sound along a ballistic arc.
"The combination of all these factors is exactly what our engineers have worked on for years, building the Ukrainian ballistic shield," he adds.
