The story behind the first CIA officers in Afghanistan after 9/11
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
11:42:40 UTC
20:42:40 KST

The story behind the first CIA officers in Afghanistan after 9/11 and the Russian chopper that flew them in
Twenty-five years ago, a Soviet-designed helicopter crossed the mountains of Afghanistan carrying the first CIA officers sent into the country after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, marking the opening move in the U.S. response that would soon become America's longest war.
The seven-man CIA team, code-named JAWBREAKER, landed in the Panjshir Valley on Sept. 26, 2001, just 15 days after the attacks, carrying millions of dollars in cash intended to help enlist and equip Afghan allies. Their mission was to gather intelligence and prepare the ground for the looming U.S. campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban — including by shoring up ties with the Northern Alliance, whose military leader, Ahmad Shah Massoud, had been assassinated by al-Qaeda operatives just two days before 9/11.
The Mi-17 that carried them there is now on display at CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, where it has undergone an extensive restoration ahead of the anniversary.
Former CIA officer David Tyson followed JAWBREAKER into Afghanistan weeks later as a member of Team Alpha, and remembers flying aboard the same aircraft before the war.
"It was shaking a lot, fuel was leaking, very noisy, and I didn't know if it was airworthy," Tyson told CBS News in an interview, "but I was assured by the pilots it was a good bird."
A helicopter built to blend in
The CIA acquired the Mi-17 in the 1990s, calculating that its Soviet origins would be an advantage in the region.
"The Northern Alliance and the Taliban both used Mi-17s," CIA historian Rob Byer told CBS News. "They're Russian helicopters and kind of the pickup truck of helicopters in that region."
"The big reason we got an Mi-17 rather than flying in a Blackhawk is because it blends in," Byer said. "And when you're going behind enemy lines, you'd like to blend in as much as you can."
It could also handle the punishing altitude. To reach the Panjshir Valley, JAWBREAKER had to cross the Anjuman Pass, which rises roughly 14,500 feet above sea level.
"The Mi-17 is one of the few helicopters that can actually make it over that pass," Byer said.
The aircraft had no transponder to identify it to American warplanes, leaving its crew to improvise. They painted "USA" and an American flag across the tops of its stabilizers, visible to friendly pilots overhead but concealed from enemy eyes on the ground. With no blue paint available, the crew left the flag unfinished. And in a reminder of the attacks that had brought them there, they gave the helicopter the call sign "9-11-01."
The Mi-17 would go on to fly more than 300 missions in Afghanistan, remaining in service until 2012.
Team Alpha goes to war
Tyson was a CIA case officer based in Central Asia who was steeped in local languages, including Uzbek, Turkmen and Russian. On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on a flight to the United Kingdom for a meeting related to the CIA's efforts to recover Stinger missiles that had remained in Afghanistan, many of which were sent there in a U.S.-backed initiative during the Soviet war.
Soon after he landed, he began planning his return, realizing his expertise would likely take him to Afghanistan.
"I knew that I would be involved given my languages and experience and so forth and where I was based in Central Asia," Tyson recalled.
On Oct. 17, less than three weeks after JAWBREAKER arrived in the Panjshir Valley, Tyson and the rest of Team Alpha were inserted into a different part of northern Afghanistan, becoming the first Americans sent behind Taliban lines. Their mission was to work with forces commanded by Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum as part of the campaign against the Taliban and al-Qaeda.
"This was something we hadn't done before," Tyson said, describing a mission that involved working with local forces to "basically prosecute a war."
His principal role was intelligence and liaison work. He worked closely with Dostum's Uzbek-speaking forces, helping his team understand the people and environment around them. The Americans traveled with Afghan fighters on horseback through the mountains, sometimes riding as long as 14 hours a day.
"The horses were not friendly," Tyson recalled. "They were stallions, they fought between each other, they bit us, they kicked us, they tried to knock us off. And the gear, the kit, the saddles were basically wooden frames with carpets thrown on them."
By late November, Taliban forces had collapsed across much of northern Afghanistan. Hundreds of foreign fighters had surrendered and were taken to Qala-i-Jangi, a sprawling 19th-century fortress near Mazar-e-Sharif.
On Nov. 25, Tyson and fellow CIA officer Johnny Micheal "Mike" Spann entered Qala-i-Jangi, where their initial task was to determine who the prisoners were and where they came from.
"For the most part, they were responding and identifying themselves as al-Qaeda members, people who had given oath of allegiance to bin Laden," Tyson said. Among the prisoners was John Walker Lindh, a California native who moved to the region in 2000 and joined the Taliban.
Hours into their mission, the prisoners rose up.
"There were explosions, gunfire, and a lot of yelling," Tyson recalled. "I started seeing things in what I would call slow motion," he said. "Things were moving slowly, but almost automatically."
At a certain point he heard Spann call his name, and began moving toward his partner through the fighting.
"I remember seeing his … silhouette or body on the ground," Tyson said. "I believe Mike was already dead when I got to him and I was able to shoot the men on top of him and took Mike's rifle from him."
Spann, 32, became the first American killed in combat in Afghanistan. His was the 79th star carved into the CIA's Memorial Wall.
Tyson fought his way to safety with Spann's rifle, which he continued using for the rest of his deployment. It is now displayed in the CIA Museum, alongside the pair of boots Tyson wore throughout his deployment. Tyson's then-8-year-old son later dubbed them "Dad's lucky boots."
"That rifle saved my life, I think, among other things," Tyson said. "It's very fitting, I think, that that rifle's in the museum. Again, it reminds us of Mike and who he was."
Restoring a piece of CIA history
After its final operational mission in 2012, the Mi-17 was brought to CIA headquarters in 2018. Its fuel lines and other components were removed and it was installed outside amid rocks meant to resemble the Afghan landscape.
Years of exposure to the elements took a toll. "The paint had faded greatly due to the sun and a few critters were getting inside as well," Byer said.
Over the past year, the CIA sealed openings in the aircraft and repainted it to more closely resemble how it looked in 2001. The green was deliberately made slightly more vivid, Byer said, so exposure to the sun will eventually fade it to the intended shade.
The restoration also brought back "607," the call sign of the Afghan pilot who flew the first mission. Painted on both sides of the Mi-17 in 2001, the number helped it pass as a Northern Alliance aircraft while signaling to allied pilots that it was friendly.
For Tyson, the artifacts preserve a much more personal history.
"As Mike would say, he wanted to be on the tip of the spear," Tyson said. "He was that, and he is today. He will be that forever. And for me to be part of that was just something that obviously I won't forget."
Tyson said he still thinks about Spann and his sacrifice on "a daily basis."
"I'd like to think he helps guide me through things," he added.
Tyson and Spann's widow, Shannon Spann DeBruyn, are now among those involved with Badger Six, a nonprofit created in 2022 and named after Spann's call sign to assist the Afghan fighters who worked alongside Team Alpha, as well as their families. The organization says it currently supports about 35 families with assistance ranging from food and medicine to relocation and resettlement support.
For Tyson, that work is part of a mission that did not end when the United States withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021 as the Taliban reclaimed power, leaving some of the Afghan partners who had fought alongside Americans behind and vulnerable to Taliban reprisals. Asked whether he feels an obligation to help where governments have not, Tyson answered simply, "Sure, yeah. That's what people do. That's what we do."

UNDP-backed assessment prioritizes 30 sand and dust storm hotspots in Iran

UNDP-backed assessment prioritizes 30 sand and dust storm hotspots in Iran
TEHRAN – A national assessment supported by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) has identified and prioritized 30 critical domestic source areas for sand and dust storms (SDS) in Iran, providing an evidence base for targeted measures to reduce risks to communities, infrastructure and vulnerable ecosystems.
Sand and dust storms are an increasingly serious environmental and development challenge in Iran, affecting public health and livelihoods, damaging infrastructure and putting additional pressure on fragile ecosystems. More than 25 provinces are affected to varying degrees, highlighting the need to shift from responding to individual storms toward prevention, preparedness and long-term resilience.
Since 2023, UNDP has been working with Iran’s Department of Environment (DOE) and the National Secretariat for Policy Making and Coordination of Management for the Sand and Dust Storms Phenomenon to support this transition.
The national assessment combines data on SDS hazard intensity, ecological vulnerability and the exposure of populations and critical infrastructure. By bringing together environmental information with data on settlements, roads, railways and agricultural areas, the assessment identifies locations where vulnerable landscapes and exposed communities overlap.
The findings provide an evidence base for directing resources to areas where interventions can have the greatest impact, ranging from vegetation restoration and soil stabilization to wetland protection and measures to safeguard infrastructure and communities.
The assessment found that 20 percent of Iran’s territory falls within high- or very-high-risk SDS categories, underscoring the importance of targeted and preventive action.
“Sand and dust storms do not respect borders. Over the past three years, our partnership with UNDP has demonstrated what collective action can achieve, advancing mitigation and adaptation
measures across four provinces and strengthening resilience to their impacts,” said Dr. Behzad Raygani, secretary of the National Secretariat for Sand and Dust Storms.
At the same time, Iran is strengthening its capacity to anticipate and manage SDS events. With support from UNDP, forecasting and early-warning capabilities have been enhanced through fixed and portable monitoring systems. Technical work has also laid the foundation for a national and regional real-time SDS monitoring application.
The initiative extends from national systems to landscapes and local communities. Technical assessments in Khuzestan, Ilam, Yazd and Semnan have incorporated SDS considerations into biodiversity and landscape planning across approximately 47,000 hectares, linking SDS mitigation with ecosystem conservation and future investment decisions.
In Semnan’s Touran landscape, the integrated approach combines vegetation restoration, more efficient water use and improved grazing management with efforts to protect one of Iran’s most important biodiversity areas. SDS mitigation measures have also been implemented across 270 hectares of the Touran Protected Area, an important habitat for the endangered Asiatic cheetah.
Provincial capacity assessments in Ilam and Khuzestan have resulted in new action plans, clearer institutional responsibilities and stronger SDS working groups, helping translate national priorities into coordinated action at the local level.
These efforts form part of a broader national shift toward proactive SDS management, including plans to establish an online system for continuous monitoring of dust source areas and a decision-support system in Khuzestan.
The work comes as governments and international partners meet in Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia, from August 17 to 28, 2026, for the 17th Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD COP17). Held under the theme “Restoring Land. Restoring Hope.”, the conference is focusing global attention on land restoration, drought resilience and sustainable land management, with sand and dust storms also addressed through a dedicated high-level event.
Iran’s experience highlights the importance of connecting scientific evidence and risk information with practical action — from identifying areas facing the greatest risks and strengthening early-warning systems to restoring vulnerable ecosystems and engaging institutions and communities in mitigation efforts.
As countries at COP17 consider ways to accelerate action against land degradation and strengthen resilience, Iran’s experience underscores the importance of addressing sand and dust storms before they become airborne hazards.
UNDP, in partnership with national stakeholders and international partners, will continue to build on these efforts to strengthen resilience to SDS across Iran. Future areas of cooperation include drawing on local and indigenous knowledge to develop mitigation and adaptation measures, promoting innovative and multifunctional land-use solutions that combine land restoration, renewable energy and SDS management, and strengthening biodiversity conservation in landscapes increasingly exposed to sand and dust storms.
By bringing together science, local knowledge and nature-positive solutions, these efforts aim to reduce vulnerability, restore degraded landscapes and strengthen the resilience of communities and ecosystems.

Suicide bombing in Pakistan’s Dera Ismail Khan kills at least 12 people
Majority of those killed and wounded are security personnel, police say.
At least 12 people have been killed and 30 wounded in a suicide bombing at a roadside police checkpoint in northwestern Pakistan, police told Al Jazeera.
The attack took place on Saturday in the Dera Ismail Khan district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, local police said.

Police chief Safdar Baloch said most of those killed and wounded were security personnel and passersby. The injured include police officers, customs personnel and two civilians.
No group immediately claimed responsibility, but suspicion fell on the Pakistan Taliban, known by the acronym TTP, said Al Jazeera’s Osama bin Javaid, reporting from Pakistan.
The armed group and its affiliates have launched a number of recent attacks in the region.
The TTP is separate from but closely allied with the Afghan Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021.
The blast occurred near Aman Mela in the Darazinda area of the district, Rescue 1122 said in a statement.
Rescue teams from the Darazinda station reached the scene and began relief operations, providing medical assistance to the wounded and taking them to hospital, the service said.
Pakistan has seen an increase in armed attacks in recent years, many of them claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, or BLA, a separatist group mainly active in neighbouring Balochistan province.
Pakistani officials have repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and have demanded that Kabul prevents cross-border attacks into Pakistan.
The latest attack comes two days after fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan along their southwestern border killed at least 13 Afghan Taliban fighters, according to Pakistan’s government.
It is the latest escalation between the neighbouring countries, following Pakistani strikes on alleged militant hideouts inside Afghanistan this week.
The renewed hostilities threaten mediation efforts by China, Turkiye, Qatar and Saudi Arabia aimed at securing lasting peace between the two countries.

Russia, Ukraine trade deadly strikes as 7 people are killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
11:32:00 UTC
20:32:00 KST

Seven people were killed in Russian and Ukrainian strikes Saturday, including four in Ukraine and three in Russia's southern Krasnodar region, local officials said, as Moscow and Kyiv continued a surge in long-range drone and missile attacks.
Russia has intensified its aerial campaign against Ukraine, deploying cruise and ballistic missiles, glide bombs and jet-powered drones as fighting along the front line has slowed more than four years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
Two women were killed after a Russian strike destroyed a home in Zaporizhzhia, trapping them beneath the rubble, according to the regional military administration. A separate Russian attack on the city of Sumy killed two people, local officials said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Saturday that Russia was escalating its attacks and urged Kyiv's international partners to respond with stronger measures.
"It is essential that our partners not forget: Russia is escalating every single day," Zelenskyy wrote Saturday. "If the Russians have chosen to make their strikes even more brutal, the world must choose stronger responses to keep the war from spreading further."
Zelenskyy said residential areas in Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia, as well as parts of the Odesa, Sumy and Kharkiv regions, had come under attack.
Ukraine's Air Force said its air defenses shot down 134 of 173 Russian drones launched overnight. The claim could not be independently verified.
In Kyiv, officials reported damage across several districts after Russian drones struck overnight. A drone hit an area between a five-story residential building and a commercial property in the Solomianskyi district, damaging an office building, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people were injured and that emergency crews were carrying out search and rescue operations. Fires were also reported near warehouses in the Darnytskyi district and at a store after a drone fell inside a shopping center in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
Two people were injured in the wider Kyiv region after a Russian drone attack caused a fire at a warehouse in the Boryspil district, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
In Odesa region, Gov. Oleh Kiper described the overnight assault as a "massive" attack on civilian infrastructure. More than 10 private and apartment buildings were damaged, along with a hotel and restaurant complex and administrative buildings at a business facility, he said.
Russia's Defense Ministry said its strikes in Kyiv damaged a data center that it claimed supported mobile internet services and Starlink satellite communications used by Ukraine's armed forces. The claim could not be independently verified.
Moscow also said its forces struck a port facility, road bridge and logistics center in the Odesa region and a dry-cargo vessel in the Black Sea that it alleged was carrying military supplies.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has continued using long-range drones to target Russian oil and industrial infrastructure, seeking to disrupt revenue streams and supplies that support Moscow's war effort.
A Ukrainian drone attack in Russia's southern Krasnodar region killed three people and injured two others, regional officials said.
Gov. Veniamin Kondratyev said the attack damaged a residential building and sparked fires at two industrial facilities in the Seversky district.
The regional emergency headquarters later said the fires had been extinguished and that about 26,000 residents were without electricity.
Ukraine's General Staff said its forces had targeted the Ilsky oil refinery in the Seversky district. Russian officials did not confirm the facility had been hit, and the claim could not be independently verified.
In neighboring Rostov region, Gov. Yury Slyusar said five people were injured in overnight Ukrainian drone attacks, including a child. He said drones struck residential buildings in Taganrog and Azov and that air defenses had downed more than 30 drones over several parts of the region.
Falling drone debris damaged apartment buildings, private homes, industrial facilities, a school, a cultural center and vehicles in Azov, according to Slyusar.
Russia's Defense Ministry separately claimed that its air defenses had destroyed 645 Ukrainian drones over 13 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea. The figure could not be independently verified.
The latest attacks underscore the continuing expansion of the war's aerial dimension, with both sides increasingly relying on long-range drones to strike targets far from the front lines.
Ukraine has sought tougher sanctions against Moscow and restrictions on trade that it says could reduce Russia's ability to finance the war. Zelenskyy renewed that appeal after the latest strikes, calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to implement additional measures against Russia and urging European leaders to impose further sanctions.
Despite repeated diplomatic efforts, there has been no confirmed breakthrough toward ending the war. Both Moscow and Kyiv deny deliberately targeting civilians and say their attacks are directed at military targets or infrastructure connected to military operations.
Independent verification of battlefield and casualty claims remains difficult because of the ongoing fighting.

Two US Army battalions are due to deploy to Lithuania in late October as part of a regular troop rotation, including a heavy unit equipped with Abrams tanks and an engineering battalion, according to Lithuanian officials.
Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas said preparations and logistical arrangements for the deployment were under way, with around 1,000 US personnel expected to arrive. The troops are due to remain in Lithuania for nine months, maintaining a US presence broadly similar in size to previous rotations.
Kaunas said: “The preparation process and logistical arrangements are currently underway, and two battalions will arrive in Lithuania at the end of October.”
One of the formations will be a heavy battalion equipped with Abrams main battle tanks and other heavy weaponry. The second will be an engineering battalion, which Lithuania says will support work connected with the development of its military division, border protection and other defence projects.
The Lithuanian Ministry of National Defence confirmed the deployment, saying: “US troops are returning to Lithuania. A US heavy battalion with Abrams tanks and an engineer battalion will deploy to Lithuania.”
Kaunas discussed the rotation during a visit to the Pentagon, where he met US Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defence Elbridge Colby. The Lithuanian minister also raised the possibility of establishing a permanent US military base in Lithuania, although he said no decision had been taken.
American forces have operated in Lithuania through successive rotational deployments, with the forthcoming nine-month rotation continuing that model rather than representing a newly announced permanent stationing arrangement.
The Lithuanian defence ministry said the presence of the two battalions would contribute to the country’s defence and NATO forces on the Alliance’s eastern flank.

The global system is entering an age of technological entropy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
11:30:47 UTC
20:30:47 KST

The global system is entering an age of technological entropy
The “profound changes unseen in a century” often mentioned by Xi Jinping are no longer merely abstract concepts found in books; they represent the systemic collapse and restructuring currently experienced by the global system.
For centuries, the world operated under a singular order – dominated by the West, characterized by linear development and a hegemonic steady state – which established fixed power structures, rules of engagement, and development paradigms. As we enter the second quarter of the 21st century, this long-standing old order has reached a critical juncture marked by runaway entropy, the collapse of paradigms, and a civilizational transition.
This entropic shift of order is essentially a global transitional state where the rules of the old system fail, its structures loosen, and its momentum wanes, while a new system undergoes pluralistic growth and iterative restructuring without yet having fully crystallized. Unlike the traditional restructuring of global patterns seen in historical dynastic changes or great-power rivalries, the core transformation of this ‘once-in-a-century’ shift is driven by the convergence of three forces: the fundamental reshaping of technology, the shifting of geopolitical centers of gravity, and the escalation of strategic competition to higher dimensions. Together, these forces are driving a comprehensive, systemic iteration of global politics, military affairs, economics, public opinion, and governance.
Adopting a holistic perspective, this article systematically deconstructs the core characteristics, underlying operational logic, and certain future evolutionary trends of this global entropic shift. Moving beyond the interpretation of fragmented events, it identifies the fundamental laws and ultimate trajectory of the transformation of the global landscape in this new era.
I. Six core characteristics of the entropic shift of order: The disintegration of the old steady state and the normalization of global pluralistic disorder
Current global geopolitical conflicts, economic fluctuations, technological rivalries, and public opinion polarization are, in essence, concrete manifestations of this entropic shift in order. The steady-state equilibrium established by the traditional Western-centric order has completely disintegrated. The global landscape now exhibits four core characteristics: intensifying headwinds, accelerating fragmentation, the resonance of risks, and the generalization of strategic competition. Uncertainty, asymmetry, and cross-domain transmission have become the new normal of the global landscape.
First, geopolitical power has undergone complete decentralization, and the absolute advantages once held by traditional major powers have fully eroded.
The geopolitical logic that prevailed for a century – where victory was determined by sheer national scale, military force, or resource endowment – has become completely obsolete; technological democratization has emerged as the core variable reshaping regional landscapes.
In the core geopolitical regions of Eurasia and the Middle East, the large-scale deployment of artificial intelligence, autonomous weapons, and intelligent reconnaissance systems has drastically lowered the threshold for war and deterrence, effectively erasing the military ‘generation gap’ that once separated traditional major powers. Europe’s security landscape has moved beyond the US monopoly; France and Germany are pursuing strategic autonomy, while Russia is leveraging intelligent hardware to challenge Western military hegemony, leading to a stratification and fragmentation of regional power. The Middle East has completely shed the old order defined by resource dominance and control by major powers; small and medium-sized states – and even non-state actors like the Houthis – can now exert asymmetric influence and disrupt regional shipping and geopolitics using low-cost intelligent equipment, causing the absolute control once held by major powers to steadily crumble.
Geopolitical power is no longer tethered to territory, troop numbers, or resource volume; instead, it is anchored in technological computing power, intelligent warfare capabilities, and the pace of technological iteration. Global geopolitical rivalry has entered a new phase where small nations can act as counterweights and non-state actors can disrupt the status quo.
Second, strategic deterrence systems have become stratified and diffuse, shifting global security risks from great-power confrontation to a state of uncontrolled volatility across all domains.
The ‘balance of terror’ established by the rigid US-Soviet bipolar nuclear standoff during the Cold War has collapsed, marking a paradigm shift in the global nuclear landscape; nuclear weapons have evolved from an ultimate deterrent for total mutual restraint into leverage for controlling regional dynamics.
Nuclear deterrence is now clearly stratified: Top-tier nuclear powers maintain a strategic last-resort capability while avoiding direct hot wars; mid-tier nuclear states rely on limited arsenals for regional self-preservation; and non-nuclear states seek security under the umbrella of major powers. Nuclear rivalry has become instrumentalized and normalized, serving as a standard tool for major powers to draw red lines and signal strategic intent.
Meanwhile, nuclear risks have become widespread; while the likelihood of direct nuclear confrontation between major powers has declined, risks associated with proliferation, technology leaks, algorithmic miscalculation, and covert regional nuclear maneuvering are rising. Compounded by the deep integration of intelligent weaponry and nuclear technology, global security governance has shifted from a model of great-power checks and balances to a complex challenge of managing risks that are multidimensional, covert, and pervasive across all domains.
Third, the global development landscape is shifting from West to East, and the Western-centric system that has prevailed for five centuries is unraveling.
The most historic transformation in this round of upheaval is the holistic shift of the global geopolitical, economic, and civilizational center of gravity from the Atlantic to the Eurasian landmass and Asia as a whole, fundamentally overturning the underlying structure of Western global dominance that has persisted for five centuries.
Economically, the interconnected development of Asian blocs – including China, ASEAN, India, and the Middle East – is accelerating the formation of a pan-Eurasian economic cycle; the era of Western dominance over global supply chains, trade rules, and economic orders is drawing to a close, while the Global South is gaining a powerful voice in development discourse. Regarding security, the security landscapes of Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific are becoming deeply intertwined; the geopolitical value of the continental landmass is making a full comeback, while the reach and control of traditional maritime hegemony continue to wane.
In terms of civilization and governance, Asian concepts of diverse coexistence and mutually beneficial cooperation are countering the Western logic of zero-sum hegemony; the resurgence of diverse civilizations is breaking the Western monopoly on civilization, emerging multilateral mechanisms are gradually replacing traditional Western-led institutions, and the pluralistic nature of global governance is becoming increasingly distinct.
Fourth, the credibility of the hegemonic system has collapsed, and the Western-led global rules-based system has comprehensively failed.
Trump’s transactional ‘America First’ diplomacy served as the critical turning point that broke the back of American-style hegemony, definitively ending the era of absolute US unilateral global control. The foundations of US hegemony – built after World War II upon alliance systems, rule-setting dominance, and the provision of public goods – have been thoroughly dismantled; alliance credibility has been squandered, multilateral systems have eroded, and the globalized order has fractured, transforming the US from an order builder into an order destroyer.
Although the Biden administration briefly attempted remedial measures, these failed to restore US credibility. Global deficits in trust and institutional confidence regarding the US have become entrenched; unilateralism and protectionism run rampant, double standards in traditional international rules have become glaring, and global governance has fallen into a vacuum of entropic change – where old rules have failed but new ones have yet to be established.
Fifth, the dimension of state-level rivalry has undergone a comprehensive escalation, with the battle for perception and public opinion emerging as a core, invisible battlefield.
The proliferation of digital technology has fundamentally restructured the model of great-power competition, shifting the focus of rivalry from traditional physical confrontation to precision-targeted cognitive warfare. Technologies such as 5G, algorithmic recommendation, and big-data profiling have constructed an information ecosystem characterized by pervasive reach, the solidification of echo chambers, and emotional dominance.
Leveraging their long-standing monopoly on discourse, the US and the West continuously export polarizing narratives, manufacture bloc-based confrontations, and fracture social consensus in other nations. The digital era has dismantled the official barriers of traditional diplomacy; ordinary citizens and non-governmental entities have become pivotal nodes in the global strategic game, with public sentiment and perception directly influencing geopolitical dynamics and diplomatic decisions. Public opinion manipulation and the shaping of perceptions achieve the strategic goal of subduing the enemy without fighting, while cognitive polarization and public opinion divides have become major drivers of disorder in the global order.
Sixth, the key actors in the global economy and governance are undergoing a comprehensive transformation, completely shattering traditional monopolistic patterns.
In the economic sphere, the traditional globalization model – which prioritized efficiency above all – has become obsolete. Geopolitical conflicts, technological blockades, and investment barriers are forcing the global economy to shift toward a development logic that prioritizes resilience and regional self-containment; regional integration is replacing global integration as a core mechanism for hedging against risk, while emerging markets and the Global South have become key stabilizers of the global economy.
In the realm of governance, the effectiveness of traditional Western-dominated institutions – such as the UN, IMF, and World Bank – is steadily declining, whereas emerging multilateral platforms like the SCO, BRICS, and G20 are rising rapidly. Global conflict resolution models are shifting from Western-led coercive intervention to diverse, consultative, and cooperative governance. Simultaneously, the global influence of non-governmental forces and industry elites continues to grow, shifting the landscape of global governance actors from one dominated solely by sovereign states to a new pattern of coexistence among governments, international institutions, and non-governmental entities.
II. Four new operational logics of order reconstruction: A new-era strategic paradigm breaking free from Western conventions
The entropic shift in the global order signifies far more than mere turbulence; it represents a fundamental and disruptive transformation of the underlying logic governing global operations. Current global competition, cooperation, and conflict can no longer be explained by the outdated Western realist paradigms of hegemony through strength, zero-sum games, and victory through force.
A new operational logic – tailored to a multipolar, digital, and regionalized world – has taken shape, fundamentally rewriting the underlying rules governing the rise of major powers, regional development, and global governance.
First, the logic of core national power: A shift from dominance through sheer scale to victory through technology and resilience.
Traditional international competition was a contest of sheer scale – territorial size, military tonnage, and aggregate economic output – whereby major powers could leverage their massive size to establish hegemonic monopolies and exert unilateral dominance. In the current era of shifting order and entropy, however, the primary benchmarks for a nation’s core competitiveness have become technological computing power, the capacity for intelligent iteration, supply chain resilience, and the ability to withstand risks.
Intelligent weaponry is reshaping the military balance of power; digital technology governs the discourse on public opinion and perception; autonomous industrial chains hedge against the risks of geopolitical sanctions; and regional closed-loop economic systems buffer against global volatility. Small and medium-sized nations can achieve asymmetric checks and balances through breakthroughs in specific technologies. Conversely, without technological innovation and systemic resilience, a major power’s sheer size risks becoming an inefficient burden – a reality that fundamentally shatters the Western historical logic equating size with hegemony.
Secondly, the logic of great power rise: shifting from hegemonic succession to rule reshaping.
Centuries of Western historical narrative have entrenched a realist paradigm – that rising implies conflict, growing strength implies a bid for dominance, and hegemony inevitably changes hands. Indeed, all Western international relations theories are essentially distillations of the history of European colonial rivalry. Yet, the current restructuring of the global landscape has completely transcended the old trap of hegemonic cycles.
The rise of emerging powers – exemplified by China – eschews military expansion, the pursuit of hegemonic status, and bloc-based confrontation; instead, it achieves developmental breakthroughs through civilizational mutual learning, regional synergy, and mutually beneficial cooperation. At its peak, the Tang Dynasty accounted for 80% of Asia’s GDP, and Zheng He’s fleet was ten times the size of Columbus’; despite possessing such overwhelming strength, China never followed the Western path of colonial conquest or regional monopoly. This proves that strength does not equate to hegemony, nor does rising equate to conflict; an Eastern logic of symbiosis is replacing the Western logic of dominance-seeking, establishing a brand-new paradigm for the rise of great powers.
Thirdly, the logic of security and stability: shifting from external balancing to autonomous resilience.
Since the Cold War, global security has maintained a precarious equilibrium based on great-power standoffs, alliance entanglements, and the balancing of forces. Control over the security agenda rested in the hands of a few Western powers, leaving most nations with no choice but to attach themselves to the strong and passively seek to avoid risk. In this era of entropic shifts in the global order, security risks have become diffuse and unpredictable, and the stability provided by external checks and balances has completely collapsed; consequently, autonomy and controllability, diversified hedging strategies, and systemic resilience have become the core pillars of security.
Militarily, nations are building autonomous defense systems powered by intelligent technologies; economically, they are establishing regional closed-loop industrial chains to mitigate the risks of decoupling; financially, they are promoting local currency settlements to hedge against the weaponization of the US dollar; and in the realm of public opinion, they are constructing independent discourse systems to break cognitive monopolies. Nations are moving away from reliance on the protection of major powers, instead seizing the initiative in their own security and development by leveraging systemic resilience and regional cooperation.
Fourth, the logic of global governance is shifting from Western monopoly to pluralistic, shared governance.
Traditional global governance was a game dominated by a handful of Western developed nations – where rules were set, standards defined, and benefits monopolized by the West, leaving developing countries to merely accept and adapt passively. The entropic shift in the global order has shattered this monopoly; the collective rise of the Global South and the growing influence of emerging multilateral mechanisms have led to a comprehensive diversification of governance actors, rules, and philosophies.
The core of governance has shifted from the strong controlling the weak to equal consultation among diverse actors; rules have evolved from self-serving Western unilateral standards into win-win principles that prioritize fairness and broad-based benefits; and the logic of development has moved beyond zero-sum plunder toward inclusive coexistence and mutual learning, marking the true entry of global governance into a new era of multilateralism.
III. Future trajectory of global order entropy change: Multipolar consolidation, resilient symbiosis, and the restoration of civilizational roles
While the current entropy change in the global order appears chaotic and fraught with risk, it is by no means random turbulence or internal attrition; rather, it represents the inevitable growing pains accompanying the demise of the old order and the birth of the new. By grounding our analysis in the fundamental logic of this transformation, we can clearly foresee the major trends of global evolution over the coming decades. Three certain trends will dominate the global landscape during the second quarter of the 21st century, effectively ending the old era of Western-centric hegemony.
First, the global landscape will shift decisively from unipolar volatility to a multipolar steady state, with hegemonic influence undergoing a continuous and irreversible decline.
The era of absolute US hegemony has definitively ended. While American hegemony will not collapse overnight, it will continue to contract and decline in relative terms, shifting from a position of global dominance to that of a regional player. The global balance of power will continue to equalize; Asia’s status as a geopolitical center will be further consolidated, and the integration of the Eurasian landmass will steadily advance.
Deep interconnectedness among Asian blocs – including China, ASEAN, India, and the Middle East – will forge a cluster of emerging powers capable of acting as a counterweight to the Western system. Old models of bloc confrontation and zero-sum games will gradually fade, giving way to a mainstream global political landscape defined by great-power competition and cooperation, diversified checks and balances, and regional autonomy. Multipolarity will evolve from a mere trend into a solidified, stable global order.
Second, global development will shift decisively from efficiency-first to resilience-first, leading to the full formation of regional symbiotic systems.
Globalization will not disappear, but it will undergo a fundamental transformation and upgrade. The old model of globalization – characterized by extensive growth, homogenization, and Western dominance – is ending, while a new model defined by precision, regionalization, and diversification is rising. Nations will continue to diversify, localize, and autonomize their industrial and supply chains, prioritizing security and stability.
Regional economic synergy and closed-loop systems will serve as the core pillars for hedging against geopolitical conflicts, trade protectionism, and technological blockades. Emerging regional mechanisms – such as RCEP, SCO economic cooperation, and BRICS cooperation – will continue to enhance quality and efficiency, building regional development systems that are mutually beneficial and independent of the West. The global economy will break free from the constraints of singular Western rules, establishing a new development landscape characterized by diverse, parallel paths and resilient symbiosis.
Third, global competition is shifting profoundly from physical confrontation to a contest of rules and civilizations, marking a comprehensive resurgence of Eastern civilizational values.
The core of future great-power competition will no longer lie in military might, territorial disputes, or resource plundering, but in the ultimate contest over technological standards, governance norms, civilizational paradigms, and cognitive narratives. The flaws of the Western civilizational logic – characterized by zero-sum games, hegemony, and confrontation – have become glaringly apparent, rendering it ill-suited to the development needs of a diverse world.
In contrast, the Asia-Pacific region’s enduring civilizational ethos – rooted in mutual learning, symbiosis, harmony amid diversity, and win-win cooperation – will serve as the core foundation for reshaping the global civilizational order. From the millennia-old legacies of Xuanzang’s translation work, Yang Liangyao’s diplomatic voyages, and Zheng He’s friendly expeditions, to the vibrant contemporary practices of mutual learning and people-to-people connectivity across the Asia-Pacific, this Eastern civilization of symbiosis will continue to counter Western narratives of conflict and rewrite the fundamental rules of global civilizational competition.
Fourth, global governance is transitioning from elite monopoly to broad-based participation, with fairness and inclusivity becoming the prevailing trends of the era.
Future global governance will thoroughly dismantle the monopoly held by a handful of Western nations and elites; the Global South will see a sustained rise in its voice and influence, emerging multilateral mechanisms will become the primary vehicles for governance, and the participation of non-governmental actors and civil society will deepen.
Global public issues – such as nuclear arms control, artificial intelligence, climate governance, and public health – will break free from the constraints of geopolitical maneuvering and bloc-based confrontation, returning to the essence of multilateral consultation and win-win cooperation. Global governance will cease to be a tool for the powerful and instead become a platform for the shared development of all humanity, with fairness, inclusivity, and mutual benefit defining the new era of global governance.
Embracing the right path of Eastern symbiosis amid order reconstruction
Viewed from a macro perspective, the essence of this once-in-a-century transformation is a process – spanning centuries – of correcting the order, restoring the civilizational balance, and reshaping the global landscape. The entropic shift in the global order represents both the entropic decay and demise of the old Western hegemonic order and the entropic reduction and rebirth of a new, diverse global order.
All geopolitical conflicts, technological rivalries, economic fluctuations, and public opinion rifts are the inevitable growing pains accompanying the transition from the old order to the new. Centuries of Western history have taught the world only about hegemonic rivalry among the strong, whereas the Asia-Pacific region – with its millennia-old cultural heritage and the practical experience of emerging powers in the new era – is teaching the world how the strong can build bridges.
Future global competition is by no means a zero-sum game of hegemonic succession; rather, it is a contest of values regarding paths, civilizations, and rules. The old era defined by unilateralism, bloc confrontation, and zero-sum games has come to an end, while a new era characterized by multilateralism, openness, inclusiveness, and mutually beneficial symbiosis is rapidly unfolding.
Standing at the historical juncture of the second quarter of the 21st century, humanity will ultimately break free from the confines of the Western-dominated order and the traps of realist power struggles. By solidifying the foundations of development through technological innovation, fostering symbiotic strength through regional synergy, and resolving differences through mutual learning among civilizations, we will build a new global order that is fairer, more stable, more resilient, and more prosperous – thereby ushering in a new stage of civilization defined by diverse coexistence and sustainable development.

Kharge also questioned whether the controversy was being reduced to the role of CEC Gyanesh Kumar while overlooking wider questions about the functioning of institutions.
NEW DELHI: Priyank Kharge on Thursday hit out at the BJP for defending the Election Commission after the Form 6 row. He said that the ruling party should allow the poll panel to answer questions over alleged differences among its members on electoral-roll decisions.The Karnataka minister's remarks came after a report by The Indian Express claimed that election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months to decisions and orders linked to electoral-roll procedures and the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.
“Why is the BJP so desperate to defend the Election Commission instead of allowing the Election Commission to defend itself? If there is nothing to hide, let the Election Commission face the questions directly. BJP leaders should stop acting as its unofficial spokespersons. Let the Commission come before the country, answer every question, disclose every fact and clear every doubt,” Kharge wrote on X.
'Gyanesh Kumar is only the pawn'
Kharge also questioned whether the controversy was being reduced to the role of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar while overlooking wider questions about the functioning of institutions.“Looks like the Modi Sarkar is preparing to sacrifice Gyanesh Kumar at the altar.
But don’t be fooled. Gyanesh Kumar is only the pawn,” he wrote.He further questioned the legal protections available to top election officials and the way power is distributed within the poll body.
“The bigger question is: who designed the system, who concentrated the power and who ensured that the Chief election commissioner received legal protection from civil or criminal proceedings for acts done in the discharge of their “official duties”?”Kharge alleged that accountability should not be limited to individual officials.“Accountability cannot stop with the pawn. The two most powerful people at the top have systematically weakened democratic institutions to cling to power and shield a system of corruption and cronyism,” he said.
Former EC raises questions over decision-making
The controversy has also drawn comments from former election commissioner Om Prakash Rawat, who said decisions of the three-member Election Commission have to be taken through consensus or a majority vote.“That is the Election Commission's system, where all three commissioners give suggestions and contribute their views on how things should be done. That is standard procedure. However, when a decision is made, it must be by consensus or by a majority vote,” Rawat said.“If two Commissioners are on one side, that forms the majority. Their objection is that while they expressed a different view, Gyanesh Kumar proceeded independently. That is the issue,” he added.Rawat, however, ruled out the possibility of cancelling elections that have already been completed.“No one can cancel an election once completed. What is done is done,” he remarked.On calls for Kumar's resignation, Rawat said a formal process would first have to be initiated.“Someone has to initiate formal proceedings. If someone moves, then the subsequent steps will be seen,” he said.
Row over Form 6
Rawat also raised questions about changes to Form 6, which is used for voter registration. He said the Election Commission could not amend statutory requirements without the required approval.He explained that Form 6 has different requirements depending on the applicant's circumstances. According to him, additional details may be sought from an older person who claims to be registering for the first time.“But what the Election Commission did this time is apply the second type of form to everyone. Even if someone is 18 years old, they are now required to provide details about where their parents were and what they did. This has led to controversy, as it effectively amounts to an amendment to Form 6. The Election Commission has amended it, even though the Election Commission has no authority to amend any form. That authority rests solely with the President,” he said.
The Election Commission, however, has said that all its decisions, including those related to the SIR exercise, were taken unanimously with the approval of both Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.Meanwhile, the Congress Working Committee is scheduled to meet in New Delhi on September 29. According to sources, the meeting is expected to discuss the Election Commission controversy, the SIR exercise and the wider political situation.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
11:25:01 UTC

Russia and Ukraine have traded accusations concerning overnight airstrikes that killed five people and injured over 20 others.
“Five people were injured in a hostile overnight drone attack. Casualties include one person in Taganrog and four in Azov — among them a child — following the impact of drones on residential buildings,” said Yury Slyusar, governor of Russia’s southern Rostov region, on Telegram on Saturday.
Slyusar said all of those injured had been hospitalised. He claimed that more than 30 drones were downed by air defences over multiple cities in the region, including the city of Rostov-on-Don, as well as over the Azovsky, Myasnikovsky and Neklinovsky districts.
In the city of Azov, falling drones damaged apartment buildings, private homes, industrial facilities, a school, a cultural center and vehicles, Slyusar stated.
Veniamin Kondratyev, governor of the neighboring Krasnodar region, said a drone attack in Seversky district damaged a residential building and caused fires at two industrial facilities in the area.
The operational headquarters of the Krasnodar region later reported that three people were killed and two others injured in the region, adding that the fires at industrial facilities have been extinguished and that about 26,000 residents are currently without electricity.
Ukraine's General Staff claimed that it launched an overnight attack on the Ilsky oil refinery, situated in the Seversky district.
The Russian Defence Ministry claimed it downed 645 Ukrainian drones over 13 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
The ministry further claimed that overnight Russian strikes in Ukraine hit a data centre that “facilitated mobile internet operations and supported Starlink satellite communication systems for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the capital Kiev.
It also claimed hitting a port facility, a road bridge, and a logistics centre in Ukraine’s southern Odesa region, as well as a dry-cargo vessel “transporting military supplies” in the Black Sea.
Strikes in Ukraine
In the Ukrainian capital, the Kiev City Military Administration said a drone struck between a five-story residential building and a commercial establishment in the city’s Solomianskyi district, where an office building was also damaged.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said five people had been injured, adding that search and rescue efforts in the area were ongoing.
He later said a fire broke out near warehouse buildings in the Darnytskyi district, while another fire occurred at a store after a drone fell on the territory of a shopping centre in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
In the broader Kiev region, two people were injured in the Boryspil district, where a fire broke out in a warehouse building, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
Meanwhile, Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper said a “massive” attack took place on the region’s civilian infrastructure, damaging the facades and windows of more than 10 private homes and apartment buildings, a hotel and restaurant complex, and administrative buildings at a business facility in the southern part of the region.
Elsewhere, in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, two people were killed and seven others injured in the regional capital, according to local authorities.
"We ask (US) President (Donald) Trump to implement the Lindsey Graham Act against Russia and everyone who props up its war financially," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X, commenting on the overnight strikes. He further called on European leaders to impose additional sanctions on Moscow.
Ukraine’s Air Force claimed that the country’s air defences shot down 134 of 173 drones launched by Russia overnight.
Independent verification of the claims is difficult due to the ongoing war.
Moscow and Kiev have ramped up strikes in recent months, targeting each other’s logistics centres, ports and energy infrastructure.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining the strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Feature: Pinglu Canal brings Chinese market closer to Vietnam's Mekong Delta
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:22:48 CST
20:22:48 KST

CAN THO, Vietnam, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- In a light drizzle at Can Tho Port in southern Vietnam, cranes unloaded containers from the first foreign trade vessel to sail through China's newly opened Pinglu Canal.
The vessel's arrival marked the maiden voyage of a direct river-sea container route linking Nanning Port in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region with Can Tho in Vietnam's Mekong Delta.
The container vessel departed from Nanning Port on Sept. 16, sailed through the Pinglu Canal and arrived at Can Tho Port on Wednesday.
It carried 252 twenty-foot equivalent units of cargo, including wood panels, sodium sulfate and auto parts, mainly from western China.
The 134.2-km canal, stretching from Hengzhou in Guangxi to the Beibu Gulf, opened on Sept. 16. It is the closest maritime outlet for much of southwest China.
Designed for vessels of up to 5,000 tonnes, the canal shortens the inland waterway journey for goods from southwest China to the sea by more than 560 km compared with traditional routes through ports in Guangdong Province.
The return cargo includes 40 containers carrying about 1,000 tonnes of rice bran from southern Vietnam to customers in inland Guangxi.
"The advantages lie in two areas: delivery time and significantly lower freight costs," said Hua Xuechun, general manager of Mekong Delta Rice Bran Co., Ltd.
Hua said rice bran and other agricultural products are sensitive to transport time, and shorter journeys help maintain product quality and accelerate cargo turnover.
Vietnamese goods bound for southwest China previously had to be transshipped at several ports, while the new route allows them to travel from Can Tho to inland Guangxi with fewer transfers, he said.
Hua estimated that the route could cut transport costs by 20 to 30 percent compared with traditional arrangements.
"This is the first time I have seen a vessel from an inland Chinese port arrive at Can Tho Port," said Hoang Xuan Nam, deputy head of the marketing and business department of Can Tho Port Joint Stock Company.
Nam, who has worked at the port for about 12 years, said the route had long been anticipated by people in Can Tho and across the Mekong Delta.
The Mekong Delta is one of Vietnam's main production areas for rice, aquatic products and fruit, while Can Tho is connected with surrounding farming areas by an extensive network of waterways.
Nam said agricultural products could be carried by barge from production areas to Can Tho Port for containerization, storage and cold-chain handling before being shipped to China.
The service could reduce road transportation and repeated cargo handling, helping exporters save time and keep agricultural products in better condition, he said.
Le Cong Ly, vice chairman of the Can Tho municipal People's Committee, said the Pinglu Canal provides a more direct maritime outlet for Guangxi's inland waterway network, while the Nanning-Can Tho route extends that connection to the Mekong Delta.
The route gives businesses more options for moving goods between southwest China and southern Vietnam, he said.
Le Quang Trung, vice president of Vietnam Maritime Corporation, said Vietnamese goods destined for inland Chinese markets previously had to be transshipped through coastal ports, adding to transport time and logistics costs.
He said the new connection could help agricultural products from the Mekong Delta reach the Chinese market more efficiently and strengthen the region's links with neighboring markets through the Mekong River system. ■

China, U.S. reach consensus on eight outcomes in Xi's visit
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:22:42 CST
20:22:42 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and his U.S. counterpart, Donald Trump, have reached a consensus on eight outcomes, according to a release made public after Xi wrapped up his U.S. visit on Friday.
The two leaders have agreed to build a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity, said the release.
They also agreed to support each other as China will host the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in November and the United States will host the G20 Leaders' Summit in December, expressing intention that they will attend each other's event.
On Iran, Xi and Trump have agreed that Tehran should fulfill its commitment not to develop nuclear weapons. No country or institution shall charge transit fees for passage through international waterways, they said.
Xi paid a state visit to the United States from Wednesday to Friday, during which he had an in-depth exchange of views with Trump on bilateral relations as well as major international and regional issues.
The release noted that the two leaders recalled that China and the United States were allies during World War II, and fought side by side to win the war.
Ahead of Xi's state visit, Chinese and U.S. economic and trade teams concluded their latest round of consultation in New York.
The two leaders acknowledged the positive role of the China-U.S. economic and trade consultation mechanism, and recognized the outcomes achieved by their respective economic and trade teams, namely the establishment and advancement of such mechanisms as a trade council, a 30-billion-U.S.-dollar reciprocal tariff reduction arrangement, and an extension of what have been achieved in the Kuala Lumpur consultation.
They instructed that those outcomes be implemented.
On bilateral counternarcotics law enforcement cooperation, Xi and Trump commended the tangible results. The release said recently, the two sides have worked closely to jointly crack multiple cases involving new psychoactive substances and precursor chemicals, and arrest dozens of suspects in both countries.
As to artificial intelligence (AI), they agreed to establish China-U.S. AI dialogue to exchange views on AI-related risks and benefits, with the next round to be held in November. A communication channel for AI-related incidents will also be set up.
The U.S. side welcomes the upcoming arrival of two giant pandas leased by China to Zoo Atlanta, according to the release.
In addition to the eight outcomes, the Chinese and U.S. militaries agreed to sign a memorandum of understanding as soon as possible on strengthening crisis communication and prevention.
The two militaries will continue cooperation on searching for the remains of U.S. soldiers in China, said the release. ■

Feature: Kenyan avocados ride Chinese-built rails to a tariff-free market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:22:41 CST
20:22:41 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- In the expansive packhouse of Vertical Agro Group, on the outskirts of Kenya's resort town of Naivasha, dozens of workers in protective gear on Thursday meticulously sorted a variety of fresh vegetables for brief storage in cold rooms and later onward shipment to overseas markets.
The packhouse is domiciled within an export processing zone directly linked to the Naivasha Inland Container Depot (ICD), a Chinese-built dry port for handling bulk cargo that is part of the logistical artery for the Mombasa-Nairobi-Naivasha Standard Gauge Railway (SGR).
Amid a beehive of activity at the packhouse, Hasit Shah, chief executive officer of Vertical Agro Group, led a group of senior government officials, foreign diplomats, industry executives and scholars, who were on a mission to learn how China's zero-tariff policy and infrastructure modernization have unlocked new markets for fresh produce companies in Kenya.
In August 2022, following the phytosanitary protocol agreed between Kenya and China, Sunripe, which is part of Vertical Agro Group, became one of the first Kenyan companies to ship fresh avocados to the Chinese market, Shah told guests.
"China is the newest and the fastest-growing of the five overseas markets, namely the United Kingdom, Europe, the Middle East, Asia and the United States," he said.
For six decades, Vertical Agro Group has operated two packhouses in Naivasha, sourcing fresh produce such as avocados, broccoli, French beans and spinach from nearby contracted farmers, Shah said.
The produce is picked, sorted, stored in cold rooms, packed to clients' specifications and transported to the dry port, where SGR wagons cover nearly 600 kilometers to deliver it to the port of Mombasa for onward shipment abroad, he noted.
A modern railway corridor has been a game changer for players in the fruit and vegetable value chains, reducing transit time, freight costs, emissions and the risk of damage to the produce, Shah said.
He hailed the Naivasha dry port, which measures 45,000 square meters with capacity to handle 2 million tonnes of cargo annually and serves Uganda, South Sudan, Rwanda, Burundi and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, for easing the transportation of fresh produce.
The planned extension of the SGR from Naivasha to Kisumu and on to Malaba, on the Ugandan border, will enable Kenyan horticulture firms to penetrate the regional market, Shah said.
When China's zero-tariff policy, covering 53 African countries, came into force on May 1, Shah was among the Kenyan avocado exporters who welcomed the move, saying it will encourage local firms to add value to the highly nutritious fruit.
Kenya is the third-largest avocado supplier to China after Peru and Chile. In 2025, the country earned 175 million U.S. dollars from total avocado exports, with exports to China valued at 6.6 million dollars, said Paul Kipronoh Ronoh, principal secretary in the State Department for Agriculture.
"Other products having great potential for exports to China under the zero-tariff policy include flowers and macadamia nuts," Ronoh said at a seminar on jointly advancing China's proposed global development and governance initiatives, held after the tour of the Vertical Agro Group packhouses.
Ronoh noted that Naivasha is one of Kenya's major horticulture farming hubs, with local exporters using both the SGR and the inland depot seamlessly, translating into lower logistical costs, enhanced market connectivity and a reduced carbon footprint.
Guo Haiyan, Chinese ambassador to Kenya, said the Mombasa-Nairobi-Naivasha SGR, a flagship project under the Belt and Road Initiative, has unlocked growth in the rural hinterland through enhanced connectivity.
Guo said China's zero-tariff policy has expanded the market in China for Kenyan avocados, Ugandan coffee, Rwandan chilli and Congolese poria.
Official statistics indicate that China imported 3,762,776 kilograms of avocados from Kenya worth 43,157,326 yuan (about 6.1 million dollars) in May-August 2026, up 63.22 percent year on year in value, compared with a 59.65 percent increase in the same period of 2025.
For roasted coffee, China imported 1,707,818 kilograms from Kenya worth 98,314,108 yuan (about 13.8 million dollars) over the four months, up 139.66 percent year on year, against a 97.33 percent rise a year earlier.
Philip Mainga, managing director of Kenya Railways Corporation, said Chinese-built transport and logistics infrastructure, including the SGR and the Naivasha dry port, has encouraged investors to set up agro-processing factories to add value to fresh produce destined for overseas markets.
"Because of the SGR and inland container depot, investors have set up export processing zones to add value to farm produce, boosting our export competitiveness, growth and regional integration," Mainga said. ■

China's modernization achievements to offer fresh opportunities for world development: VP
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:22:36 CST
20:22:36 KST

Chinese Vice President Han Zheng meets with United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Sept. 25, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Ling)
UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 25 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice President Han Zheng said on Friday that China will offer fresh opportunities for world development with new achievements of Chinese modernization.
Han made the remarks while meeting with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Han said that the current international situation is fraught with turmoil and the international system with the United Nations at its core is facing multiple challenges.
This year marks the 55th anniversary of the restoration of the lawful seat of the People's Republic of China at the UN. Over the past 55 years, China has always adhered to true multilateralism and supported the UN in playing a central role in international affairs, Han said.
Looking to the future, China will continue to play its role as a responsible major country and actively promote the alignment of its own concepts with the UN agenda, Han said.
Upholding multilateralism and improving the global governance system are the common calls of the international community, Han said, noting that the vast majority of member states, especially developing countries, have always had high expectations for the United Nations.
China stands ready to work with the United Nations to pool global efforts for sustainable development and advance the implementation of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
China will also support the United Nations in continuing to mobilize the international community to address major challenges such as climate change, actively advancing global governance in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, and will continue to support the Security Council in fulfilling its primary responsibility for maintaining world peace and security.
For his part, Guterres expressed gratitude to China for its long-term firm and strong support for the cause of the United Nations, saying that cooperation between the two sides has now reached a new level.
The world today is facing serious challenges, while multilateralism is encountering headwinds, Guterres said.
China has always been actively committed to promoting international cooperation, addressing common challenges, and upholding fairness and justice, playing a key role in advancing important UN agendas and making significant contributions to global development, he said.
Guterres said the United Nations stands ready to further deepen cooperation with China in an all-round way, reform and improve global governance, promote the building of a multi-polar world, and safeguard the common interests of the international community. ■

How Xi looks to history and culture to deepen China-U.S. understanding
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
19:22:25 CST
20:22:25 KST

WASHINGTON, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, visited the U.S. National Archives in Washington on Friday, accompanied by U.S. President Donald Trump and his wife, Melania Trump, before departing for Beijing after a three-day state visit.
Established in 1934, the National Archives houses the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution and the Bill of Rights -- three documents central to the founding of the United States and essential to understanding its history over more than two centuries.
At the final stop of his U.S. trip, Xi said the archives carry the wisdom of the forebears and offer insights for the future. Over the past 250 years, the American people have pursued the American Dream and built a prosperous country and a beautiful home on the North American continent.
The Chinese people, inheriting 5,000 years of Chinese civilization, have continued to make new achievements on the new journey toward realizing the Chinese Dream of the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, Xi said.
As two distinctive countries, China and the United States have different histories and cultures, social systems and development paths, Xi said.
However, the people of the two countries share the same aspiration for a better life despite the differences, he said.
A day earlier, Peng and Melania also visited the National Museum of Asian Art in Washington, a renowned U.S. institution dedicated to the collection, research and exhibition of Asian art.
The tour to the National Archives and the art museum echoed the special arrangements China made for Trump during his previous trips to Beijing. During the U.S. president's state visit to China in May, Xi invited him to see the Temple of Heaven, a more than 600-year-old landmark near the southern end of the Beijing Central Axis.
Standing inside the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests, the iconic centerpiece of the temple, Xi explained to Trump that in ancient times, state rituals were held in the temple, where then Chinese rulers prayed for national prosperity, social harmony and favorable weather for good harvests.
Describing the Temple of Heaven as "great" and "incredible," Trump said the two countries should deepen mutual understanding and strengthen friendship between their peoples.
During Trump's first state visit to China in 2017, Xi accompanied him on a tour of the Forbidden City, or the Palace Museum, another historic landmark along the axis.
Inside the ancient royal palace, Xi briefed Trump on its history, architecture and culture as they toured the three main halls, each bearing the Chinese character "He," meaning peace and reflecting the Chinese people's longstanding aspiration for peace and harmony.
Such interactions reflect Xi's longstanding commitment to promoting exchanges and mutual learning among different cultures.
"For any country in the world, the past always holds the key to the present and the present is always rooted in the past. Only when we know where a country has come from, could we possibly understand why the country is what it is today, and only then could we realize in which direction it is heading," Xi once said.
Xi has noted on many occasions that both China and the United States are great countries, and both the Chinese and American peoples are great peoples. While the two countries differ in histories and cultures, social systems and development paths, he believes that those "differences should not become an obstacle to growing China-U.S. relations."
For Xi, understanding these differences can create more space for dialogue and coexistence between countries, pointing the way toward avoiding the so-called Thucydides Trap and sustaining the steady development of the world's most consequential bilateral relationship.
At the state dinner held by Trump in the White House on Thursday, Xi recounted the history of China-U.S. exchanges that stretches back more than 200 years, including their joint fight against Japanese aggression in World War II, and Ping-Pong diplomacy.
"Exchanges have helped promote heart-to-heart communication between our peoples and cemented public support for China-U.S. friendship and cooperation," he said.
During his just-concluded visit to Washington, Xi announced a series of new initiatives to further boost people-to-people bonds between the two countries, including an invitation for 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchanges and study in the coming five years.
Just as Xi has said, if the two countries recognize and respect their differences, deepen mutual understanding and learn from each other, seek the biggest common denominator, expand the list of areas for cooperation, and properly manage differences, China-U.S. relations will enjoy steady and sustained growth. ■

Zelenskyy imposes sanctions on 44 individuals involved in sham elections in temporarily occupied territories
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has brought into force sanctions against 44 individuals involved in holding sham elections to the State Duma (lower house of the Russian parliament) in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories.
Source: president of Ukraine's website
Details: This concerns individuals acting in Russia's interests and facilitating the occupation of territories in Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, as well as Crimea and Sevastopol.
Those sanctioned include Russian propagandist Irina Kuksenkova and former Ukrainian MP Yurii Onyshchuk, who began collaborating with the Russians after the occupation of Melitopol.
Some individuals on the list have previously already been "elected" as members of local councils established by the Kremlin-appointed occupation authorities.
The President's Office stressed that the so-called "elections" held by Russia in occupied Ukrainian territories are illegal, and their results carry no legal force.
Information on the sanctioned individuals is planned to be shared with international partners so they can introduce similar restrictions within their own jurisdictions.
Background: Russia held sham elections to the lower house of its parliament, the State Duma, in the temporarily occupied part of Kherson Oblast with the help of themed polling stations styled after different periods of history – from the Russian Empire to the post-war USSR.

HUANGSHAN, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Eating rice cakes during the Mid-Autumn Festival is a traditional custom dating back to ancient Huizhou, which included Huangshan and neighboring areas, as the word "cake" sounds like "high" in Chinese, symbolizing promotion and steady progress.
