====================================================================================================

China Focus: Zooming in on WorldSkills -- How China is reshaping skills in an age of AI, automation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:29:13 CST
18:29:13 KST

SHANGHAI, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- In the foyer of the WorldSkills Conference in Shanghai in east China, several overseas participants gathered around a robot, curious to see how it would handle an unusual request, namely marriage advice.
When a male participant asked what to do if his wife talked too much, the robot suggested a "three-second rule" before responding. The exchange drew laughter, with one participant joking that it could make a decent marriage counselor.
This light-hearted exchange touched on a broader question being discussed at this year's WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai: which skills are difficult for AI to replace, and what new capabilities will people need in an age of AI?
WHAT AI CAN'T REPLACE
At the digital interactive media design venue, contestants move from product planning to image processing, video production and interaction design during more than 20 hours of competition.
Notably, even as AI begins to take over some basic work in the industry, the training remains highly demanding. Zhou Jiaxiang, a member of China's national training squad, described a six-hour video-production module in which contestants may have to adjust dozens or even hundreds of parameters, fine-tune transitions frame by frame and repeatedly render the footage.
AI can generate some visual effects within seconds, Zhou said, but the output is often not ready for delivery. Text, a character's gaze, fingers or facial movements may still contain visible flaws, requiring professionals to identify the problem, give precise instructions for revision, and further process the results with conventional software.
A professional designer, as Kuang Ying, a professor at East China Normal University's Faculty of Education, put it, can "train AI like a doctoral student," using expertise and judgment to push it toward better results. She said the judgment and aesthetic sense of highly skilled designers remain difficult to replicate.
The same question extends beyond creative work. At the retail competition, contestants first build up a store setting, arranging merchandise and visual displays before moving on to face-to-face sales and simulated after-sales complaints. This event also tests online livestreaming and staff training.
Beyond the competition arena, AI is already gaining ground in retail. During the first four hours of this year's "618" shopping festival, the number of merchants using JD.com's AI-powered digital hosts for livestreaming surged sixfold year on year, generating more than 70 million yuan (10.37 million U.S. dollars) in sales, according to the company.
Yet Lu Chunhua, the venue manager for the WorldSkills retail competition, said: "The core competitiveness of retail is providing emotional value and touching people. That is something AI cannot replace."
ONE SPECIALTY, MULTIPLE CAPABILITIES
AI's impact, experts said, is not limited to taking over parts of existing work. It is also raising demand for workers who can combine a core specialty with digital and cross-disciplinary skills.
At the Industry 4.0 competition, contestants worked to integrate production equipment and other manufacturing resources into a unified system. The project simulates the operation of a smart factory, requiring skills ranging from mechanical assembly and electrical wiring to PLC programming, data collection and analysis, and production scheduling optimization.
"Skilled workers in the new era need 'one specialty plus multiple capabilities,'" said Zhang Rui, deputy director of the engineering training center at Tianjin University of Technology and Education in north China. She added that workers who can use digital tools, work across disciplines, and think innovatively are likely to be increasingly sought after.
This shift is also reshaping what counts as expertise in software. At the Web Technologies competition, contestants are expected to do more than write code -- they have to understand client needs, design solutions, build databases and programs, and test and debug the final product.
Wu Yingxiang, a technical expert and coach for the Chinese team in WorldSkills Web Technologies, said AI is making code generation much faster, pushing programmers toward broader roles. "Every programmer may now become a project manager and a product manager," he said.
Data shows that demand for AI-related skills has risen rapidly in China in recent years. Newly posted campus-recruitment positions in AI increased 47.3 percent year on year in the first five months of 2026, according to data from the talent research arm of Maimai, a Chinese networking and recruitment platform.
Over the past five years, more than 20 newly recognized occupations have been closely related to AI, with over 40 percent directly linked to future industries.
China is moving quickly to address the emerging talent gap. In April, five government departments, including the Ministry of Education, issued an "AI Plus Education" action plan, with measures including upgrading traditional vocational programs, developing new curricula and training systems, and strengthening school-company cooperation for emerging AI-related jobs.
The ministry added 27 programs to the country's vocational education catalog in July, covering fields like the digital economy, AI, the low-altitude economy and advanced equipment, with new offerings related to humanoid robots.
Schools are adjusting their programs accordingly. Ge Rui, principal of Shanghai Information Technology College, said the college is planning to reshape its professional clusters around areas including AI and industrial digitalization during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), in response to Shanghai's evolving industrial landscape.
As training changes, the question is no longer whether workers will use AI, but how they will work with it. Francis Hourant, president of WorldSkills International, said that adapting to the changes in the future is not an either-or choice between humans and AI.
"It is not AI in the end. It is the combination of humans and AI," he explained.
Asked what young people need most to keep pace with this change, Hourant gave a short but telling answer: "Lifelong learning." ■

Cambodia establishes 1st-ever genetic conservation area to protect Siamese crocodiles
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
17:29:12 CST
18:29:12 KST

PHNOM PENH, Sept. 26 (Xinhua) -- Cambodia has officially established its first crocodile genetic conservation area to safeguard the natural genetic diversity of the critically endangered Siamese crocodile, conservationists announced in a joint press release on Saturday.
The newly designated area offers formal legal protection for a critical nesting habitat, ensuring the species can continue to breed and thrive in the wild while supporting the long-term, in-situ conservation of its unique gene pool.
Officially announced by the Ministry of Environment, the Boeung Veal Veng site features a 315-hectare nesting area. Located in the O'Som commune of Pursat province, the area is home to the largest remaining wild population of Siamese crocodiles at approximately 40 individuals.
Minister of Environment Eang Sophalleth noted that Boeung Veal Veng is Cambodia's first-ever genetic conservation area established specifically for a single animal species.
Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Dith Tina called the establishment of the conservation area a milestone in the kingdom's long-term mission to rescue the endangered reptile from the brink of extinction.
The Siamese crocodile (Crocodylus siamensis) is currently listed as critically endangered on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List.
Khvay Atitya, an undersecretary of state and spokesperson for the Ministry of Environment, said fewer than 1,000 Siamese crocodiles remain worldwide, with more than 300 in Cambodia. ■

Trump ‘rejects’ Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal. What’s next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:28:19 UTC
18:28:19 KST

Trump ‘rejects’ Iran’s seven-day ceasefire proposal. What’s next?
Analyst says Trump may opt to resume attacks on Iran after November midterm elections.
United States President Donald Trump has reportedly ruled out an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week, according to unnamed US officials cited by The Wall Street Journal.
Trump’s rejection comes just hours after Iran put forward a new roadmap to opening the strait, through which one-fifth of global oil and natural gas is shipped during peacetime – and days after the US president threatened to “annihilate” Iran from the floor of the UN General Assembly.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump hails ‘very productive’ talks with China’s Xi Jinping
- list 2 of 3Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
- list 3 of 3Iran war squeezes Iraq’s economy as oil revenues fall and prices rise
Here’s what we know about Trump’s response to the proposal and what could come next in the conflict.
What was in Iran’s seven-day proposal?
The proposal lays out a roadmap to open the Strait of Hormuz with normal maritime passage within a week.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iran’s Foreign Minister, Abbas Araghchi, said the proposal calls for the US to take actions it committed to under the failed June 17 Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) on an accelerated timeframe.
Those actions include releasing $12bn in frozen Iranian assets, lifting Iranian oil sanctions and ending the US’s naval blockade on Iranian ports, Araghchi told reporters at a private media briefing on Thursday, according to The New York Times. He also said all hostilities, including in Lebanon, where Israel still occupies part of the south of the country, must cease during the seven-day period.
Araghchi said once the US conditions are met – which he estimated would take four or five days – the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and negotiations with the US on a “final deal” would start on day seven.
He said the process could begin as soon as the US accepts the plan.
“The choice now rests with the United States,” said Araghchi. “Iran does not accept coercion, threats or intimidation.”
How has the US responded?
The US government has not publicly responded to the plan.
However, The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump had quickly ruled it out, citing unnamed US officials.
They said Trump was sceptical about whether Iran would fulfil US demands. Trump’s most persistent demands have been that Iran never be able to acquire a nuclear weapon and that it restore free passage in Hormuz.
Iran says it will not discuss its nuclear programme until the conditions it has laid down are met, which has led to an impasse between the two sides.
Meanwhile, a US official has told Al Jazeera that Washington is in no hurry to respond to Iran’s proposal and that it sees itself as being in a strong position with respect to the Strait of Hormuz.
Late on Friday night, Trump posted an image of a map on his Truth Social platform that labelled it “Trump Strait”.
Trump has previously said the US has “total control” over the waterway and threatened to designate it as a US territory. Iran strongly denied that, saying it has complete control of the strait.
Are peace negotiations still happening?
Yes, but mostly indirectly. At the UN General Assembly in New York this week, Qatar has been passing messages between the two sides as an intermediary.
Both the US and Iran have said the door to diplomacy remains open and a US official told Al Jazeera that ongoing mediated talks are “positive and constructive”.
Qatar, a key mediator in the conflict, said its foreign minister spoke with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Friday about de-escalation and the conditions for renewed dialogue.
Earlier this week, US officials, including special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, held mediated discussions with Iranian counterparts in New York, a meeting Trump described as “very good”.
Nevertheless, there is “an enormous amount of scepticism in Washington that the two countries are on the same page,” according to Thomas Warrick, senior fellow at the Atlantic Council.
“I think that the best we can hope for is that this offer from the Iranian foreign minister does lead to further discussions to try to clarify what preconditions Washington is willing to work with,” Warrick told Al Jazeera.
Where does the US-Iran standoff go from here?
Possibly towards renewed hostilities.
According to the US officials cited in The Wall Street Journal, Trump told his aides he expects to carry out a new bombing campaign against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
That comes after Trump told the UN General Assembly he was considering whether to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell” in the absence of a deal.
At the same time, Trump has said he believes a deal to end the conflict will come shortly after the midterms.
Paul Musgrave, an associate professor of government at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera that Trump “doesn’t want to end the war on unfavourable terms” and that the result of November’s elections will likely help steer his policy.
If Trump’s Republican party suffers severe setbacks in the elections – and loses its majority in Congress – he may opt for “unilateral actions, including perhaps a resumption of warfare”, said Musgrave.
“That would also mean that Iran would have delivered a really stinging political blow to President Trump,” Musgrave continued, adding this could trigger short-term escalation, “followed by negotiation so that the White House doesn’t look like it’s just surrendering”.

Why is the Swiss government opposing stricter neutrality rules?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:24:21 UTC
18:24:21 KST

Why is the Swiss government opposing stricter neutrality rules?
The Swiss government and parliament are urging voters to reject a proposal during an upcoming referendum that would strengthen the country’s neutrality policy by constraining Bern’s ability to impose unilateral sanctions.
The motion is being pushed by pro-sovereignty politicians, who have criticized the government’s decision to largely adopt EU sanctions against Russia following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022.
Under the current system that the Federal Council seeks to preserve, the seven-member ruling body decides on a case-by-case basis whether Switzerland should copy restrictions imposed by other Western nations.
The proposed amendment will be put to a nationwide vote on Sunday, September 27.
Why do sanctions matter?
Switzerland largely aligned itself with the EU sanctions regime targeting Russia after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022.
As of July, Bern reported freezing 8.5 billion Swiss francs ($10.3 billion) in assets owned by Russian companies and individuals targeted by Brussels and another 6.8 billion francs ($8.2 billion) in funds owned by the Russian Central Bank. The Swiss Federal Council has rejected calls to confiscate the money.
Moscow has repeatedly accused Switzerland of abandoning its traditional neutrality by taking the sanctions path, arguing that it had lost its standing as a “trusted neutral mediator.”
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov reiterated Moscow’s stance to Swiss Federal Councillor Ignazio Cassis personally, when the two met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly session in New York in July 2025.
Russia as well as several other non-Western nations reject any sanctions not authorized by the UN as illegal under international law and consider them a form of economic warfare.
What is at stake in Sunday’s vote?
The “Safeguard Swiss neutrality” initiative was launched by the Pro Schweiz (For Switzerland) pro-sovereignty movement and figures associated with the conservative Swiss People’s Party (SVP), which strongly backs the proposal.
It would define Switzerland’s neutrality in the Constitution as “perpetual and armed.” Switzerland would be barred from joining or cooperating with military or defense alliances unless it was facing a direct military attack.
The country would also be prohibited from imposing sanctions against belligerent states, with exceptions for measures mandated by the UN and those intended to prevent sanctions circumvention.
A newly-strengthened neutrality policy would be used to “prevent and resolve conflicts” and “to act as a mediator,” if the proposal is passed.
Who is against it?
The Swiss Federal Council argues that the more rigid interpretation would restrict Switzerland’s freedom of action and could weaken its national security. Parliament has also recommended rejecting the initiative.
“Anyone who waits until the crisis is already here before they are willing to cooperate is too late,” Cassis has said.
The government is particularly opposed to surrendering its ability to decide whether to adopt sanctions.
“Neutrality does not require an automatic response,” the councillor said. “It requires us to take responsibility and weigh up our interests.”
Who backs it?
SVP President Marcel Dettling has accused Cassis and Swiss diplomats of seeking to erode neutrality and “play the big shot everywhere in the world.”
“Switzerland is neutral. This means we do not interfere in foreign affairs. Every individual is entitled to their own opinion, but official Switzerland is neutral and offers its good offices to all parties in conflict,” he said.
SVP member Christoph Blocher, who was a member of the Federal Council in the 2000s, rejected the notion that neutrality should be “flexible,” denouncing it as “dangerous nonsense.”
The SVP argues that fixed constitutional rules would make Swiss policy more predictable and enhance the country’s credibility as a mediator. It also contends that unilateral sanctions against parties to a conflict are incompatible with staying neutral on it.
What do the polls say?
Recent surveys show substantially more respondents opposing the neutrality initiative than supporting it.
A LeeWas survey for 20 Minuten and Tamedia, conducted earlier this month among 12,948 eligible voters, found 31% supported the initiative and 68% opposed it. Support had fallen by five percentage points compared with the previous survey wave.
Historically, Swiss voters have often sided with the Federal Council’s recommendations.
In June, they rejected the SVP-backed proposal to cap Switzerland’s population below 10 million through 2050, with 54.79% voting against and 45.21% in favor. The Federal Council had opposed the initiative.
On the same day, voters approved stricter rules governing access to alternative civilian service by 52.46% to 47.54%. That measure intended to preserve participation in the mandatory military service was backed by the Federal Council and parliament, with the SVP being among the supporting parties.
How does Swiss direct democracy work?
Switzerland has one of the world’s most extensive systems of direct democracy, with voters deciding national issues up to four times a year, often with several proposals on the ballot at once.
A popular initiative seeking to amend the Constitution requires 100,000 valid signatures collected within 18 months before it can proceed through the political process toward a nationwide vote. Constitutional amendments require a double majority – a majority of voters nationwide and a majority of the cantons – to pass.
Rules are less restrictive for optional referendums on laws passed by parliament.

Israeli director Erez Tadmor takes ‘Matchmaking 3’ to New York - and reveals its unlikely secret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:20:51 UTC
18:20:51 KST

The Matchmaking crowd is back in a new movie, Matchmaking 3, which opened in theaters throughout Israel on Thursday.
This time, director Erez Tadmor has taken his heroes to the Big Apple, where they try to find a groom for the daughter of an American haredi (ultra-Orthodox) billionaire, played by Michael Rapaport.
The first two movies were among the most popular in Israeli history, selling millions of tickets during the pandemic and the war, and bringing together secular and observant audiences who laughed and cried together with the protagonists.
“The audience chose a second and a third film by loving these characters,” said Tadmor in an interview just ahead of the new movie’s opening.
“Audiences wanted to know what happened to Baruch [the hero of the series, played by Maor Schwietzer], so we wrote a third film about how he is trying to pay for a wedding to Ruth [Niv Sultan, Schwietzer’s real-life wife] and build a home with her.”
Matchmaking fans have high expectations for the third installment in this trilogy, and they won’t be disappointed.
New York setting proves to be a highlight of new movie
The New York scenes at the core of the movie are the highlight, and feature the funniest urban mugging sequence in decades, with the young matchmaker Baruch and his mentor and sometimes frenemy, Malki (Irit Kaplan), trying to talk their way out of the situation with their Israeli-accented English.
“Malki understands money and bargaining, and her English is better. When a mugger appears, of course she negotiates. The idea came from a producer who was robbed in New York by a man dressed as Spider-Man,” said Tadmor.
“The costumed characters in Times Square can feel like figures out of a fairy tale suddenly turning hostile.”
As viewers will recall, Baruch, who is not considered a catch by the standards of haredi society because he is not a star yeshiva student, has no money, and doesn’t come from a prestigious family, is engaged to Ruth (Niv Sultan), a pastry chef who is also not seen as top drawer because she has a brother (the gifted young actor Eliyahu Shaki) with Down Syndrome.
Now that it’s time for them to get married, they don’t have the money for the kind of wedding Baruch wants.
Then he learns that Michael Gerstel (Rapaport, who gives a relaxed and completely authentic performance) is looking for a groom for his daughter, Rivka (Naya Bienstock), and is offering $100,000 to anyone who can find the right guy.
Sensing his chance, Baruch sets off with Malki in tow and tries to fix up Gerstel’s daughter with learned yeshiva students. But there’s a twist: Gerstel is a different kind of father than Baruch is used to dealing with.
“Gerstel wants a son-in-law who can eventually take over his business,” said Tadmor. “He sees talent in Baruch, who has had to survive without many advantages. Baruch is street-smart, but he’s not corrupt or fixated on doing anything to make money; he has principles. … He sees the man he once was in Baruch.”
AS IN ANY good romantic dramedy, the couple is torn apart for a time. For a while, it seems that Baruch might be the perfect match for Gerstel’s daughter, while Ruth is courted by a young man she once dated (played by Yadin Gellman), who has a sister with Down Syndrome, whom Ruth’s brother falls for.
So, there is some real suspense among the laughs. “It moves against the expected romantic-comedy pattern. I love a story that can be serious and suddenly funny,” said Tadmor.
Tadmor collaborated with Hava Divon, Yaki Reisner on new movie
The director, who is secular, developed the movie with Hava Divon, one of the creators of the beloved television series about national-religious young people, Srugim, and Yaki Reisner, a producer/writer/businessman from a Litvak ultra-Orthodox family in Bnei Brak who plays Malki’s husband.
Tadmor wrote the screenplay with Divon, Sarel Piterman, and Sharon Maymon.
He admitted that the huge success of the first Matchmaking film took him by surprise.
“People wondered who would see a movie about haredim, whether secular audiences would be interested, and whether religious audiences would go to a movie theater,” he said.
“But secular people were curious, and religious viewers also came. The film ran for months; some people saw it over and over, both religious and secular moviegoers.”
Tadmor's prolific career
Tadmor is one of Israel’s most acclaimed and prolific directors.
In addition to the Matchmaking trilogy, he has made diverse films such as Strangers, about a romance between a Palestinian woman and an Israeli man in Europe, co-directed by Guy Nattiv; A Matter of Size, co-directed by Sharon Maymon, about Israelis who become sumo wrestlers; and Soda, a drama about Holocaust survivors starring Lior Raz and Rotem Sela that was based on his grandfather’s life.
Unlike many Israeli directors who struggle to get their movies made, he releases a film just about every year.
Through working on the Matchmaking trilogy, he has become far more knowledgeable about ultra-Orthodox life, and his affection for his characters shines through all three movies.
But he comes to this community with an outsider’s eye and looks at its problems as well as its positive sides.
The first film focused on Moti (Amit Rahav), an Ashkenazi groom courting a Mizrahi bride, while his buddy Baruch came to the forefront in the second movie.
Audiences sympathized with his struggle to prove himself, and the second movie introduced Ruth, who is resigned to never getting married because having a brother with an intellectual disability made her undesirable in the eyes of haredi society.
“Our films each have criticisms of the world they portray,” he said, although he emphasized that he admires the way haredim support each other. He did not think the current controversy over drafting haredim into the military would affect ticket sales for the movie.
While he is excited about the film’s release, he is also working on several upcoming movies: some he can talk about, such as a documentary about Iranian women, and some he can’t.
“I make movies all the time. I have to keep making movies; it’s what I do,” he shared. And while he wouldn’t give any details, he did make one promise that will please Matchmaking fans: there is a fourth movie in the works.

====================================================================================================

Not sheepish: Israel Museum reveals a different side of Menashe Kadishman’s art
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:20:49 UTC
18:20:49 KST

Mention the name Menashe Kadishman to most Israeli art consumers, and the knee-jerk response will invariably be something along the lines of: “Oh, the sheep painter!”
But, as an exhibition currently on display at the Israel Museum clearly demonstrates, there was a lot more to the late, internationally renowned Israel Prize-winning artist than just funky renditions of woolly farm animals.
The “Urban Nature” collection, curated by Amitai Mendelsohn, with assistance from Mika Nachtailer, includes not one single sheep. True, it is far from an expansive set, with only around 20 or so works in the cozy Hagit Gallery space, but it offers the public a new perspective on the larger-than-life character and his oeuvre.
Walking the walk
Kadishman, who died in 2015 at the age of 82, was a colorful figure who walked the walk throughout his 50-plus-year career. He was constantly on the prowl for new lines of aesthetic, disciplinary, and philosophical departure, and was forever leapfrogging boundaries and diving headlong into new, surprising territory.
He sprung the aforementioned leitmotif creature, for example, on the unsuspecting world at the 1978 Venice Biennale, where, as Israel’s representative at the art world’s most prestigious event, he unveiled a flock of sheep, bearing a slew of hues. At the time, he explained that the work blurred the line between art and nature.
That yin-yang feature reemerged numerous times as his portfolio evolved. Many of his outdoor iron and steel statues incorporated gaps or hollows, and, when strategically positioned in suitable urban spots, one could espy through them leafy trees or parts of city green lungs. In so doing, he seamlessly straddled the interface between Mother Nature and humankind’s intervention in her vibrant verdant continuum.
“URBAN NATURE” focuses on Kadishman’s output between 1969 and 1979. That was a formative passage in his artistic growth, as he forsook minimalist sculpting and gravitated toward his trademark sheep-based presentations. But, always ready to bring anything and everything into his creative sphere, he also embraced everyday objects.
That was sparked by an out-of-sync time-lapse predicament in which he found himself on a trip to New York. Jet-lagged and unable to sleep, at 4 a.m. he was fired with creative fervor and, bereft of any suitable raw materials through which he could expend some of his nervous energy and pent-up conceptual foraging, he turned to a hotel bedside accoutrement.
Looking out his window at the nighttime Manhattan skyline, he ripped out a page from a telephone directory, took a pen, and began drawing the structural contours in view.
Perhaps, for folks who weren’t around in the pre-Internet world, I should explain that every city in the world had a – generally – fat tome or, in larger places such as New York or London, several volumes, with lists of names of locals, together with their address and telephone number. That is how we mostly found and communicated with each other, in addition to writing letters and, if we were in a hurry, sending telegrams.
Telephone directory topography
Kadishman took the directory’s textural topography and ran with it, spinning out lines that followed the shapes of the buildings around him. That opened the thematic floodgates, and, in the following years, similar pages formed the substratum of hundreds of works that fed off urban and other dynamics.
Several relevant specimens appear in the Israel Museum exhibition, including a particularly attractive work Kadishman created in honor of the illustrious art repository’s 10th anniversary, in 1975.
A few years later, he expounded on his newfound course of visual expression: “I related to each column as if it were a building, a skyscraper.” He subsequently took the structural concept into more abstract climes. “Later, I related to the page itself, not what I saw around it, only to what was on the page,” Kadishman explained. “I arrived at a whole landscape, paths between the letters, a cardiogram of the page.”
That also involved taking a cerebral and philosophical leap of faith, as Kadishman took the dry information in the directories into corporeal domains, as he reimagined the data as a direct and accurate reflection of the street-level reality of millions of New Yorkers, Londoners, or other city dwellers, their houses, and day-to-day lives.
Characteristically, he didn’t just stick to a simple artistic extension of the urban facts on the ground. He took ordered page structures, with their neat, easily legible and accessible rows and columns, and created unfettered feral arrangements that exuded dynamism and high energy.
Rather than keep that adventurous visual notion to himself, he enlisted the help of numerous professional colleagues, from Israel and abroad alike, to take his telephone directory initiative a step or two further in all sorts of directions.
His siblings in boundary-pushing arms included similarly inclined graphic-leaning artist and educator Raffi Lavie, modernist painting pioneer Yehezkel Streichman, abstract painter Lea Nikel, and lyrical abstraction proponent Moshe Kupferman. All Kadishman’s partners were A-listers in the field, and some of the results of that project – originally exhibited at the museum in 1979 under the “Kadishman Connection” banner – feature in “Urban Nature.”
Artistic balancing acts
Kadishman not only delved into different and apparently disparate artistic disciplines; he also fused them almost against their will. That applied equally to areas of life that feed off contrasting energies and sources.
The delicate balancing act between contemporary civilization and the environment appears repeatedly in the placement of his creations.
That spawned jarring yet, somehow, harmonious confluences that seem to scream out at town dwellers: “Look at me!”
One such venture in 1970s New York produced an unmissable display of large, rectangular, yellow metal boards affixed to the trunks of trees in Central Park.
“He didn’t ask for a permit to do that,” explains Nachtailer. “He just put them up. They were removed a day later,” she laughs. He pulled a similar antic in Uruguay, too.
That was typical of the man. He had a gentle demeanor yet an iron will to follow his ideas through to their artistic denouement, come what may.
A change of garb for the president
He had an imposing presence, with his impressive girth, loose-fitting shirts and ubiquitous short pants. He simply trod his own unique path. Mind you, he did make the odd compromise, actually donning long pants for the Israel Prize ceremony at the President’s Residence in 1995.
That was very good of him, to defer to ceremonial protocol, but he made no concessions when it came to his envelope-pushing work, across the disciplinary and material board.
He pushed on with his interventionist dialogue with nature on his home patch, too. A tree in the museum compound came in for the yellow treatment, as did a spot on the ground in the neighboring Valley of the Cross.
Yellow is the color
Kadishman clearly had a thing about yellow. That harked back to his stint on Kibbutz Ma’ayan Baruch, where he lived for three years and worked as a shepherd.
“For him, yellow was the color of the tractor plowing the field,” Nachtailer enlightens me. I’m assuming the kibbutz used John Deere tractors, easily recognizable by their iconic green-and-yellow color scheme.
The equilibrium-imbalance confluxes line of thought, for the artist, was both an extension of, and an oxymoronic adjunct to, what grows out of the soil as the Good Lord intended.
“I wanted to work with the Creator’s forest, the organic forest, and incorporate into it a man-made mechanical forest, which would have forms that clash with nature,” he noted in the context of his favored hue.
“The shadows of the branches and tree trunks were reflected on the yellow panels, changing with the movement of the sun,” he observed, referencing his projects in New York and Uruguay.
It was very much a matter of harnessing terrestrial and celestial kinetics and seeing how they affect his seemingly dissonant input.
“In nature there are thousands of forms that change with the movement of the sun. My shade of yellow doesn’t exist in the forest’s color palette.”
Kadishman maintained his ding-dong synergy with his natural surroundings and enjoyed a long, fruitful relationship with the Israel Museum, periodically recruiting its expansive hilltop grounds and its vegetation, of an arboreal ilk, as a milieu for his creations.
Getting into trees
Trees often underpinned new aesthetics, including some of his own making, such as in his eponymous work that comprised naive-looking blue metal tree shapes interspersed in forested parts of the museum site.
Back in the day, there were others around the world who interacted with nature, including Joshua Neustein, Georgette Battle, Dani Karavan, and particularly Itzhak Danziger, who, like Kadishman, studied at the Slade School of Fine Art in London.
Despite his abundant range of outdoor metal pieces, Kadishman didn’t work exclusively with rigid addenda. He was all for allowing his works to take up the attraction mantle and communicate themselves to the public.
In 1975, he assembled his Laundry Forest installation near the then-entrance plaza of the Israel Museum. The set comprised large white canvas sheets, suspended from cables, with tree shapes cut out of them. The absence of the natural figure drew the observer into completing the picture themselves, enlisting them in the creative process.
Ever alert to the dynamics of the world around him, he planned the installation to make optimal use of the ebb and flow of daily life and meteorological conditions, animating and complementing his design.
Communicating with the public
He was also keen to bring others into the creative fold, and visitors to the museum could walk through the work as the material flapped in the wind and reflected the dovetailing momentum of sun and shadow.
Laundry Forest had a nostalgic element. Kadishman talked about childhood memories of playing betwixt freshly laundered sheets his mother hung on a line outside the family home in Tel Aviv.
The exhibition at the Israel Museum offers a behind-the-scenes glimpse of the machinations behind setting up the installation in Jerusalem, with a couple of monochrome photographs that conjure up the ambiance of the day and the artist’s mien.
Art lovers used to viewing Kadishman’s more monumental alfresco efforts, or locked into his famed sheep-themed works, will get a peek at other areas of his adventuresome oeuvre and, thus, a better handle on his artistic and human makeup.
It might be stretching matters somewhat to call Kadishman mercurial, but there is ne’er a dull moment in his professional timeline as he constantly strove to marry the quotidian urban continuum with the forces of nature through his fearless artistic acts.■
“Urban Nature” closes in November 2027.
For more information:
www.imj.org.il/en/exhibitions/
menashe-kadishman-urban-nature

The last 15 years: Sarit Brown brings intimate musical ‘The Last Five Years’ to Jerusalem - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:20:15 UTC
18:20:15 KST

Our thriving Jerusalem English-speaking theater scene boasts active theater companies and many plays, musicals, and performances, yet it’s small enough that we get to see the same actors showing their chops in different productions. We have our own lineup of stars alongside those of Hollywood and Broadway, and we fondly follow these talented thespians who invest so much in keeping us entertained. Thus, when one of them strikes out in a new direction, we take notice.
Sarit Brown, who has performed in a good number of productions over recent years, has recently taken the leap into the role of director to make a longstanding dream of hers come true: staging The Last Five Years, an intimate musical about ambition and the breakdown of love.
Written and composed by Jason Robert Brown (no relation to Sarit) after his own marriage broke up, it premiered in Chicago in 2001 and has since been produced widely, finally reaching Broadway last year. Brown staged it earlier this year at Psik Theater’s Ma’agalim Festival and is now offering a full run at the Fringe Center of Beit Mazia Theater, on Hol Hamoed Sukkot and the following week.
Non-spoiler: The marriage doesn't survive
This production stars Sarit Brown as Cathy, a struggling actor, and Avi David-Rene Cohen as Jamie, an up-and-coming writer. Jamie is Jewish but Cathy is not – one song is actually titled “Shiksa Goddess” (and for those opposed to intermarriage, I have good news: The marriage doesn’t survive – no spoiler here, this is the actual premise!).
The pair share the tale of their five-year relationship through music, with Jamie recounting events from when they met and Cathy working backward from the breakup; they meet in the middle, at the marriage itself. There are two sides to any relationship, and here we get both points of view (and can decide with whom we will side, if we want).
Both Cohen and Brown trained at Maslul, the Tel Aviv Musical Theater Academy, where they became good friends. While I have yet to attend the show, two of Brown’s fellow Jerusalem theater directors were impressed by what they saw.
Brown was “unsurprisingly, given her past record, excellent as Cathy,” says Yael Valier of Theater and Theology. Of Cohen, 28, a former Parisian now based in Haifa, Valier says he “can really sing! His handling of Jamie’s ‘Nobody Needs to Know’ scene with convincing emotional complexity was a high point for me,” while Encore’s Aviella Trapido highlights his “great energy and emotional depth.”
Brown, 36, is a theater educator at Psik Theater and co-founded Living Room Productions with Alexa Solace. Explaining the name, she says: “Originally we thought we would actually perform in a living room, an intimate space. Ultimately we were given the opportunity for a larger stage – but we still work out of our living rooms!”
This aligns with the writer’s intentions: He has shared that, after his large-scale musical Parade, he wanted to create a show small enough to play in his own living room.
Smart, intimate, and imaginative
Jerusalem audiences may enjoy the musical’s Jewish elements, among them “The Schmuel Song,” a whimsical tale of an old Jewish tailor and his magical clock. Musical accompaniment is provided by Paul Salter, who helmed Encore theater productions for many years and has numerous credits as musical director to his name.
For this show, which Valier sums up as “smart, intimate, and imaginative,” Brown describes “a unique staging concept” that she has been developing for almost 15 years (see box). The concept certainly sounds intriguing.
Valier affirms that Brown “designed the space with a flair not just for the visuals but for the way in which it drew the audience in without ever feeling forced,” and Trapido praises “really creative staging choices that brought a fresh perspective.”
If you are still debating whether to book tickets for The Last Five Years, Trapido’s assessment might be just the push you need: “A thoughtful and engaging interpretation of a show I love very much!”

Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii, Mexico with flooding, high surf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:17:00 UTC
18:17:00 KST

People on Hawaii’s Big Island were bracing for another potentially catastrophic storm Friday as Hurricane Nolo churned south of the islands, threatening to unleash flash floods, powerful winds and dangerous surf through the weekend.
Nolo’s maximum sustained winds increased to 105 mph (165 kph) Friday, with the storm expected to strengthen into a major hurricane Saturday. Its center was about 145 miles (235 kilometers) south of Hawaii’s southernmost point.
Forecasters warned that parts of the Big Island could receive up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) of rain, with isolated totals reaching 25 inches (64 centimeters). The forecast was revised downward from an earlier projection of as much as 35 inches (89 centimeters).
Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, urged residents to remain indoors and in safe locations as the storm approaches.
“People are going to want to kind of shelter in place on the Big Island, be in their safe place, certainly by later today, tonight, well into Saturday,” Brennan said Friday. “Don’t venture out if you don’t have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down.”
The hurricane center also warned that heavy rainfall could affect Hawaii’s other islands. Maui faced the threat of intense rain, potentially life-threatening flooding and mudslides, forecasters said.
Crews on the Big Island spent hours Friday trying to build berms to guide water and move large debris ahead of the worst of the rain, said Erika Kapu, Hawaii program manager for the humanitarian nonprofit CORE.
CORE and other nonprofit partners spent the week packing and shipping supplies such as camp stoves and hygiene products by air cargo from Oahu to the Big Island for a community relief hub that has been active since August’s Hurricane Lala.
President Donald Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for the state of Hawaii, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate assistance from across the federal government and provide funding support for emergency measures.
Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits, and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed in some areas.
Hawaii County officials on the Big Island urged residents in flood-prone areas to consider taking refuge at shelters being set up or other locations.
The heaviest rain from Nolo was likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island that was hit by Lala and where the ground remained wet from additional precipitation. The storm surge could reach 1 to 3 feet (30 to 91 centimeters), creating large and dangerous waves and coastal flooding, the hurricane center said.
Hawaiian Electric, the state’s primary utility, said crews that had been helping restore power in Kauai after this month’s Hurricane Lowell would return to Oahu, Maui and the Big Island in preparation for the coming storm.
Residents and tourists on the Big Island were busy preparing.
In Hilo, where light rain was falling Friday, residents filled bags with sand and gravel at Francis Wong Stadium, where authorities had set up a sand distribution center.
Dean Taise said water was starting to get into his driveway from the street, so he decided to get a few sandbags ready ahead of possible flooding.
“They say, prepare for the worst, right? Hope for the best,” Taise said.
Piles of sandbags lined the terminal at Hilo International Airport, where Daniela Mendoza was trying to get home to Oahu after Southwest Airlines canceled flights. Only Hawaiian Airlines was still flying out of the airport Friday afternoon.
“I hope I can leave,” Mendoza said. “My cats are waiting for me.”
Meanwhile, Mexico was under threat from Hurricane Polo as it headed toward the Baja California peninsula after bringing storm conditions to the southwestern coast.
The hurricane center said Polo gained significant strength overnight into Friday morning and doused parts of Mexico’s Pacific coast. No major damage or flooding was reported along the coast overnight into Friday.
By midday Friday, attention had turned to the peninsula, where the hurricane was expected to turn back and make landfall between Monday and Tuesday. Local authorities were preparing shelters, and Mexico’s government announced Friday afternoon that it was closing ports in the region as dark clouds swirled overhead.
The latest estimated sustained winds were 175 mph (280 kph).
Residents stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes in some coastal areas Thursday. Mexican authorities opened shelters and cleared people from beaches, and 15,000 security personnel were deployed across the coast. Schools were closed.
In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán, seawater swept through homes, leaving wooden planks and furniture strewn across the streets. Residents and government officials were clearing debris and shoveling thick mud that coated much of the town.
Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 15-foot (4.5-meter) waves. She worried about how she would recover financially, saying she has no other source of income.
Brennan said some moisture associated with Polo would be pushed into parts of the southwestern U.S. by Monday, possibly producing scattered flash flooding in the Four Corners region, particularly in parts of Arizona and New Mexico.
Biologists on Friday relocated eggs from two olive ridley sea turtle nests on Southern California beaches to the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach over concerns about high tides and hazardous surf as officials monitored Hurricane Polo.
El Niño is prompting major environmental shifts across the world, fueling drought in some areas and flooding in others. It traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season, while it tends to increase tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific because of moist air and low wind shear.
A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was at Category 4 status and remained far from land Friday, roughly 955 miles (1,537 kilometers) west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.
Two other powerful storms were churning in the Atlantic Ocean but were not near land.
In the northern Atlantic, Tropical Storm Fay reformed early Thursday. As of Friday, it was about 1,040 miles (1,674 kilometers) west-southwest of the Azores, the hurricane center said. Off Africa’s western coast, Tropical Storm Gonzalo strengthened early Friday as it approached the Cabo Verde Islands.

Ebola outbreak deepens as Congo fails to trace most contacts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:16:00 UTC
18:16:00 KST

Health authorities battling an Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo have identified only about 30,000 people who may have been exposed to the virus, far short of the more than 400,000 contacts expected to be traced, a senior African health official told Reuters.
Dr. Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, said the gap underscored how deeply the outbreak remained embedded in communities despite signs of progress.
More than 80% of newly confirmed cases were being detected among people who were not already on contact lists, suggesting transmission was continuing beyond the reach of surveillance efforts.
For every confirmed Ebola case, health authorities would expect to identify about 60 people who had direct or indirect contact with the infected person, Kaseya told Reuters on Friday on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
With nearly 7,900 confirmed cases, that would translate into about 474,000 contacts. "But currently, we have just 30,000 people in the contact list," Kaseya said.
"When the outbreak is at community level, we cannot talk about control," he added.
The Ebola outbreak was detected in May and has become the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The outbreak is also approaching the scale of the 2014-2016 Ebola epidemic in West Africa, which remains the largest Ebola outbreak on record.
The World Health Organization said Friday that the outbreak had spread to two additional health zones, Bulu in Sud-Ubangi province and Dungu in Haut-Uele province near the South Sudan border, bringing the number of affected health zones to 63 across seven provinces.
Last week, United Nations and Congolese government officials said there were signs transmission was slowing in some of the worst-affected parts of Ituri, the epicenter of the outbreak.
Congolese Prime Minister Judith Suminwa Tuluka described the outbreak Wednesday as a major test for the country and said the response had begun producing tangible results.
"We see some improvement, but the outbreak is still serious," Kaseya said.
Even if the Democratic Republic of the Congo were still recording 50, 60 or 70 new cases a day, Kaseya said he would be less concerned if they were people already identified and monitored as contacts because it would mean health authorities knew where transmission was occurring.
Kaseya declined to predict when the outbreak would be brought under control, saying he wanted to see substantially better surveillance and other improvements before putting a timetable on the response.
"If there is a game I didn't want to play since we declared this outbreak, it was to predict when we can bring this outbreak under control," he said.
Kaseya said that if new confirmed cases were identified through contact lists, zero deaths were occurring in communities and there were no new infections among health care workers, he could be in a position to forecast whether the outbreak could be fully controlled within four weeks.
But for now, he said, the high proportion of cases being discovered outside contact lists remained evidence of uncontrolled community transmission.
Africa CDC said nearly $2.9 billion was pledged for the Ebola response at a U.S.-convened meeting in New York on Thursday, including $886 million from the United States.

The White House indicated Friday night that CNN would be excluded from the media pool aboard Air Force One for President Donald Trump’s trip Saturday, marking the latest escalation in the administration’s ongoing dispute with the news organization and raising fresh First Amendment concerns.

The decision came hours after journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico returned to the White House with television cameras after a federal judge granted the news organizations a temporary reprieve. Trump’s administration had barred the three outlets from the White House grounds last week.
The latest media-access decision adds to a growing confrontation between the administration and news organizations over press access and coverage of the president.
U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily struck down the ban in an overnight ruling early Thursday, but his decision addressed “hard passes” for access to the White House grounds and did not directly address pool duties.
The temporary order from the judge also said nothing directly about Air Force One.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., the news outlets’ attorney, did not immediately respond to an email or phone call from The Associated Press seeking comment Friday night.
Earlier Friday, on “The Lead with Jake Tapper,” Boutrous said the plaintiffs believe the recent court ruling also covers the issue of pool access.
The White House did not immediately respond to an email from Associated Press (AP) seeking additional details about the decision.
For a while during the day, the U.S. network video pool for the White House was back in operation for the first time since Trump banned the three news outlets in an extraordinary showdown over media access.

“As of now, all systems are go,” said a person familiar with the pool, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the fluidity of the situation.

The spot that was meant for CNN on this flight has long been reserved for a member of the U.S. network video pool, which Real America’s Voice News is not part of.
CNN did not comment directly earlier Friday, referring instead to its editorial coverage. But Brian Stelter, the network’s media analyst, posted on X that CNN had a pool assignment at the National Archives event and that the White House had approved the network’s credentials.
Throughout his second term, Trump has increasingly targeted media outlets whose coverage irritates him, taking administrative or legal action against several.
Early last year, he banished AP reporters from White House events because the organization was not abiding by his executive order changing the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America.” AP’s guidance says to acknowledge the new name when relevant.
The case is on appeal after a federal district judge ruled in AP’s favor.
The press pool was created decades ago by the White House Correspondents’ Association, a group of journalists who cover the president, to ensure that a rotating roster always travels with the president.
The pool distributes in-person reports and imagery to the broader press corps and is designed to help hold the nation’s chief executive accountable on behalf of the American public.
The association did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

Record heat grips European seas, threatens fisheries, marine life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:14:00 UTC
18:14:00 KST

As drought gripped Europe and wildfires swept across the continent this summer, record-breaking heat also spread into the surrounding seas.
European waters recorded their hottest summer since satellite monitoring began providing reliable data in 1982, according to a Reuters analysis of sea-surface temperatures.
Records were broken from the English Channel to the Mediterranean. An offshore buoy near Mallorca recorded 33.02 degrees Celsius (91.44 degrees Fahrenheit) on Aug. 5, the highest temperature ever recorded by Spain's port authority buoy network.
Scientists warn that marine heatwaves like those seen this summer are becoming more frequent, intense and widespread as greenhouse gas emissions drive temperatures higher worldwide.
The oceans absorb most of the planet's excess heat and retain it far longer than land or the atmosphere.
The warming is reshaping marine ecosystems, with severe consequences for some European fisheries and the communities that depend on them, according to a review of scientific research and interviews with more than a dozen researchers, fishing industry representatives and analysts.
Species that have supported coastal communities in Spain and southern England for generations are disappearing, while unfamiliar species are moving into waters that are becoming increasingly hospitable to them.
"What is surprising is the speed at which this occurs," Jean-Pierre Gattuso, senior research scientist at France's National Centre for Scientific Research, said of Europe's warming seas. "Records are broken almost every day in many places."
Taken together, European seas averaged 21.6 degrees Celsius (70.9 degrees Fahrenheit) between June and August, the highest in 45 years of available data.
Few areas strayed further from the norm than the Bay of Biscay, off the Atlantic-facing coast of France and Spain.
Stretching from Cape Ortegal in Galicia to Pointe de Penmarch in southern Brittany, the bay's traditionally cool waters averaged 21.4 degrees Celsius (70.5 degrees Fahrenheit) between June and August, more than 2.4 degrees Celsius (4.4 degrees Fahrenheit) above the 1991-2020 average.
Readings from the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration peaked at 23.2 degrees Celsius (74 degrees Fahrenheit) on Aug. 13, the highest of the satellite era.
Scientists define a marine heatwave as five or more days of water temperatures well above an area's historic norm. In the 1980s, the Bay of Biscay averaged a handful of heatwave days per year. By the end of August, it had logged 186 this year, more than three out of every four days, Reuters found.
The Bay of Biscay's cool waters, long prized by Spaniards seeking relief from the heat of the Mediterranean coast, were immortalized in Ernest Hemingway's 1926 novel "The Sun Also Rises." The book's protagonist recovers after weeks of dissipation on the northern beaches of San Sebastian.
"Now if you want to swim in cold water, you have to go to the westernmost portion of Galicia," in the far northwestern corner of Spain, said Jose Manuel Rico Ordas, a professor of marine ecology at the University of Oviedo in the northern Asturias region.
Galicia benefits from strong winds that push warm surface water away from the coast during the summer months, allowing cold, deep-sea water to take its place in a process known as upwelling.
Rico Ordas has been spending summers on the bay since he was a child and now studies its transformation.
Back then, there were extensive underwater forests of kelp, which provide vital food, shelter and nurseries for dozens of species that sustain the region's small-scale fisheries. But he estimates roughly 95% of the large, brown seaweed stands have disappeared, based on sampling along the rugged Asturias coast since 2010. He attributes the decline primarily to climate change.
Kelp needs cold water, typically below 20 degrees Celsius (68 degrees Fahrenheit), to survive. Higher temperatures were once exceptionally rare in the bay, Rico Ordas told Reuters.
"Now, it's the opposite," he said.
Fish overgrazing, in particular by dreamfish, which thrive in warmer temperatures, has added to the kelp's decline, he said.
The impacts have been stark.
"We are finding no more lobster, no more crayfish, no more sea urchins and many other species that are associated with the good status of kelp forests," Rico Ordas said.
Concerned fishermen have been teaming up with scientists and environmental activists to try to restore kelp forests by planting seedlings grown in laboratories.
Manuel Angel Reiriz Gonzalez, president of a local fishermen's guild in Galicia, recently ferried members of one such project in a boat he uses for sport fishing charters out of the port of Ribeira. The group brought a box full of small stones seeded with kelp, which they tossed into the choppy waters.
Climate change threatens a way of life that has sustained Gonzalez's community for generations, he said. His family has been diving for sea urchins and harvesting clams for more than a century. But now, he said, recurring heatwaves are hurting shellfish stocks.
The area has also seen an influx of Portuguese man o' war and triggerfish from warmer climes to the south, species that prey on local fish and crustaceans.
"We had some very bad years for clam production, but we worked on seeding them, and the species gradually adapted," Gonzalez said.
He hopes the seabed restoration efforts can do the same for kelp forests.
The disappearance of kelp could lead to the decline of sea urchins and other species fishermen depend on, he said. "At that point, as a fishing guild, we would cease to exist."
In other European waters, new, invasive species from the Red Sea and beyond are entering the Mediterranean through the Suez Canal, displacing native populations, reshaping food chains and threatening fisheries, researchers say. In all, there are more than 1,000 nonindigenous species in the Mediterranean, according to a recent report by the Cyprus Academy of Sciences, Letters and Arts, based on surveys by scientists in 11 countries.
Some native species are coping with the warmer temperatures better than others.
A massive swarm of jellyfish shut down reactors at France's Gravelines nuclear power plant in August when they clogged its cooling system, for the second time in as many years. The plant in northern France is cooled from a canal connected to the North Sea.
Fishermen on the south coast of England are reporting a surge in landings of common octopus. Around 2,600 metric tons were caught last year and upward of 3,000 tons so far this year, according to figures compiled by the UK Marine Management Organisation. Before 2025, annual landings were less than 30 tons.
Octopus larvae are carried into British waters on currents from breeding grounds near the Channel Islands, Brittany and places farther south, said Bryce Stewart, senior research fellow at the Plymouth-based Marine Biological Association (MBA).
Previously, many didn't survive the frigid temperatures. But since 2022, the English Channel has been under heatwave conditions for around six months out of the year on average, logging more than 900 days in all, the Reuters analysis found.
"Now they're actually breeding in UK waters quite prolifically," Stewart said.
For Ian Perkes, owner of the eponymous fish merchant in the south Devon seaside town of Brixham, the octopus bloom has proved a boon.
There is a ready market in southern Europe for the once-rare species and no fishing quotas, he said. "There was one week where we had 200,000 kilos (200 tons)."
But not everyone profits from the shellfish-loving octopuses, which feed on local lobsters, brown crabs and scallops.
For members of the South Devon and Channel Shellfishermen's Cooperative, 2026 has been an "octopus apocalypse," according to its executive officer, Beshlie Pool. One recent fishing trip yielded a single crab all day, she said.
The MBA estimates the octopus bloom could account for about 10 million pounds ($13.25 million) in lost shellfish catches against about 12 million pounds in octopus landings between January and September 2025.
But the benefits are not evenly distributed. Some shellfishermen have switched to catching octopuses, but many do not have the necessary equipment, Pool said. Four of the cooperative's 90-some vessels have gone out of business in the past 12 months.
The unpredictability of the changes makes it hard to adapt, Stewart added.
"Will the octopus still be here next year?" he asked. "If they've eaten all the crabs and lobsters, and the octopus die off, then what do we do?"

Bangkok declares flood disaster as torrential rain inundates city
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:06:00 UTC
18:06:00 KST

Bangkok authorities declared a flood disaster across the Thai capital Saturday after nearly 48 hours of torrential rain overwhelmed canals, submerged roads and forced residents to wade through waist-deep water.
Bangkok Gov. Chadchart Sittipunt urged residents to remain at home after nearly 300 millimeters (11.8 inches) of rain fell, while Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul cut short a trip to London to return to Thailand and oversee the response.
“The water keeps coming in. It’s hard to go out now. It’s like at my waist level now,” said Somkid Pheuk-ngam, 67, a vendor living near a canal north of central Bangkok.
“I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now,” she told Agence France-Presse (AFP), saying flooding was common in the area but that “I think this time is worse than the 2011 flood.”
The devastating 2011 floods killed more than 500 people across Thailand and damaged millions of homes, leaving large parts of the country under water for months.
Chadchart said midafternoon Saturday that the situation had “stabilized,” adding, “If more rainwater doesn’t fall in the area, it will be solved.”
“If the rain stops, it is expected that it will take two to three days to drain the floodwater,” he said in an update broadcast on social media.
Almost continuous rain since Thursday afternoon has swollen Bangkok’s network of canals, sending murky water into surrounding homes, restaurants, shops and alleyways.
Chadchart said at least 13 roads were also flooded, and AFP reporters saw residents in several neighborhoods forced to wade through high water.
The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration declared a disaster for all 50 districts of the city, a move that gives local organizations special powers to act.
But the governor urged residents not to worry about potential food shortages caused by blocked roads, stressing that “the public don’t have to panic.”
Chadchart said around 980 people were staying in temporary shelters, while authorities had transferred 36 bedridden people to hospitals.
“I woke up to go to work and the street in front of my house was flooded,” said motorbike rider Samruay Nakkamnueng in the Ari neighborhood.
“I worried if my motorbike would be able to wade through this much floodwater.”
In the On Nut neighborhood, an AFP reporter saw locals filling sandbags to take home to protect their homes and businesses.
Flooding was worst in the east of the city and along the canals, and Chadchart urged residents to move their belongings to higher ground.
“Our problem is that the canals are full,” Chadchart said in his afternoon update.
“We are cooperating with nearby provinces and trying to drain water out through other sides, minimizing the amount that flows into Bangkok.”
Once dubbed the “Venice of the East,” the city is built on former marshland and sits about 1.5 meters (5 feet) above sea level.
The BMA earlier said the city’s pumping stations were operating at full capacity, pumping about 1,200 cubic meters per second combined.
Municipal workers were also busy Saturday trying to keep the roads clear.
“Our job is to make sure rubbish along the road doesn’t block the drains, so the water can drain away quickly,” said Kwan Nobnom, one of a group wearing bright orange raincoats.
“We thought this year would be dry, so we didn’t expect the flooding to be this bad.”
September is the peak of the rainy season in Bangkok, but it has been wetter than usual, according to figures from the drainage and sewage department.
The capital recorded 487 millimeters of rain between Sept. 1 and 25, compared with an average of nearly 269 millimeters for the same period from 1991 to 2020.
Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to warm because of fossil fuel emissions.
The Department of Disaster Prevention and Mitigation warned of low pressure across eastern, northeastern and central Thailand through Sunday.

Iran awaits US response on plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:05:00 UTC
18:05:00 KST

Iran awaited a formal U.S. response Saturday to a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days and halt fighting across the Middle East, after The Wall Street Journal reported that President Donald Trump had rejected the initiative.
The proposal, presented by Iran at the United Nations General Assembly in New York and conveyed to Washington through Qatari mediators, calls for a pause in hostilities and the eventual reopening of the strategic waterway, a vital route for global energy shipments.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Friday that Tehran had prepared the framework for a deal and was ready to move quickly if Washington showed a willingness to reach an agreement.
"If there is seriousness on the U.S. side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," Araqchi told reporters at the United Nations.
But the Journal, citing unnamed U.S. officials, reported that Trump was privately skeptical that Tehran would meet his demands and had told aides that he expected a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterm elections.
Reuters could not immediately independently confirm the Journal's report. Earlier, a U.S. official said discussions with Iran through mediators had been "positive and constructive."
Under Tehran's proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz after a seven-day period during which hostilities would be halted across the region, including in Lebanon.
In return, Araqchi said Washington would have to lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release frozen Iranian funds and waive oil sanctions.
If those conditions were accepted, the two sides could move into broader negotiations on issues they mutually agree to discuss, potentially including Iran's nuclear program.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran would not make concessions on what it considers its nuclear rights, including uranium enrichment or the transfer of its highly enriched uranium out of the country. The official said the strait would remain closed until Washington met all of Iran's conditions.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview with CBS' "Face the Nation" that Tehran was prepared to negotiate on its nuclear program and other issues but would not accept what he described as "bullying or coercion."
"Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks," Pezeshkian said.
He also said Iran had already agreed that it should not develop nuclear weapons.
Trump has repeatedly said Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon. Tehran has denied seeking one.
The diplomatic effort comes after months of fighting that have disrupted energy shipments and intensified pressure on economies across the region.
The conflict began Feb. 28 with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Iran and has since moved through periods of reduced fighting followed by renewed strikes. The fighting has killed thousands, weakened Iran's conventional military capabilities and placed additional strain on its economy.
Iran and allied groups have also expanded attacks across the region.
The Strait of Hormuz has become a central pressure point in the conflict because of its importance to global energy markets. Before the war, the waterway carried roughly a fifth of global oil and gas shipments, making its disruption a major concern for energy markets and international trade.
Iran shares control of the strategic waterway with Oman and has used its position there as leverage in negotiations with Washington.
Tehran has also opened communication with its longtime regional rival Saudi Arabia over shipping through the strait.
Araqchi briefed Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan on an understanding between Iran and Oman concerning safe shipping routes, according to Iran's Foreign Ministry.
The outreach comes as Saudi Arabia faces a growing security threat from Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement.
The Houthis have launched missiles and drones toward Saudi territory and have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea. The attacks have added another layer of risk to regional energy supplies while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains heavily disrupted.
Saudi-led forces said Saturday that they had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched toward Khamis Mushait and two drones headed toward Riyadh.
The Houthi attacks have also raised concerns over the Red Sea, an alternative route for Gulf energy exports when traffic through Hormuz is restricted.
The widening conflict has pushed Saudi Arabia and its partners to strengthen military coordination.
Defense officials from Türkiye and Pakistan met in Riyadh on Friday with Saudi counterparts to discuss intelligence cooperation, military coordination and the integration of forces, according to Saudi Arabia's Defense Ministry.
The meeting followed talks between the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers under the framework of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement.
The escalation has also deepened humanitarian concerns in Yemen.
UNICEF said Friday that acute malnutrition among children was rising as renewed violence worsened conditions in the country.

China, US to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit, White House says
White House says the two countries agreed to open a ‘bilateral communication channel’ for artificial intelligence incidents.
The United States and China have agreed to establish a “communication channel” for artificial intelligence (AI) incidents, the White House said after a summit in Washington, DC.
US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping discussed matters ranging from AI and trade to the stalled war in Iran during a three-day state visit, and confirmed that they would meet for a third and fourth time this year at international summits in China and the US.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump praises US-China friendship at state dinner with Xi Jinping
- list 2 of 3From ‘cheats’ to ‘great friendship’: How Trump’s rhetoric on China changed
- list 3 of 3The Trump-Xi summit exposes a US disadvantage in the Global South
The White House said on Friday that the nations agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents. There was no immediate comment from Beijing on the White House statement.
The announcement came after a summit short on breakthroughs that was dominated by ceremony, according to Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher, reporting from the White House.
“There was a lot of ceremony and a lot of pomp. In fact, there was a lot more pomp than progress,” Fisher said. The two sides agreed to extend a trade truce due to expire in November, pushing the deadline to January “to give both sides the chance to talk”.
Trump said the visit had strengthened his personal rapport with Xi, which he said would benefit the US in the long run.
“We’ve had a tremendous visit from two spectacular people, and we really enjoyed it, and I think we’ve made tremendous strides,” Trump said. “We’ve made great strides, very positive for both countries.”
Calling on both nations to pursue “a healthy competition” that acts as “a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses”, President Xi stated that as “leading nations in artificial intelligence”, the two powers share “the capability and responsibility to develop and manage AI for good”.
Fisher reported that Xi used the summit to press specific aims, seeking assurance that China would be “treated more fairly” in future dealings and laying out guidelines he wants to shape upcoming talks between the two countries.
Xinhua reported Xi also urged Trump to “handle the Taiwan issue prudently” along with discussions on the Middle East, Ukraine, and the Korean Peninsula.
On trade, the White House said China agreed to import at least 10 million metric tonnes of US coal in 2027-2028, with more favourable tariffs on $30bn of “non-sensitive goods” each way. Two pandas are also set to arrive at a US zoo.
The visit featured a state banquet, a military parade and a tour of the National Archives, where the leaders viewed the Declaration of Independence and Constitution. Trump noted the US “goes 250 years; theirs goes 6,000 years”.
The two leaders will meet again at the APEC summit in Shenzhen in November and the G20 in Miami in December.
Fisher said the continuation of dialogue was “perhaps the biggest deliverable for both sides”.

Six designs that freshen up the humble toothbrush
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-26
09:00:14 UTC
18:00:14 KST

Six designs that freshen up the humble toothbrush
After Dyson recently hit headlines with its tech-driven toothbrush, we revisit eight projects from the Dezeen archives that add polish to the everyday dental tool.
Accessories is a collection of toothbrush add-ons, designed specifically for people with dexterity challenges.
It has more than 142 designs, including handles with chunky grips and ridged edges, which make them easier to hold. They also come in a range of textures and colours, which lend them a decorative, homeware-like appearance.
The designer said the project was sparked by accessible design research that had found "users hacking toothbrushes in functional but extremely uncomfortable ways".
Find out more about Accessories ›
Sustainable Sonic Toothbrush by Suri
One of the most recognisable toothbrush brands on the market today, Suri was launched to tackle global dependence on plastic toothbrushes.
In 2022, it released the Sustainable Sonic Toothbrush, with an aluminium body and plant-based brush head that are both recyclable. More recently, it updated its design with Suri 2.0, which has features such as a pressure sensor and wireless induction charging.
"We wanted to create a brush that champions design, performance and sustainability without compromise," Suri told Dezeen.
Find out more about Sustainable Sonic Toothbrush ›
Benjamin Brush by BleepBleeps and MAP
Designed to make brushing teeth more enticing for children, the Benjamin Brush featured an integrated speaker that played music for the recommended two-minute brushing time.
The prototype product had a blue silicone body, designed to be easily held, and interchangeable "pom pom" brush heads that added a playful look.
Find out more about Benjamin Brush ›
Dyson's first dental hygiene product is an electric, tech-driven toothbrush with an integrated mouthwash jet.
Named the Dyson CameraJet, the product has a camera set near the oscillating brush head, which identifies gaps between teeth and negates the need for flossing.
"By combining a camera, machine learning, precision fluid dynamics, advanced brushing technologies, connectivity and WiFi, Dyson CameraJet introduces an entirely new way to keep your mouth healthy," said founder James Dyson.
Find out more about Dyson CameraJet ›
The Misoka toothbrush is designed to clean teeth without toothpaste. Instead, users just need to dip the brush in water.
This is because the bristles are coated in nano-sized mineral ions that, after being loosened by water, are transferred to the teeth. These ions are then able to remove stains and form a protective coating on the enamel, according to its creator, Kosho Ueshima.
The Ara toothbrush was launched in 2017 with integrated artificial intelligence, intended to help users improve their oral health.
A low-energy Bluetooth connection linked it to an app, which displayed brushing data including frequency, duration and areas covered.
