A grand display for Xi reveals the limits of Trump's summitry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
21:04:47 UTC
06:04:47 KST

A grand display for Xi reveals the limits of Trump’s summitry
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Calls for Trump to negotiate a meaningful framework on artificial intelligence fell on deaf ears.
- Trump repeatedly patted Xi on the back, a gesture considered highly inappropriate in Chinese political culture.
WASHINGTON — Expectations were low entering President Trump’s meetings with China’s leader, Xi Jinping, this week, after officials on both sides tempered hopes for a breakthrough. Yet the summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
It was a visual affair designed to project a new phase of managed competition between a prevailing superpower and a rising one — a message that Washington and Beijing are ultimately capable of responsible leadership. But even a cursory look beneath the surface revealed the challenges ahead for the world’s most consequential bilateral relationship.
Industry pleas and bipartisan calls for Trump to negotiate a meaningful framework on artificial intelligence fell on deaf ears. A trade truce between the two sides was extended for a mere two months. And Trump again warned Xi not to assist Iran as the U.S. war there continues — a warning that, so far, has gone unheeded, with millions of dollars’ worth of crucial Chinese parts reportedly arriving in Tehran by the planeload.
“The U.S.-China relationship has settled into a managed stalemate. It has stabilized at the top without stabilizing underneath,” said Craig Singleton, a senior fellow on China at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
Xi Jinping, president of China, issued a call from the White House on Thursday that artificial intelligence remain “under human control” as the world’s two superpowers race for technological supremacy.
“The elaborate pageantry matters precisely because there is still relatively little substantive progress to showcase,” Singleton said. “Trump appears to value the personal relationship as an end in itself. Xi treats his relationship with Trump as a means to shape U.S. choices and forestall future competitive actions.”
The summit followed a playbook from Trump that has become familiar over the last decade, placing his direct relationships at the center of diplomacy and reducing the complexities of statecraft to blunt attempts at charm.
As he did during his lavish state visit to Beijing this spring, Trump repeatedly patted Xi on the back, a gesture considered highly inappropriate in Chinese political culture that nevertheless reflected Trump’s strategic focus on personal friendship.
He toured Xi around a series of controversial renovations to the White House, including the South Lawn — now paved over with a massive helipad designed as the presidential seal — and the Rose Garden, also paved over in order for Trump to host al fresco dinner parties.
Before entering a heavily gilded Oval Office, Trump walked Xi along a renovated colonnade now adorned with gold-framed portraits of U.S. presidents. He paused at one for his predecessor, President Biden, replaced with a mocking image of an autopen, suggesting the former president was incapable of signing documents himself.
Trump patted Xi on the back once more, and the two men laughed, in a moment that generated outrage online.
“Let’s be very clear on this one point,” John Delaney, a former Democratic member of Congress, wrote on social media. “The President mocking a former President in front of the communist leader of China is the most un-American thing an American president has ever done.”
Part of the state visit included a dinner at the White House that was attended by some of the country’s most prominent tech executives, such as Elon Musk, Sam Altman and Mark Zuckerberg. The tech giants’ presence at the event was notable given that there was heightened public interest in knowing how China and the United States are planning to regulate artificial intelligence.
During the visit, Xi called for artificial intelligence to remain “under human control” as the two countries race for technological advancement in the industry. Lawmakers and AI industry leaders have also called for guardrails on the nascent technology, which experts warn could soon surpass human understanding. Trump, however, has been reluctant to embrace limits on the industry, and it is unclear how much the topic was discussed while Xi was in Washington.
Xi Jinping’s remarks reflect growing concern within China over whether governments in Washington or Beijing will be able to contain a technology with potentially transformative capabilities, according to a U.S. official.
President Trump’s rare welcome of Xi and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the airport, as well as the bilateral and cultural events the leaders attended were closely covered — and praised — by Chinese state media. Those who watched at home saw a China elevated in status.
But the visit showed a surprising alignment of visions between the U.S. and Chinese presidents, embracing fierce competition that avoids miscalculation and conflict. Both stressed the importance of dialogue, with Xi invoking the concept of the Thucydides trap, a historical paradigm that holds that rising powers inevitably clash with established ones.
“I don’t think anyone will be surprised if there are no significant agreements,” said David Ochmanek, a senior researcher at Rand. “My sense is that Xi sees little reason to compromise with us on anything right now.”
The two men are expected to meet twice more this year, alongside other world leaders, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, and the Group of 20 summit in Miami.
“We do not need to avoid mentioning competition, but our competition should be a healthy one, and should be kept within bounds,” the Chinese president said Thursday from the Cross Hall of the White House. “It should be a race of catching up with one another, not a wrestle in which one either wins or loses. China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict, and no confrontation between us.
“Our two militaries should maintain regular dialogue, and improve mechanisms for crisis communication and prevention,” he continued. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome.”

Houthi attack on Mecca, Medina would cross ‘red line’, Pakistan PM tells UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:59:43 UTC

Houthi attack on Mecca, Medina would cross ‘red line’, Pakistan PM tells UN
Shehbaz Sharif speaks as Islamabad, Riyadh and Ankara army chiefs meet to discuss Mecca pact, closer military ties.
Pakistan’s prime minister has condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, warning that any “threat to the sanctity” of the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina is a “red line that must never be crossed”.
Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Friday, Shehbaz Sharif denounced recent Houthi attacks as “deplorable”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Pakistan PM calls Houthi threats to Saudi holy sites a ‘red line’
- list 2 of 3Oil prices jump after Yemen’s Houthis claim attacks on Saudi facilities
- list 3 of 3Netanyahu’s UN belligerence wins cheers at home as world walks out
He added that an attack by the Iran-aligned Yemeni group, which Riyadh says targeted Mecca, “outraged Muslims across the globe”. The Houthis have dismissed the accusations as a “heinous lie”.
Last month, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed a trilateral defence pact, formally known as the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement. The pact states that an attack on any member will be treated as an attack on all. However, Islamabad and Ankara have refrained from getting involved in Riyadh’s ongoing fight with the Houthis.
The military chiefs of all three countries met in Riyadh on Friday and discussed enhancing intelligence sharing and military coordination, the Pakistani military said. The chiefs reviewed the security situation and threats facing Saudi Arabia, affirmed a commitment to collective defence and pledged to turn Mecca Agreement commitments into effective cooperation, the army added.
It is not clear what, if any, support Ankara and Islamabad may provide to Riyadh. In a written interview published by the US media outlet Newsweek on Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said support could include “intelligence, logistics or ammunition, with more extensive military assistance possible depending on the scale of the threat”.
Iran and Palestine
In Sharif’s UN address, he also referenced the US-Israeli war that was launched against Iran in late February, as well as Islamabad’s role as a co-mediator.
Pakistan’s efforts culminated in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, signed by Washington and Tehran, which was intended to help end the conflict.
The accord has since unravelled while regional countries push for a conclusive end to the war, which has caused a global energy crisis and exacerbated tensions across the Middle East.
“Yet amid the roar of missiles, drones and guns, the voice for diplomacy must echo even louder and stronger,” Sharif said.
He added that the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has effectively blockaded, and the Bab al-Mandeb waterway, which is now largely under Houthi control, are “arteries of the global economy” that should remain free and safe.
The Pakistani prime minister also denounced what he described as Israel’s “genocidal agenda” in Palestine, while condemning “Israeli aggression against Lebanon and Syria”. These were sentiments echoed earlier in the day by Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam in his UN General Assembly address.
India, Kashmir, Afghanistan
Closer to home, Sharif’s speech touched on tensions with Pakistan’s neighbours.
Criticising India, he accused New Delhi of weaponising the Indus waters, which both countries have jointly managed for more than six decades. The two neighbours heavily rely on the Himalayan river network.
Sharif warned that “any attempt to stop, impede or divert Pakistan’s share of the waters will be treated as an act of war”.
He also called for what he described as a “just and fair solution” to the Kashmir dispute, which both Pakistan and India claim in its entirety. Sharif alleged that there have been attempts to “alter the legal status” of Kashmir through demographic engineering.
Another pressing issue for Islamabad is the threat posed by the Tehrik-e-Taliban (TTP), or Pakistani Taliban. Sharif said groups operate from “sanctuaries inside Afghanistan, with the aim of destabilising Pakistan”, insisting that attacks launched from Afghanistan “must come to a grinding halt”.
This comes as the latest cross-border fighting left several Afghan Taliban fighters dead on Friday.

US Supreme Court allows Trump administration to use database to check voter citizenship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:54:45 UTC
05:54:45 KST

The US Supreme Court has granted a Trump administration request to allow the use of a federal database to weed out potential non-citizens from the voter rolls.
A majority of the nine justices on the top court joined the unsigned opinion, providing a victory to President Donald Trump ahead of the November mid-term elections.
The three liberal justices on the conservative-dominated court dissented.
Trump has stated for years that many non-citizens vote in US elections and that mail-in ballots are vulnerable to fraud.
Friday's Supreme Court decision lifted a lower court order that had blocked the use of a Department of Homeland Security program known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) to verify the citizenship of individuals on the voter rolls.
SAVE is used to identify citizenship status to determine whether someone is eligible for benefits.
Ruling against the Trump administration in June, the lower court said, "States have partnered with the federal government to access the database and are actively removing United States citizens from voter rolls based on inaccurate information.
In its ruling, the Supreme Court said the federal government "has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters."
The lower court order blocking the use of SAVE "prevents the Federal Government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task."
“Victory for election integrity”
US Attorney General Todd Blanche welcomed the Supreme Court ruling as a "huge victory for election integrity," saying it will "allow states to clear the voter rolls of illegal voters."
Election experts, however, said the ruling is unlikely to have a major impact on the November elections because most US states ban purges of voters 90 days ahead of an election.
"Both the majority and dissent agree that this case is likely to have limited impact on the midterms," Rick Hasen, a law professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, said in a blog post.
"Compared to the recent mail-in voting case, this one is not very important substantively."
Hasen was referring to a Supreme Court decision earlier this month that blocked a Trump plan that would have restricted the use of mail-in ballots.
Trump reacted furiously to that ruling, calling it "horrible" in a Truth Social post.

Sudanese army says it captured strategic North Kordofan city of Sodiri

Adel Abdelrheem, Rania Abushamala

The Sudanese army said Friday it had seized control of Sodiri in North Kordofan state after fierce clashes with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).
“Our forces liberated the city of Sodiri in North Kordofan state today after fierce battles that inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment on the terrorist militia,” the army said in a statement, referring to the RSF.
The announcement followed accounts from military sources who told Anadolu earlier Friday that army troops and allied forces had entered Sodiri and taken control after intense fighting with the RSF.
Sodiri has been a key RSF stronghold in northern North Kordofan. It lies near Hamrat al-Sheikh and Umm Badr, close to the borders with North Darfur to the west and West Kordofan to the south.
Army personnel and members of allied armed movements also posted videos on social media that they said were filmed inside Sodiri after its capture. The footage showed destroyed combat vehicles they said belonged to the RSF.
The RSF had not commented on the developments as of 1845GMT.
The army’s reported capture of Sodiri follows a series of advances elsewhere in North Kordofan that have increased pressure on RSF forces in the state’s far northwest, particularly around Al-Mazrub, Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Badr.
It also comes days after the army announced that it had captured 11 areas in North Kordofan, one of its largest reported advances in the state in recent weeks. On Sept. 6, the army said it had taken Hamrat al-Waz in Jabra al-Sheikh locality.
Since late July, the army has reported gaining extensive territory in North Kordofan, including the city of Bara and areas around Jabra al-Sheikh and Umm Sayala. It also said it had secured the main road linking Bara to Omdurman, west of the capital, Khartoum.
Sudan’s three Kordofan states — North, West and South — have witnessed continued clashes between the army and the RSF since last October.
The war between the two sides began in April 2023 and has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced around 13 million, according to UN and international estimates.

Thieves Stole ‘Nvidia’ Trailers. They Got 20 Tons of Sand
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:30:40 UTC
05:30:40 KST

On Thursday morning, a top executive at self-driving truck developer PlusAI received an unexpected congratulatory text message from an acquaintance. “I have been proud of you for your adventure and success at Plus. Just saw two of your trucks near my work place! :)” the message said.
But PlusAI’s trucks weren’t supposed to be near this person’s office, in Newark, California. As of the last the company knew, the trailers were docked outside its warehouse, half a mile away. Soon, according to a police statement, cops were on the scene to help recover the two trailers, emblazoned with logos for PlusAI and Nvidia, the most valuable company in the world. The two companies are working together on AI software and autonomous truck technology.
That’s when PlusAI employees gave police a hint as to why whoever hooked their own cabs up to the trailers and drove away might have abandoned the whole thing after breaking them open: Each trailer was full of about 20,000 pounds of sand.
“PlusAI uses simulated loads in its trailers to assist with research and development testing,” says Lauren Kwan, a company spokesperson. The trailers were recovered with “40,000 pounds of sand intact.”
PlusAI’s tech-enabled truck cabs—where the driver typically sits and controls the vehicle—were parked inside its warehouse and weren’t taken, Kwan says. The trailers were secured with hand locks, which were broken.
The case is under investigation, and no arrests have been made, says Amy Gee, a spokesperson for the Fremont Police Department.
Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
The incident comes at a time of rising theft targeting high-value computer equipment, especially chips and other electronics meant for use in data centers. In August, WIRED revealed two California incidents in which thieves deliberately struck the vehicles of security escorts that follow high-value tech loads to ensure they reach their destinations. The trucks involved were then driven to another destination. As of August, millions of dollars of data center equipment onboard had not been recovered.
This year, thieves have also targeted Tesla batteries and various bitcoin mining machines. Authorities have arrested suspects in some cases, but many crimes remain unsolved.
Some of the most common targets of cargo theft in recent months across the US include metals and enterprise-grade computer and networking equipment, according to Verisk CargoNet, an analytics and risk assessment firm.
This story has a happier ending. By Thursday afternoon, the sand trailers were back with PlusAI, the Fremont Police Department said.

====================================================================================================

The big 'what if': Do those chanting 'from the river to the sea' really mean it? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:15:36 UTC
05:15:36 KST

What if they mean what they are saying?
How many times must we hear “Free Palestine from the river to the sea” at concerts, on university campuses, and city streets?
How many politicians, celebrities, and people of influence must repeat those words before we confront the question hiding in plain sight: What if they actually mean it?
Between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea live approximately seven million Jews. Let us be clear: a Palestinian state replacing Israel across this entire territory is not suggesting a two-state solution.
What happens to the Jews who live there, some for generations?
Where do they go? Who protects them? And what happens if they refuse to leave?
These are not hypothetical questions about a distant future. They concern the survival of a people whose history includes persecution, expulsion, and attempted annihilation.
Yet the international debate increasingly treats Israel’s elimination as a legitimate political aspiration without demanding an explanation of its consequences.
Consider the regional realities.
Israel is surrounded by Arab states that are not liberal democracies. The Palestinian Authority has not held a presidential election since 2005. Hamas, which seized control of Gaza in 2007, perpetrated the October 7 massacre.
In September 2026, the US again denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas an entry visa for the UN General Assembly, citing objections to Palestinian leadership conduct. Abbas has also made statements widely condemned as Holocaust denial.
The PA and Hamas are the political institutions and movements against which promises of coexistence must be evaluated.
Israel withdrew its settlements and permanent ground forces from Gaza in 2005. Rather than creating a peaceful model of Palestinian governance alongside Israel, Hamas built military capabilities and ultimately launched October 7.
What credible guarantees would protect seven million Jews suddenly transformed from a sovereign majority into a vulnerable minority?
October 7 was not the whole plan
Evidence uncovered since October 7 makes this question considerably more urgent.
Hamas documents examined by The New York Times revealed that Yahya Sinwar sought to enlist Iran and Hezbollah in a broader assault against Israel.
In July 2023, a senior Hamas official discussed the planned attack with an Iranian Revolutionary Guard commander. According to the reported documents, Iran and Hezbollah welcomed the plan in principle but needed more time to prepare.
Sinwar proceeded.
Meanwhile, Israel subsequently exposed Hezbollah’s preparations for its own invasion of the Galilee.
The IDF reported discovering underground compounds, tunnels, weapons, motorcycles, and operational infrastructure intended to support attacks and military operations on northern Israeli communities.
How can anyone assess the foreseeable consequences of Israel’s elimination while ignoring the intentions and conduct of armed organizations seeking its destruction?
Three choices for seven million Jews
The first choice is departure, but to where?
At the 1938 Évian Conference, most participating countries refused to expand immigration opportunities for Jews fleeing Nazi persecution.
In 1939, the St. Louis, carrying more than 900 Jewish refugees, was denied entry to Cuba and the US. Forced back to Europe, many passengers subsequently perished in the Holocaust.
The second possibility is remaining under Palestinian sovereignty.
Would Hamas protect Jewish religious freedom? Would the PA guarantee Jewish property rights? What independent judiciary, police force, or military would protect Jewish communities against extremists?
The third possibility is resistance.
Millions of Israeli Jews could refuse to surrender their country and fight.
The consequences could include regional war, mass displacement, and catastrophic loss of life.
If a movement knowingly pursues a political objective whose implementation entails mass expulsion or destruction, can its proponents avoid scrutiny simply by calling their objective liberation?
Apply the same genocide standard
Israel has faced accusations of genocide in Gaza. Amnesty International’s December 2024 finding relied on officials’ statements, patterns of conduct, and cumulative consequences. Israel rejects the accusation.
The Genocide Convention requires specific intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. That intent may be inferred from evidence; it need not be announced explicitly.
Now, apply the same methodology to a movement demanding Israel’s elimination.
Examine its rhetoric and the conduct of organizations pursuing that objective. Examine historical context, foreseeable consequences, and the willingness to accept mass harm.
If the intended outcome of “Free Palestine from the river to the sea” is the forced departure of seven million Jews, the issue is ethnic cleansing.
If the intended outcome includes killing Jews who refuse to leave, or deliberately imposing conditions calculated to destroy them as a group, the issue becomes genocide.
And if advocates knowingly accept such consequences, their declared objective of liberation cannot automatically absolve them of responsibility.
Intent cannot require inference when Israel is accused but suddenly require an explicit confession when Jews are the prospective victims.
Not every demonstrator intends genocide. But those demanding Israel’s elimination must explain how their objective could be implemented without mass expulsion, persecution, or killing.
Why does the Palestinian refugee problem endure?
Following the Holocaust, Jewish survivors were resettled, including in the newly established State of Israel.
Approximately 850,000 Jews left or were expelled from Arab countries and Iran in the decades surrounding Israel’s establishment. Many were absorbed by Israel despite enormous challenges.
The Palestinian refugee question followed a different trajectory.
UNRWA began operations in 1950, serving approximately 750,000 refugees. Today, approximately 5.9 million people, including descendants, are eligible for its services.
Why has a permanent solution proved so elusive?
Could the enduring refugee problem itself have become a strategic instrument in the long-term struggle against Israel?
Harder to understand is why so many in Europe and America have embraced demands framed around eliminating the one Jewish state among a multitude of Arab states.
Diaspora Jews
The danger does not stop at Israel’s borders.
Israel has sovereign institutions, intelligence services, and an army. Diaspora Jews depend on their host governments for protection.
In America, the warning signs are unmistakable.
According to the American Jewish Committee’s 2025 survey, published in February 2026, 91% of American Jews said violent antisemitic attacks had made them feel less safe. Thirty-one percent reported personally experiencing antisemitism during the preceding year.
CNN’s July 2026 analysis found that Israel’s average net favorability had fallen from plus 51 during Trump’s first term to minus 16, a staggering 67-point reversal.
Among Democratic voters, sympathy for Palestinians now exceeds sympathy for Israelis by 60% to 16%.
For Israel, the implications extend to its diplomatic relationships. For American Jews, already confronting rising antisemitism, the changing environment raises additional questions about their security and place in American society.
History has repeatedly demonstrated what happens when Jews become politically powerless, and societies cease to protect them.
The Holocaust is not ancient history. October 7 was less than three years ago.
At the UN this month, the world is being asked to normalize political demands whose implementation could place millions of Jews in existential danger.
Those advocating peaceful coexistence must explain how to achieve it. Those advocating expulsion or destruction must be judged by the same standards applied to anyone threatening a protected population.
And those who chant without considering the consequences must confront the genocidal implications of their words.
Because the concern is no longer just simply what the slogan’s genocidal meaning is.
The concern is what happens if someone attempts to turn it into reality, as Iran and Hamas tried on October 7.
For those of us who laughed at the many demonstrators who couldn’t tell you which river and which sea, perhaps laughing was a very inappropriate response.
What if some of them really mean what they are saying?
The writer is a global strategist and a strategic adviser at the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs. Follow him on X: @jeffkahn2020

How online toxicity silences the majority and fuels power users
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:00:37 UTC
05:00:37 KST

In online political discussions, a small fraction of highly active users typically generates the vast majority of content while most people silently observe. A recent experiment reveals that polite and constructive environments encourage silent readers to post their first comment, but the most active users are driven to post more when discussions become toxic. These findings were published in the journal Science Advances.
Online spaces are central to modern political discourse, yet they suffer from a stark participation divide. A vocal minority often dominates the conversation, creating a distorted picture of public opinion. Researchers refer to these highly active individuals as power users, while the vast majority who consume content without posting are known as lurkers.
This uneven participation raises concerns about a spiral of silence. This is a theory where citizens withhold their views if they believe those views are unpopular. In the modern attention economy of social media, extreme or hostile content often gains the most visibility.
If only a specific type of user feels comfortable producing this content, online discussions may look much more polarized than the actual public. A cycle emerges where moderate voices retreat, leaving the platform to those who thrive on conflict.
To understand what drives people into these distinct roles, researchers need to observe communities as they form. Lead author Lisa Oswald, a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, alongside colleagues William Small Schulz and Philipp Lorenz-Spreen, designed a study to track exactly how users select into active or silent roles. They also wanted to test whether financial rewards or strict civility rules could level the playing field.
The researchers recruited 520 participants from the United States through advertisements on the social media platform Reddit. After participants completed an initial survey about their political views and online habits, they were randomly assigned to one of six private Reddit communities created specifically for the study.
Over four weeks, the research team prompted the groups with 20 different political issues. They asked participants to discuss topics ranging from immigration and gun control to universal basic income and artificial intelligence.
To test ways to close the participation gap, the researchers applied different conditions to the communities. Two communities served as a control group with standard platform settings. In two other communities, participants received a financial incentive, earning two dollars for every day they wrote a substantive comment.
The final two communities operated under a moderation condition. In these groups, users received frequent reminders to stay civil and respectful alongside automated spam filters.
Participants completed weekly surveys about their experiences and perceptions of the group dynamics. The researchers then categorized the users into two groups. One group consisted of those who never commented, while the other included those who wrote at least one comment.
For the active users, the team tracked the total number of comments they contributed. The results revealed a mirrored psychological mechanism driving both initial participation and heavy posting.
Participants who remained silent were more likely to view the group as polarized and toxic. These users indicated they preferred environments that felt respectful, knowledgeable, and constructive. If a community felt hostile, they chose to simply read the posts and say nothing.
For users who crossed the threshold to write at least one comment, the exact opposite held true. The active users posted more frequently when they perceived the group as polarized, toxic, and lacking in knowledge.
The researchers noted that an abrasive environment suppresses the voices of the silent majority. At the same time, it acts as a catalyst for a less sensitive minority to dominate the conversation. The objective toxicity of the group interacts with a user’s personal sensitivity to hostility to determine their behavior.
The interventions designed to improve the conversation had mixed results. Financial incentives did encourage more people to speak up, narrowing the participation gap between lurkers and power users. Providing a direct reward successfully motivated hesitant users to join the conversation.
The moderation condition failed to change participation levels or improve the quality of the discourse. Reminding users to remain civil did not reduce the participation gap, nor did it lower the toxicity of the comments. The researchers observed that simply asking for polite behavior is unlikely to change the underlying dynamics of online engagement.
The researchers also analyzed how social feedback influenced user behavior. They found that receiving positive votes on comments was associated with increased posting the following day. When participants received negative feedback through downvotes, they were less likely to continue participating.
The experiment also tracked whether engaging in these political discussions changed participants’ minds. Over the four weeks, the research team found no statistically significant differences in political attitude changes between the treatment groups and the control group. Measures of political trust and polarization remained relatively stable regardless of the community rules or incentives.
Descriptively across all groups, participants reported lower levels of political interest and issue knowledge by the end of the study. The researchers suggested this might be due to an intimidation effect. The comments posted during the study were considerably longer and more detailed than typical Reddit posts, which may have led some participants to feel they could not add anything to the conversation.
The study took place in a uniquely controlled environment that differs from organic social media use. The participants were predominantly liberal, meaning the discussions lacked the deep ideological clashes often found in broader public forums. Additionally, the overall toxicity of the comments during the experiment was exceptionally low from the start.
This low baseline of toxicity left little room for the moderation treatment to make a measurable impact. Future research could explore whether strictly enforced rules, such as banning hostile users rather than just reminding them to be civil, might yield different outcomes. Scientists also plan to investigate how these group dynamics function on other platforms with different community structures and algorithms.
The study, “Disentangling participation in online political discussions with a collective field experiment,” was authored by Lisa Oswald, William Small Schulz, and Philipp Lorenz-Spreen.

Fabrizio Corneli creates dramatic installation for glasses brand Lindberg
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
20:00:15 UTC
05:00:15 KST

Fabrizio Corneli creates dramatic installation for glasses brand Lindberg
Promotion: Danish eyewear brand Lindberg has presented a site-specific installation for the Armory Show in New York City, created with Italian artist Fabrizio Corneli.
Called Enigma of Vision, the minimalist installation opened on 24 September as part of the city's annual Armory Show of contemporary art.
Lindberg, which distinguishes itself from other eyewear brands through its sharp, architectural approach to design, commissioned Corneli to design the site-specific work for the exhibition.
Enigma of Vision presents two interconnected artworks by Corneli, whose portfolio of site-specific pieces is defined by experiments with light and shadow.
The first is Seed, a sculpture featuring a concealed light source. When visitors interact with the sculpture, it reveals an image of the globe.
Lindberg explained that the piece encourages visitors to reflect on humanity's connected future through the interplay of space, form and light.
The second artwork is called Eyecatcher. This piece centres on a selection of Lindberg's most recognisable glasses, transforming the frames into sources of striking shadows, which are a familiar motif in Corneli's work.
Together, both pieces express Lindberg's philosophy of stripping away design to its essential parts, while also exploring how perception is shaped equally by what we see and "what remains hidden".
Since 1986, Lindberg has been producing lightweight glasses in materials like titanium and wood, without the need for screws or rivets.
The brand has since ventured into the art world and has been an active participant in the industry since 1986.
Lindberg was first present at the Armory Show in 2024, when it collaborated with American photography and sculpture artist Letha Wilson.
Last year, Brooklyn-based artist Yuko Nishikawa created a Lindberg installation of delicate sculptural mobiles for the show.
The brand considers Enigma of Vision to be a progression of Lindberg's commitment to the arts.
"Lindberg's collaboration with Corneli is a natural extension of the brand's design philosophy, where technical mastery and artistic expression converge to challenge perception and reveal beauty through simplicity," said the founder, president, and CEO of Kering Eyewear, which owns Lindberg, Roberto Vedovotto.
To learn more about Lindberg, visit its website here.

Potential weekend disruptions follow an equipment outage on Monday that forced carriers to cancel hundreds of flights bound for the New York area and Philadelphia.

04:59:21 KST

US President Donald Trump warned Chinese President Xi Jinping against providing support to Iran during talks in Washington this week and received assurances that China would not do so, the US ambassador to China said on Friday.
The warning came amid reports that China had supplied Iran with shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers and that Tehran had found ways to evade sanctions on its oil sales with Chinese help.
David Perdue, Trump's ambassador to Beijing, said in a CNBC interview that Trump reiterated to Xi that direct or indirect support for Iran was "totally unacceptable."
Asked separately on Fox News if that meant China would stop assisting Iran, Perdue said Washington received assurances from Beijing on Thursday.
"We've seen movement ... on that already. That's what the commitment is. They assured us yesterday they're not doing that," Perdue told Fox News' "America's Newsroom" program.
Trump later on Friday acknowledged that the two leaders discussed the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran in late February, without giving details.
Missile launchers, sanctions dodge
US lawmakers had urged Trump to confront Xi over reports of Chinese assistance to Iran, raising concerns that Chinese entities may have given targeting help that led to US casualties in the conflict.
Chinese officials have assured Iran that even after the Trump-Xi meeting, China will not limit its economic, political or military ties with Tehran under pressure from the US president, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
Reuters reported in July that Iran was expected to receive within weeks a first shipment of up to 400 Chinese-made shoulder-fired air-defense missile launchers.
Iran has also used a barter-like arrangement to bypass sanctions on its oil sales and buy billions of dollars’ worth of goods from China, including military gear, two senior Iranian sources and three other people familiar with the matter told Reuters earlier this month.
Chinese state newswire Xinhua reported on Thursday that Xi had urged the US and Iran to return to negotiations to end the war, but Xi has not publicly commented on Chinese support for Iran.
Trump and Xi did not take formal questions during the three-day state visit to Washington.
Earlier this month, Trump brushed aside a report that Iran acquired satellite images of a base in Jordan from Chinese entities before an attack that killed three US troops there in July.
"They basically do what we do," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on September 13. "When they say China spies on us, I say you're right, and we spy on them too."

Eritrea's Blue Revolution: Inside the movement challenging one of Africa's longest-serving rulers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:58:55 UTC
04:58:55 KST

In a side street in south Tel Aviv, there sits a small office where a group of men is hard at work. Most of that work concerns a country none of them has seen for years, but which remains present in almost everything they do.
Michael, also known as Atakliti Abraham, does much of the talking during The Jerusalem Post’s visit. Alongside him are Mulue Sultan, international coordinator of the Israeli wing of the Eritrean Blue Revolution Front, and Awat Hagos, the movement’s social affairs coordinator in Israel.
The office is part political headquarters, part community organization, and part meeting place for Eritreans who believe their time in Israel should eventually come to an end.
Their days are spent speaking with members of their community, dealing with Israeli police and politicians, organizing activities for children, and maintaining contact with a much larger opposition network stretching across Europe, North America, and Africa.
They speak about football pitches and computer courses alongside political prisoners, military service, and an Eritrean opposition movement attempting to reinvent itself. Phones appear throughout the conversation, photographs are pulled up and passed across the table, and names of friends still inside Eritrea are treated with caution.
For most Israelis, the Eritrean community has entered the national conversation through a familiar set of arguments. “Asylum seekers” to some, “infiltrators” to others, Eritreans are a population concentrated heavily in south Tel Aviv whose presence has produced years of political battles.
Immigration, refugee status, crime, deportation, and the responsibility Israel bears toward people who crossed its border after fleeing Africa are all aspects pertaining to these political battles.
The men in the office approach the issue from another direction. They have built lives in Israel, some have raised children in Israel, and all speak warmly about the country that gave them refuge. Yet when Michael is asked what he actually wants for his future, he answers almost immediately.
“If the regime falls tomorrow, tomorrow we go home.”
It is a useful starting point for understanding almost everything else happening in the room.
The organization they represent is today called the Eritrean Blue Revolution Front (EBRF), an international opposition movement that emerged from Brigade N’Hamedu. This blue-clad grassroots movement began organizing Eritrean government opponents across the diaspora several years ago.
In Israel, the work has a distinctly local character. The movement holds regular meetings and stays in touch with parts of the Eritrean community around the country.
Hagos and the others speak proudly of soccer programs they say now involve hundreds of Eritrean children, as well as computer courses and other activities intended to give teenagers somewhere to go and something to belong to. A recent EBRF Congress in Israel attracted 1,300 people.
The problem becomes more pronounced as those children get older. Many were born in Israel or arrived at such a young age that Hebrew became one of their first languages. They attend Israeli schools, follow Israeli football clubs, have Israeli friends, and know Eritrea largely through their parents.
Mulue later returned to the subject in a voice message because, he says, he felt it was important enough to add even after the interview had ended.
“We have many children who have studied in the State of Israel,” he says. “They feel Israeli. They don’t really know Eritrea; they only know that they have a country.”
For their parents, Eritrea is a place they remember. For some of their children, it is an inherited country waiting somewhere across the Red Sea.
Michael’s own relationship with Eritrea is considerably more immediate. He says he entered the military system in November 1997 at the age of 14 and remained there until 2011. Some of the young men who entered alongside him, he says, were still trapped within the system long after he had escaped.
“I came here so that I could speak like a human being, so that I could write like a human being,” he notes. “In my country, I couldn’t write, I couldn’t speak about the dictator.”
The route that eventually brought him to Israel was not one he describes as a search for work or a better salary. Eritreans fleeing north moved first through Sudan, then under Omar al-Bashir, where many feared arrest and being sent back. From there came smugglers, traffickers, and the route across Sinai.
“We didn’t come here to work,” Michael says. “We came to save our lives.”
Over a decade later, he now spends much of his time helping run an organization whose declared ambition is to make that refuge unnecessary.
To understand why, one must go back to the extraordinary promise with which modern Eritrea began.
The country they left behind
Few countries entered independence with as much reason to celebrate as Eritrea.
The struggle that produced the modern state had lasted roughly three decades, beginning in 1961 after years of growing resistance to Ethiopian rule. By the time Eritrean guerrillas entered the capital Asmara in 1991, generations had grown up knowing little other than war.
Two years later, Eritreans finally voted on independence in a referendum monitored by the United Nations. Turnout exceeded 98%, and 99.8% of those who cast ballots voted for independence. UN observers concluded that the referendum had, overall, been conducted freely and fairly.
On April 27, following the referendum result, Eritrea declared itself an independent and sovereign state.
At the center of the victory stood Isaias Afwerki, one of the principal leaders of the Eritrean People’s Liberation Front. This movement had fought a much larger Ethiopian military and now had to transform itself from a revolutionary army into a state government.
For a time, there were reasons for optimism.
Eritrea had emerged from one of Africa’s longest wars with a powerful sense of national identity and a leadership that enjoyed enormous prestige for defeating successive Ethiopian governments.
Work began on a constitution, and in 1997 a new document was adopted that promised civil rights, political institutions, and limits on executive power.
It never came into force, and the young state soon found itself at war again.
Eritrea finds itself at war again
In May 1998, a border dispute between Eritrea and Ethiopia erupted into a devastating interstate conflict. Trenches and massed infantry and artillery returned to a frontier that had only recently become an international boundary.
Fighting continued, with interruptions, until 2000, displacing vast numbers of people on both sides before the two governments agreed to a cessation of hostilities and later signed the Algiers Agreement in December that year.
The war left a deep imprint on Eritrea’s political system. National service, introduced earlier in the decade and legally limited to 18 months, became effectively indefinite after the 1998 emergency. The country remained heavily militarized even after the guns fell silent.
The political opening that many Eritreans had expected after independence narrowed further.
In 2001, senior figures from within the ruling movement itself – the group that became known as the G-15 – publicly demanded reform, an implementation of the constitution, and greater accountability from Afwerki.
The response was comprehensive. Reformist officials were detained, privately owned newspapers were closed, and journalists were arrested.
On September 18, 2001, Eritrea shut down its independent press. Several of the journalists arrested during the crackdown have never been seen publicly again.
Twenty-five years later, the basic political structure remains largely unchanged. Eritrea has held no national elections since independence, the 1997 constitution remains unimplemented, the legislature has not met since 2010, and no political party other than the ruling People’s Front for Democracy and Justice is permitted to operate.
Human Rights Watch continues to document arbitrary detention, enforced disappearance, and restrictions on religion, expression, and association.
National service remains one of the defining institutions of Eritrean life.
Legally, it should end after 18 months. In practice, Human Rights Watch reported again this year that Eritreans continue to serve for years and sometimes decades, often for little pay and with no clear end-of-service date.
Since 2003, thousands of secondary school pupils have been required to complete their final year at a military training camp in Sawa, which combines education with army practice and political instruction.
When Michael talks about entering the system as a teenager and watching years disappear, his story fits into a much larger national experience.
Mulue argues that the consequences are now returning to haunt the government.
“Many people, women and men, were in the army for decades,” he says. “They have experience in all kinds of roles.”
Large numbers of Eritreans who escaped the system eventually found themselves scattered across Sudan, Ethiopia, Israel, Europe and North America. Many carried their military training with them, along with anger at the state that had kept them in uniform.
“If there is a place to organize and begin fighting,” Mulue said, “we don’t need much time to learn military things. We already have people who are ready.”
It is one of the stranger legacies of post-independence Eritrea. A government that spent decades keeping much of its population under arms has helped create a diaspora in which thousands of people already know how to use them.
For many years, however, the opposition abroad remained notoriously divided. Groups split along political, generational, ethnic, and religious lines; older organizations carried baggage from arguments stretching back into the liberation struggle, while younger Eritreans often had little interest in joining them.
Brigade N’Hamedu emerged from a different generation and through a different type of politics.
Its activists appeared in blue at demonstrations against festivals associated with Eritrean embassies and government supporters abroad.
What began as a protest movement grew quickly, especially among younger diaspora members, and confrontations with regime supporters began spreading across Europe and North America.
Eventually, its leaders decided street protests had taken them as far as they could.
The next stage would be much more ambitious.
From protest movement to international front
When the Post later spoke at length with senior EBRF figures outside Israel, the transformation from Brigade N’Hamedu to the organization that exists today was the first subject raised.
Dawit Teferi, EBRF’s director of finance and a member of its diplomatic team, describes it as an attempt to turn a movement capable of filling streets into one capable of wielding political power.
“We are attempting to evolve from a grassroots movement into creating a political wing,” he tells the Post.
Brigade N’Hamedu had succeeded in attracting attention and mobilizing Eritreans who had previously remained outside established opposition structures.
Demonstrations outside regime-linked festivals generated international headlines, but they also increasingly produced violence, arrests and police investigations.
Teferi argues that continuing down that path risked letting the movement be defined by clashes in European cities rather than by what it wanted to achieve inside Eritrea.
“We have precisely cut down on our activities internationally in terms of protest,” he said, “and we’re focusing on building the operational side and the diplomatic side.”
EBRF now describes itself as a front rather than a conventional political party. Its leaders speak of a council meant to represent different branches and participating groups, a central committee that functions as an executive body, and a smaller leadership nucleus at the center.
The numbers they gave the Post varied according to what was being counted. At one point, EBRF representative Beyene Gerezgher spoke of 17 or 18 national chapters, including Israel; elsewhere, the movement referred to roughly 70 local chapters or representative organizations participating through a wider council.
Teferi cites an official estimate of around 100,000 supporters worldwide and at least 30,000 active members, figures that cannot currently be independently verified.
Publicly, the movement appears to be expanding well beyond the demonstrations from which it emerged. EBRF has developed an operation in Washington and retained professional representation in the United States.
US Justice Department filings under the Foreign Agents Registration Act identify EBRF representatives, including Teferi and Gerezgher, and list the organization’s address in Addis Ababa.
Teferi speaks about cultivating support across party lines and says EBRF has held discussions with members of Congress and their offices.
He wants American policymakers to view Eritrea through strategic as well as human-rights considerations: a country stretching along the Red Sea, facing Yemen and positioned close to one of the world’s most important maritime arteries.
Ethiopia, however, is where the most sensitive part of the project is taking shape.
“The operational side is based in Ethiopia,” Teferi says. “And it has its own command structure as well.”
For Eritreans, that sentence would have been unthinkable just a few years ago, since Eritrean nationalism was forged in resistance to Ethiopian rule and given that independence came only after a 30-year war, with the two states then returning to combat within five years of separating.
Even today, Addis Ababa’s renewed discussion of access to the Red Sea can raise immediate suspicions in Eritrea.
EBRF has chosen to engage with the issue rather than dismiss it.
Gerezgher, who works on the movement’s political and diplomatic affairs, says the Addis Ababa operation gives EBRF access to Eritrean refugees, as well as the wider diplomatic world centered on the African Union, Western embassies, and international organizations.
He insists the movement has no authority to sign away Eritrean interests or promise access to its coastline while it remains an opposition organization.
Any agreement involving Ethiopian use of Eritrean ports, he says, would have to be negotiated by a future constitutional government with the legal authority to do so.
“We don’t have anything to give at this time,” he tells the Post. “We don’t have anything to promise at this time.”
At the same time, he acknowledges that EBRF’s presence in Ethiopia depends upon a political environment that allows it to operate.
“We are operating from here,” he says, “but for sure, we are protected by the Ethiopians.”
The relationship is one of the ways EBRF is attempting to break with older Eritrean opposition politics. Teferi argued that endless suspicion of Ethiopia has helped trap Eritreans inside the political worldview created by Afwerki himself.
If a future government can negotiate mutually beneficial arrangements while protecting Eritrean sovereignty, he sees little reason why old enemies must remain enemies forever.
The Jewish state as an EBRF litmus test
Israel fits into the same line of thinking.
When Teferi discusses how the EBRF decides which other opposition groups it can work with, he says their attitude toward Ethiopia provides one test.
Then comes another: “Israel is the litmus test.”
He argues that groups incapable of discussing cooperation with Israel without immediately retreating into older ideological arguments are unlikely to fit within EBRF’s coalition.
The front, he says, is intended to be broad enough to include people from very different political backgrounds. Gerezgher speaks of civic organizations, women’s groups, academics, investors, political organizations, and members of Eritrea’s various communities all operating within the same structure.
Yet there are boundaries. Teferi says he would oppose the participation of groups he regards as Muslim Brotherhood-aligned or extreme Christian political movements, arguing that a future Eritrean state should remain secular.
Those limitations raise questions that any movement promising democracy eventually has to answer: Where does protection of a secular political order end and exclusion of political opponents begin?
The larger unanswered question concerns force.
EBRF leaders repeatedly tell the Post that they would prefer the least violent route possible. Information campaigns, diplomatic pressure, civil resistance and the development of contacts within the country all feature heavily in their explanation of how change might occur.
“When we say regime change, it doesn’t mean a war or violence,” Gerezgher says. “There are a lot of mechanisms to bring change into Eritrea.”
Operating from a place of hope
Eritrea provides almost no space to measure public opinion, let alone a place where a clandestine opposition network can operate openly. EBRF’s assessment that large parts of the population and military are waiting for an opportunity to turn against the government remains just that: the movement’s assessment.
Teferi nevertheless has little doubt about the workforce he believes could be mobilized.
“I have thousands and thousands of people who are willing to fight for the country.”
The emphasis on military capability is accompanied by a surprisingly detailed discussion about what would happen if Afwerki’s system actually collapsed.
This is an important question for an Eritrean opposition movement because the current president was once a revolutionary leader himself.
Afwerki and many of his generation spent decades fighting a government they regarded as oppressive. However, victory did not ultimately produce the constitutional system many Eritreans had expected.
Gerezgher says EBRF envisages a transitional government lasting roughly two or three years, during which the country would stabilize and move toward constitutional rule.
“We will have an interim government for two or three years,” he says.
Teferi speaks of presidential term limits, a legislature, and competitive politics, while drawing on aspects of the unimplemented 1997 constitution and studying constitutional arrangements elsewhere.
Nevertheless, the first challenge would be far more immediate than writing a constitution.
Eritrea contains a huge population of armed or recently armed conscripts. If central authority simply disappeared, thousands of men with weapons and little money could suddenly find themselves outside the system that had controlled them for decades.
“The first thing we’re going to do is not go after justice,” Teferi says.
His idea is to seek international financial help to pay soldiers and conscripts to return home, surrender weapons, and begin civilian lives while new institutions establish control.
Only then, he says, should the country begin dealing comprehensively with crimes committed under the old system.
“Vengeance is not part of it, but legal justice is,” he explains to the Post. Teferi acknowledges, however, how difficult that would be in a society where ordinary citizens have been pressured to report on everybody from family to friends and neighbors.
“The regime makes everybody a spy,” he says. “You can’t go after everybody.”
The movement therefore talks about concentrating first on senior security and intelligence figures capable of threatening a transition, while eventually establishing a mechanism to investigate serious abuses.
All of that remains theoretical. EBRF controls no Eritrean city and governs no population. Afwerki has remained in Asmara for more than three decades after independence.
Yet the movement is growing, and it is transforming itself into a legitimate movement.
A diaspora protest movement that once made its name confronting government festivals abroad is now hiring lobbyists in Washington, organizing from Ethiopia, drafting political road maps, talking about contacts inside Eritrea, and debating how to demobilize soldiers after a government it has not yet removed.
And yet one of the events that pushed the movement toward that transformation did not happen in Asmara or Addis Ababa. It happened on the streets of Tel Aviv.
When Eritrea’s conflict came to Israel
On September 2, 2023, south Tel Aviv erupted.
Hundreds of Eritreans opposed to Afwerki’s government gathered to protest an event connected to the Eritrean embassy. Supporters of the government were also present, and what followed developed into hours of fighting between rival groups and clashes with Israeli police.
Stones, pieces of wood, metal bars and other improvised weapons appeared on the streets. Police used stun grenades, tear gas and, when officers said they believed their lives were in danger, live fire.
More than 100 people were wounded, including around 30 police officers, and dozens were arrested.
The images shocked Israelis who had paid little attention to the politics inside the Eritrean community. Men dressed in the blue associated with opponents of Afwerki fought supporters of the government – both groups that were ostensibly thought to have been left behind.
From Michael’s and the men in the Tel Aviv office’s perspective, the violence had a history.
For years, opposition activists had protested embassy-linked festivals and events marking Eritrean national occasions. They viewed such gatherings as an extension of the regime’s political activity abroad and resented Eritreans who claimed asylum while openly supporting the government.
“If you celebrate together with the Eritrean ambassador,” Michael says, “that means you don’t have a political problem” with the regime.
They also allege that pro-government networks intimidate opponents, pressure families, and maintain links to institutions in Eritrea. Human-rights organizations have documented Eritrean government intimidation of diaspora communities abroad, although individual allegations made by EBRF members in Israel are often difficult to verify.
The violence, however, did not end on September 2.
Further clashes between Eritrean government supporters and opponents broke out elsewhere in Israel during the weeks and months that followed, including fatal incidents in Netanya and Tel Aviv.
Michael says four members of the anti-government community and four regime supporters were ultimately killed across subsequent episodes of violence.
He returns repeatedly to the deaths of men from the opposition community, some of whom were buried in Jerusalem.
Michael says their families could not safely return the bodies to Eritrea because the dead were known opponents of the government. Supporters of Afwerki who died abroad, he argues, faced no such problem and could be repatriated.
The violence also created a political opening inside Israel.
One of the lawmakers who became closely involved was Yisrael Beytenu MK Yulia Malinovsky.
Malinovsky and the Israeli response
Malinovsky does not present herself as an expert on the internal factions of the Eritrean opposition.
She encountered government opponents during a tour of south Tel Aviv and later in Knesset committee hearings, particularly while advancing legislation dealing with Eritreans who support the government they claim to have fled.
“I didn’t get involved in their internal struggles as an opposition,” she tells the Post, “but I can judge from their activity on social media that they are quite organized.”
Her conclusions about what was happening on the streets were considerably firmer.
“Reality proves that every time there is an event such as Revolution Day or Eritrean Independence Day, there is a pogrom carried out mainly by regime supporters,” she says, adding that Israeli civilians and security personnel have also been caught up in the violence.
“From the impression I received during my tour of south Tel Aviv, there is harassment of regime opponents by regime supporters.”
“Pogrom” is Malinovsky’s description, and a strong one.
The September 2023 violence involved participants from opposing camps, and anti-government Eritreans were themselves involved in attacks on police and pro-regime activists. Her argument is that much of the organized intimidation stems from supporters of Afwerki.
After those riots, she says, the idea behind her legislation began to take shape.
During a Knesset Internal Affairs Committee discussion attended by a representative of the UN Refugee Agency, Malinovsky asked what she regards as a basic question.
“If asylum-seeker status comes from the danger to asylum seekers in their country, then what do infiltrators who openly declare themselves supporters of the regime have to look for here?” she recalls. “After all, their lives are not in danger in their homeland.”
According to Malinovsky, the UN representative accepted the logic of the question and told the committee that regime supporters were damaging the reputation of other Eritreans seeking protection.
The legislation that followed passed its final Knesset readings in June 2025. It allows the interior minister, after receiving an opinion from the Population and Immigration Authority and giving the person concerned an opportunity to respond, to revoke the residency permit of an infiltrator identified as a supporter of their country’s regime when the presumption that return would be dangerous has not been established.
Malinovsky stresses that the law is broader than the shorthand often used to describe it. It also addresses infiltrators who have committed serious criminal offenses, irrespective of their position toward their home government.
What frustrates her now is implementation.
“The law is absolutely not being implemented as I would like, and that is because of the government’s failure,” she says.
According to information Malinovsky said she received from the Israel Police, one person identified as both a regime supporter and criminal offender has so far been deported.
Seven others, she says, are currently candidates for removal but remain in Israel because the authority needed to approve the deportations has not been exercised.
Her figure immediately echoes something Michael had raised during the earlier interview. He showed the Post photographs of men he describes as pro-government activists who had been arrested and later released, asking repeatedly why Israeli authorities allowed people whom the opposition regards as dangerous to remain.
There is, however, a clear limit to how far Malinovsky is willing to follow EBRF.
Asked whether Israel should begin treating the organization as a political interlocutor and engage with its plans for a post-Afwerki Eritrea, she is unequivocal.
“The State of Israel has enough problems of its own,” she says. “We cannot deal with all the world’s problems and intervene in regimes in other countries.”
Her position is considerably narrower than the one EBRF would like Israel eventually to adopt. Israel can decide whom it protects inside its borders, how it handles violence, and whether people who openly support the government from which they claim asylum should continue to receive that protection.
Regime change in Asmara, in Malinovsky’s view, remains Eritrea’s business.
“We have enough problems of our own,” she says. “It is not our place to intervene in other regimes, however problematic they may be.”
The road home to Eritrea
For EBRF, convincing Israelis that Eritrea should matter strategically is part of a much longer-term project.
Teferi readily talks about agriculture, technology, investment, and security, areas in which he believes a future Eritrean government could learn from Israel and cooperate closely with it.
Eritrea’s coastline runs along the Red Sea opposite Yemen, close to the route leading through Bab el-Mandeb, and Houthi attacks over recent years have demonstrated how directly instability there can affect Israeli shipping and trade.
“We have an interest in working together with Israel on ensuring that the Red Sea becomes a peaceful place for business to trade,” Teferi tells the Post. “We can become a reliable ally.”
Gerezgher is prepared to contemplate an even deeper future relationship. Discussing the difficulty a relatively small Eritrean state would face securing such a long and strategically important coastline, he raises the possibility of allowing partners such as Israel or the United States to maintain military facilities there.
“We could have their own military base there in order to secure their benefits,” he says.
The proposal comes from an opposition figure discussing a government that does not yet exist, and no agreement of this kind is currently on offer.
But its relevance lies more in what it says about the foreign policy EBRF imagines: an Eritrea closely connected to Western and regional partners rather than defined by decades of suspicion and isolation.
The relationship EBRF’s Israel branch talks about is also more personal.
When Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, Michael says members of the Eritrean opposition community began volunteering within days. They helped at the L. Greenberg Institute of Forensic Medicine at Abu Kabir alongside the Brothers in Arms organization, later worked at Expo Tel Aviv, and assisted in agriculture at a time when farms across Israel were struggling with severe labor shortages.
Michael says that on some days, around 150 Eritreans took part, while community members later visited Golani Brigade soldiers and prepared food for them. They asked whether they could serve more directly, he says, but volunteering was where they could be useful immediately.
For Michael, the war never belonged solely to the Israelis around him.
“The missiles that come here don’t only come for Israelis. They come for us too,” he explains, stating that friends from the Eritrean community were murdered in Netivot on October 7.
“What happens here happens to all of us, together.”
The experience of watching Israeli reservists leave their families and return to uniform inevitably struck men whose own understanding of military service had been formed in Eritrea.
Michael describes the contrast almost ruefully. Israelis are mobilized when war comes and eventually return to normal life – to jobs, studies, and families. In Eritrea, he says, people enter the military system and sometimes disappear into it for years.
Yet the deepest connection to Israel may eventually belong to the generation that never experienced Eritrea at all.
Mulue thinks often about the children who have grown up around them.
“They have love for their friends, their teachers, Israeli citizens,” he says. “They have a very good connection, and they feel Israeli.”
If a political change eventually allows their parents to return, he believes many of those children will follow, carrying Hebrew, friendships, and years of Israeli life with them.
“They will feel that Israel is their second country.”
There is something almost paradoxical in an opposition movement spending years building a community in Israel while defining success as the moment that community can begin to leave. But the men do not appear troubled by it.
Israel gave them somewhere to build families while they waited. They now want to create an Eritrea to which those families could return without fear.
Near the end of the conversation in south Tel Aviv, Michael picks up his phone again.
This time he shows photographs of graves in Jerusalem.
They belong, he says, to friends from the anti-regime community who died during the violence that has accompanied the political split among Eritreans in Israel. Their bodies remained in the country because returning them home was considered impossible while Afwerki remains in power.
For Michael, that fact carries an emotional weight almost separate from the politics that produced it.
The men had left Eritrea because they believed they could not live there freely. Some, he says, could not even return there after death.
He does not believe they will remain in Jerusalem forever.
“Our friends will remain here until we remove the dictator,” Michael says. “The moment we remove him, we will take our friends back to our country, to their own soil.”
The living are waiting for the same journey.
EBRF’s leaders can talk for hours about operational structures, constitutional transitions, lobbying in Washington, diplomacy in Addis Ababa, and the strategic value of the Red Sea. In Tel Aviv, those ambitions eventually return to something considerably simpler.
Michael wants to go home.
Mulue wants children raised in Israel to be able to discover the country their parents left and still carry Israel with them when they do. And somewhere in Jerusalem are men whose friends believe they, too, are waiting for the road back to Eritrea.

Thousands of Christians set to arrive in Jerusalem for Sukkot celebrations, support of Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-25
19:58:29 UTC
04:58:29 KST

Around 3,000 Christians from more than 70 countries are arriving in Israel for the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem’s (ICEJ) annual Sukkot conference set to begin Friday evening.
The conference will call for “strong support for Jewish communities in Judea and Samaria, against the backdrop of a growing wave of economic sanctions imposed by European countries,” according to a statement released by the embassy.
“We are excited to once again celebrate the biblical Feast of Sukkot together with Christians from around the world,” said ICEJ President Dr. Jürgen Bühler.
Bühler said that Sukkot celebrations are taking place as a series of “deeply troubling sanctions imposed by European countries on Jews living in Judea and Samaria, the Golan Heights, and even Jerusalem” take place.
International measures ‘suffocate existence of Jewish communities,’ Bühler says
“These discriminatory measures are intended to suffocate the existence of Jewish communities that, in an extraordinary return to history, have come back to life in the heart of the ancient Land of Israel after centuries of Jewish exile among hostile nations,” he said. “These acts of economic warfare, targeting hundreds of thousands of Israeli Jews, are racist and bear far too much resemblance to boycotts imposed on Jews in the past.”
The International Christian Embassy Jerusalem, established in 1980 in Jerusalem, represents Christian Zionists from around the world.
The organization intends to invite community leaders from Judea and Samaria to address the event’s participants, as well as display products from Judea and Samaria for sale in the exhibition hall, and organize tours for Christians from Europe and elsewhere to stores, wineries, and biblical sites throughout Judea and Samaria, according to its statement.
In addition, the organization invited US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee to be the guest of honor at the event, and he is expected to make an appearance on Monday.
This year’s celebrations are also set to “highlight the extensive efforts undertaken by the Christian Embassy in recent years to assist Israeli communities along the Gaza border in recovering and rebuilding their homes and communities following the October 7 terror attack,” the organization added.
Embassy expanding rehabilitation projects
The embassy has been working on nine major rehabilitation projects in the Gaza envelope area, and plans to unveil a tenth during the celebrations.
Its new project aims to help rebuild the central community facility in Kibbutz Nir Oz, one of the hardest-hit kibbutzim during the October 7 massacre.
The conference will be held at the International Convention Center (Binyanei HaUma) in Jerusalem until September 30.

Iran will make no nuclear concessions, Iranian official says

Iran will show no flexibility over its nuclear program even if the United States accepts its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, which calls for steps including the lifting of a US naval blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Friday.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the waterway would remain closed until the United States meets “all of Iran’s conditions.”
According to a US official later on Friday, the United States is having positive, constructive discussions with Iran through mediators and continues to discuss nuclear issues.
Under Iran’s proposal, Tehran has offered to reopen the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz. Within seven days, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon; the United States would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran’s frozen funds, and waive its oil sanctions, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Thursday.
Araghchi reiterated to reporters at the UN on Friday that the “choice rests with the US” to accept and implement Iran’s proposed seven-day plan. The conditions outlined in the plan are not new, he said, as they were already included in the June MoU. He added that the Strait of Hormuz would not reopen until the plan’s conditions were fulfilled. “Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure,” Araghchi said.
The proposal follows a sharp escalation in Middle East tensions after seven months of war between Iran and the United States, with Iran-backed Houthi militias in Yemen launching missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia.
The strait has become the central bargaining chip in efforts to end the US-Iran conflict, with Iran seeking relief from the US blockade that is choking its economy and Washington seeking free passage for ships on the global oil supply route now blocked by Tehran.
Pezeshkian hopes a deal with Washington can be reached before US midterms
In a meeting with journalists on Thursday on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said he hoped a deal with Washington to end the hostilities could be reached before the US midterm elections on November 3.
Tehran said it would be prepared to engage in detailed negotiations over its nuclear program only after its conditions are met by the US.
But the official said Iran would give no concessions over its rights, including enriching uranium or shipping its highly enriched uranium out of the country, one of the main US demands.
Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.
The International Atomic Energy Agency estimates that Iran had 440.9 kg of uranium enriched to 60% when Israel and the US attacked Iranian nuclear facilities in June 2025. How much of that has survived is unclear.
Iranian authorities have said that Iran could agree to dilute its most highly enriched uranium.
In May, Reuters reported that Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has issued a directive that the country's HEU should not be sent abroad, according to two senior Iranian sources.

A U.S. doctor survived a deadly strike in Gaza. Why he plans to go back.
